senses.d: A kind of close carriage with two or four wheels, usually a public vehicle.
The covered part of a locomotive, in which the engineer has his station.
A Hebrew dry measure, containing a little over two (2.37) pints.
A cottage or small house; a hut.
q: A hunting cabin in the west. E. Everett.

senses.d: A small room; an inclosed place.
q: So long in secret cabin there he held Her captive. Spenser.

senses.d: A room in ship for officers or passengers.

Cabin.etym: [OF. caban, fr. W. caban booth, cabin, dim. of cab cot, tent; or fr. F. cabane, cabine, LL. cabanna, perh. from the Celtic.]

senses.d: To live in, or as in, a cabin; to lodge.
q: I'll make you . . . cabin in a cave. Shak.

senses.d: To confine in, or as in, a cabin.
q: I am cabined, cribbed, confined, bound in To saucy doubts and fears. Shak.

senses.d: A box or inclosure, wholly or partly of openwork, in wood or metal, used for confining birds or other animals.
q: In his cage, like parrot fine and gay. Cowper.

senses.d: A place of confinement for malefactors
q: Stone walls do not a prison make, Nor iron bars a cage. Lovelace.

senses.d: An outer framework of timber, inclosing something within it; as, the cage of a staircase.
A skeleton frame to limit the motion of a loose piece, as a ball valve.
The box, bucket, or inclosed platform of a lift or elevator; a cagelike structure moving in a shaft.
The drum on which the rope is wound in a hoisting whim.
The catcher's wire mask.

Cage.etym: [F. cage, fr. L. cavea cavity, cage, fr. cavus hollow. Cf. Cave, n., Cajole, Gabion.]

senses.d: To confine in, or as in, a cage; to shut up or confine.
A small mass of dough baked; especially, a thin loaf from unleavened dough; as, an oatmeal cake; johnnycake.
A sweetened composition of flour and other ingredients, leavened or unleavened, baked in a loaf or mass of any size or shape.
A thin wafer-shaped mass of fried batter; a griddlecake or pancake; as buckwheat cakes.
A mass of matter concreted, congealed, or molded into a solid mass of any form, esp. into a form rather flat than high; as, a cake of soap; an ague cake.
q: Cakes of rusting ice come rolling down the flood. Dryden.

Cake.etym: [OE. cake, kaak; akin to Dan. kage, Sw. & Icel. kaka, D. koek, G. kuchen, OHG. chuocho.]

senses.d: To form into a cake, or mass.
To concrete or consolidate into a hard mass, as dough in an oven; to coagulate.
q: Clotted blood that caked within. Addison.

senses.d: To cackle as a goose.
Wolfram, an ore of tungsten.
Any great misfortune or cause of misery; — generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evil, either to communities or individuals.
q: Strokes of calamity that scathe and scorch the soul. W. Irving.

senses.d: A state or time of distress or misfortune; misery.
q: The deliberations of calamity are rarely wise. Burke.
Where'er I came I brought calamity. Tennyson.

Calamity.syn: Disaster; distress; affliction; adversity; misfortune; unhappiness; infelicity; mishap; mischance; misery; evil; extremity; exigency; downfall.
Calamity.etym: [L. calamitas, akin to in-columis unharmed: cf. F. calamité]

senses.d: The indian cane, a plant of the Palm family. It furnishes the common rattan. See Rattan, and Dragon's blood.

A species of Acorus (A. calamus), commonly called calamus, or sweet flag. The root has a pungent, aromatic taste, and is used in medicine as a stomachic; the leaves have an aromatic odor, and were formerly used instead of rushes to strew on floors.
The horny basal portion of a feather; the barrel or quill.
A large kettle or boiler of copper, brass, or iron. [Written also cauldron.]

Caldron.etym: [OE. caldron, caudron, caudroun, OF. caudron, chauderon, F. chaudron, an aug. of F. chaudière, LL. caldaria, fr. L. caldarius suitable for warming, fr. caldus, calidus, warm, fr. calere to be warm; cf. Skr. çrā to boil. Cf. Chaldron, Calaric, Caudle.]

senses.d: The young of the cow, or of the Bovine family of quadrupeds. Also, the young of some other mammals, as of the elephant, rhinoceros, hippopotamus, and whale.
Leather made of the skin of the calf; especially, a fine, light-colored leather used in bookbinding; as, to bind books in calf.
An awkward or silly boy or young man; any silly person; a dolt.
q: Some silly, doting, brainless calf. Drayton.

senses.d: A small island near a larger; as, the Calf of Man.
A small mass of ice set free from the submerged part of a glacier or berg, and rising to the surface.
The fleshy hinder part of the leg below the knee.

Calf.etym: [OE. calf, kelf, AS. cealf; akin to D. kalf, G. kalb, Icel. kālfr, Sw. kalf, Dan. kalv, Goth. kalbō; cf. Skr. garbha fetus, young, Gr. �����, Skr grabh to seize, conceive, Ir. colpa, colpach, a calf. √222.]

senses.d: One who calks.
A calk on a shoe. See Calk, n., 1.
To command or request to come or be present; to summon; as, to call a servant.
q: Call hither Clifford; bid him come amain Shak.

senses.d: To summon to the discharge of a particular duty; to designate for an office, or employment, especially of a religious character; — often used of a divine summons; as, to be called to the ministry; sometimes, to invite; as, to call a minister to be the pastor of a church.
q: Paul . . . called to be an apostle Rom. i. 1.
The Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. Acts xiii. 2.

senses.d: To invite or command to meet; to convoke; — often with together; as, the President called Congress together; to appoint and summon; as, to call a meeting of the Board of Aldermen.
q: Now call we our high court of Parliament. Shak.

senses.d: To give name to; to name; to address, or speak of, by a specifed name.
q: If you would but call me Rosalind. Shak.
And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. Gen. i. 5.

senses.d: To regard or characterize as of a certain kind; to denominate; to designate.
q: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Acts x. 15.

senses.d: To state, or estimate, approximately or loosely; to characterize without strict regard to fact; as, they call the distance ten miles; he called it a full day's work.
q: army is called seven hundred thousand men. Brougham.

senses.d: To show or disclose the class, character, or nationality of.
q: This speech calls him Spaniard. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To utter in a loud or distinct voice; — often with off; as, to call, or call off, the items of an account; to call the roll of a military company.
q: No parish clerk who calls the psalm so clear. Gay.

senses.d: To invoke; to appeal to.
q: I call God for a witness. 2 Cor. i. 23

senses.d: To rouse from sleep; to awaken.
q: If thou canst awake by four o' the clock. I prithee call me. Sleep hath seized me wholly. Shak.

Call.syn: To name; denominate; invite; bid; summon; convoke; assemble; collect; exhort; warn; proclaim; invoke; appeal to; designate.
Call.etym: [OE. callen, AS. ceallian; akin to Icel. & Sw. kalla, Dan. kalde, D. kallen to talk, prate, OHG. kallōn to call; cf. Gr. γηρύειν to speak, sing, Skr. gar to praise. Cf. Garrulous.]

senses.d: To speak in loud voice; to cry out; to address by name; — sometimes with to.
q: You must call to the nurse. Shak.
The angel of God called to Hagar. Gen. xxi. 17.

senses.d: To make a demand, requirement, or request.
q: They called for rooms, and he showed them one. Bunyan.

senses.d: To make a brief visit; also, to stop at some place designated, as for orders.
q: He ordered her to call at the house once a week. Temple.

senses.d: The act of calling; — usually with the voice, but often otherwise, as by signs, the sound of some instrument, or by writing; a summons; an entreaty; an invitation; as, a call for help; the bugle's call.
q: I rose as at thy call, but found thee not. Milton.

senses.d: A signal, as on a drum, bugle, trumpet, or pipe, to summon soldiers or sailors to duty.
An invitation to take charge of or serve a church as its pastor.
A requirement or appeal arising from the circumstances of the case; a moral requirement or appeal.
q: Dependence is a perpetual call upon humanity. Addison.
Running into danger without any call of duty. Macaulay.

senses.d: A divine vocation or summons.
q: St. Paul himself believed he did well, and that he had a call to it, when he persecuted the Christians. Locke.

senses.d: Vocation; employment.
A short visit; as, to make a call on a neighbor; also, the daily coming of a tradesman to solicit orders.
q: The baker's punctual call. Cowper.

senses.d: A note blown on the horn to encourage the hounds.
A whistle or pipe, used by the boatswain and his mate, to summon the sailors to duty.
The cry of a bird; also a noise or cry in imitation of a bird; or a pipe to call birds by imitating their note or cry.
A reference to, or statement of, an object, course, distance, or other matter of description in a survey or grant requiring or calling for a corresponding object, etc., on the land.
The privilege to demand the delivery of stock, grain, or any commodity, at a fixed, price, at or within a certain time agreed on.
A kind of head covering; a caul.
The act of one who calls; a crying aloud, esp. in order to summon, or to attact the attention of, some one.
A summoning or convocation, as of Parliament.
q: The frequent calling and meeting of Parlaiment. Macaulay.

senses.d: A divine summons or invitation; also, the state of being divinely called.
q: Who hath . . . called us with an holy calling. 2 Tim. i. 9.
Give diligence to make yior calling . . . sure. 2 Pet. i. 10.

senses.d: A naming, or inviting; a reading over or reciting in order, or a call of names with a view to obtaining an answer, as in legislative bodies.
One's usual occupation, or employment; vocation; business; trade.
q: The humble calling of ter female parent. Thackeray.

senses.d: The persons, collectively, engaged in any particular professions or employment.
q: To impose celibacy on wholy callings. Hammond.

senses.d: Title; appellation; name.
q: I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son His youngest son, and would not change that calling. Shak.

Calling.syn: Occupation; employment; business; trade; profession; office; engagement; vocation.

senses.d: Freedom from motion, agitation, or disturbance; a cessation or absence of that which causes motion or disturbance, as of winds or waves; tranquility; stillness; quiet; serenity.
q: The wind ceased, and there was a great calm. Mark. iv. 39.
A calm before a storm is commonly a peace of a man's own making. South.

Calm.etym: [OE. calme, F. calme, fr. It. or Sp. calma (cf. Pg. calma heat), prob. fr. LL. cauma heat, fr. Gr. καυ̑μα burning heat, fr. καίειν to burn; either because during a great heat there is generally also a calm, or because the hot time of the day obliges us seek for shade and quiet; cf. Caustic]

senses.d: To make calm; to render still or quiet, as elements; as, to calm the winds.
q: To calm the tempest raised by Eolus. Dryden.

senses.d: To deliver from agitation or excitement; to still or soothe, as the mind or passions.
q: Passions which seem somewhat calmed. Atterbury.

Calm.syn: To still; quiet; appease; allay; pacify; tranquilize; soothe; compose; assuage; check; restrain.

senses.d: Not stormy; without motion, as of winds or waves; still; quiet; serene; undisturbed.
q: Now all is calm, and fresh, and still. Bryant.

senses.d: Undisturbed by passion or emotion; not agitated or excited; tranquil; quiet in act or speech.
q: Such calm old age as conscience pure And self-commanding hearts ensure. Keble.

Calm.syn: Still; quiet; undisturbed; tranquil; peaceful; serene; composed; unruffled; sedate; collected; placid.

senses.d: The place where Christ was crucified, on a small hill outside of Jerusalem.

A representation of the crucifixion, consisting of three crosses with the figures of Christ and the thieves, often as large as life, and sometimes surrounded by figures of other personages who were present at the crucifixion.
A cross, set upon three steps; — more properly called cross calvary.

Calvary.etym: [L. calvaria a bare skull, fr. calva the scalp without hair. fr. calvus bald; cf. F. calvaire.]

senses.d: To bring forth a calf.
To bring forth young; to produce offspring.
q: Canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? Job xxxix. 1.
The grassy clods now calved. Molton.

senses.d: To throw off fragments which become icebergs; — said of a glacier.

A turning or sliding piece which, by the shape of its periphery or face, or a groove in its surface, imparts variable or intermittent motion to, or receives such motion from, a rod, lever, or block brought into sliding or rolling contact with it.
A ridge or mound of earth.

Cam.etym: [Dan. kam comb, ridge; or cf. W., Gael., and Ir., cam bent. See 1st Comb.]

senses.d: Crooked.
A slender rod of cast lead, with or without grooves, used, in casements and stained-glass windows, to hold together the panes or pieces of glass.

Came.etym: [Cf. Scot. came, caim, comb, and OE. camet silver.]

senses.d: A large ruminant used in Asia and Africa for carrying burdens and for riding. The camel is remarkable for its ability to go a long time without drinking. Its hoofs are small, and situated at the extremities of the toes, and the weight of the animal rests on the callous. The dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) has one bunch on the back, while the Bactrian camel (C. Bactrianus) has two. The llama, alpaca, and vicuña, of South America, belong to a related genus (Auchenia).

A water-tight structure (as a large box or boxes) used to assist a vessel in passing over a shoal or bar or in navigating shallow water. By admitting water, the camel or camels may be sunk and attached beneath or at the sides of a vessel, and when the water is pumped out the vessel is lifted.

Camel.etym: [Oe. camel, chamel, OF. camel, chamel, F. chameau L. camelus, fr. Gr. κάμηλοσ; of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. gāmāl, Ar. jamal. Cf. As. camel, fr. L. camelus.]

senses.d: The ground or spot on which tents, huts, etc., are erected for shelter, as for an army or for lumbermen, etc.
A collection of tents, huts, etc., for shelter, commonly arranged in an orderly manner.
q: Forming a camp in the neighborhood of Boston. W. Irving.

senses.d: A single hut or shelter; as, a hunter's camp.
The company or body of persons encamped, as of soldiers, of surveyors, of lumbermen, etc.
q: The camp broke up with the confusion of a flight. Macaulay.

senses.d: A mound of earth in which potatoes and other vegetables are stored for protection against frost; — called also burrow and pie.
An ancient game of football, played in some parts of England.

Camp.etym: [F. camp, It. campo, fr. L. campus plant, field; akin to Gr. κη̑ποσ garden. Cf. Campaign, Champ, n.]

senses.d: To afford rest or lodging for, as an army or travelers.
q: Had our great palace the capacity To camp this host, we all would sup together. Shak.

senses.d: To pitch or prepare a camp; to encamp; to lodge in a camp; — often with out.
q: They camped out at night, under the stars. W. Irving.

senses.d: To play the game called camp.
An old spelling of Camphor.
an obs. form of began, imp. & p. p. of Begin, sometimes used in old poetry. [See Gan.]
q: With gentle words he can faile gree. Spenser.

senses.d: A drinking cup; a vessel for holding liquids.
q: Fill the cup and fill can, Have a rouse before the morn. Tennyson.

senses.d: A vessel or case of tinned iron or of sheet metal, of various forms, but usually cylindrical; as, a can of tomatoes; an oil can; a milk can.

Can.etym: [OE. & AS. canne; akin to D. Kan, G. Kanne, OHG. channa, Sw. Kanna, Dan. kande.]

senses.d: To preserve by putting in sealed cans
To know; to understand.
q: I can rimes of Robin Hood. Piers Plowman.
I can no Latin, quod she. Piers Plowman.
Let the priest in surplice white, That defunctive music can. Shak.

senses.d: To be able to do; to have power or influence.
q: The will of Him who all things can. Milton.
For what, alas, can these my single arms? Shak.
Mæcænas and Agrippa, who can most with Cæsar. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To be able; — followed by an infinitive without to; as, I can go, but do not wish to.
q: Yet he could not but acknowledge to himself that there was something calculated to impress awe, . . . in the sudden appearances and vanishings . . . of the masque De Quincey.
Tom felt that this was a rebuff for him, and could not but understand it as a left-handed hit at his employer. Dickens.

Can.syn: Can but, Can not but. It is an error to use the former of these phrases where the sens requires the latter. If we say, “I can but perish if I go,” “But” means only, and denotes that this is all or the worst that can happen. When the apostle Peter said. “We can not but speak of the things which we have seen and heard.” he referred to a moral constraint or necessety which rested upon him and his associates; and the meaning was, We cannot help speaking, We cannot refrain from speaking. This idea of a moral necessity or constraint is of frequent occurrence, and is also expressed in the phrase, “I
Can.etym: [OE. cunnen, cannen (1st sing. pres. I can), to know, know how, be able, AS. cunnan, 1st sing. pres. ic cann or can, pl. cunnon, 1st sing. imp. cūðe (for cunðe); p. p. cūð (for cunð); akin to OS. Kunnan, D. Kunnen, OHG. chunnan, G. können, Icel. kunna, Goth. Kunnan, and E. ken to know. The present t

senses.d: A descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham, and grandson of Noah.
A Native or inhabitant of the land of Canaan, esp. a member of any of the tribes who inhabited Canaan at the time of the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt.
A zealot.
Of or pertaining to Canaan or the Canaanites.
A slender, cylindrical body of tallow, containing a wick composed of loosely twisted linen of cotton threads, and used to furnish light.
q: How far that little candle throws his beams! So shines a good deed in a naughty world. Shak.

senses.d: That which gives light; a luminary.
q: By these blessed candles of the night. Shak.

Candle.etym: [OE. candel, candel, AS, candel, fr. L. candela a (white) light made of wax or tallow, fr. candëre to be white. See Candid, and cf. Chandler, Cannel, Kindle.]

senses.d: An instrument or utensil for supporting a candle.
A name given to several peculiar palms, species of Calamus and Dæmanorops, having very long, smooth flexible stems, commonly called rattans.
q: Like light canes, that first rise big and brave. B. Jonson.

senses.d: A walking stick; a staff; — so called because originally made of one of the species of cane.
q: Stir the fire with your master's cane. Swift.

senses.d: A lance or dart made of cane.
q: Judgelike thou sitt'st, to praise or to arraign The flying skirmish of the darted cane. Dryden.

senses.d: A local European measure of length. See Canna.

Cane.etym: [OE. cane, canne, OF. cane, F. canne, L. canna, fr. Gr. κάννα, κάννη; prob. of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. qāneh reed. Cf. Canister, canon, 1st Cannon.]

senses.d: To beat with a cane.
To make or furnish with cane or rattan; as, to cane chairs.
A corroding or sloughing ulcer; esp. a spreading gangrenous ulcer or collection of ulcers in or about the mouth; — called also water canker, canker of the mouth, and noma.
Anything which corrodes, corrupts, or destroy.
q: The cankers of envy and faction. Temple.

senses.d: A disease incident to trees, causing the bark to rot and fall off.
An obstinate and often incurable disease of a horse's foot, characterized by separation of the horny portion and the development of fungoid growths; — usually resulting from neglected thrush.
A kind of wild, worthless rose; the dog-rose.
q: To put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose. And plant this thorm, this canker, Bolingbroke. Shak.

Canker.etym: [OE. canker, cancre, AS. cancer (akin to D. kanker, OHG chanchar.), fr. L. cancer a cancer; or if a native word, cf. Gr. � excrescence on tree, � gangrene. Cf. also OF. cancre, F. chancere, fr. L. cancer. See cancer, and cf. Chancre.]

senses.d: To affect as a canker; to eat away; to corrode; to consume.
q: No lapse of moons can canker Love. Tennyson.

senses.d: To infect or pollute; to corrupt.
q: A tithe purloined cankers the whole estate. Herbert.

senses.d: To waste away, grow rusty, or be oxidized, as a mineral.
q: Silvering will sully and canker more than gliding. Bacom.

senses.d: To be or become diseased, or as if diseased, with canker; to grow corrupt; to become venomous.
q: Deceit and cankered malice. Dryden.
As with age his body uglier grows, So his mind cankers. Shak.

senses.d: Affected with canker; as, a cankered mouth.
Affected mentally or morally as with canker; sore, envenomed; malignant; fretful; ill-natured.
The larva of two species of geometrid moths which are very injurious to fruit and shade trees by eating, and often entirely destroying, the foliage. Other similar larvæ are also called cankerworms.
Am, is, or are, not able; — written either as one word or two.
A head, or chief officer
q: A trainband captain eke was he. Cowper.
The Rhodian captain, relying on . . . the lightness of his vessel, passed, in open day, through all the guards. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: A military leader; a warrior.
q: Foremost captain of his time. Tennyson.

Captain.etym: [OE. capitain, captain, OF. capitain, F. capitaine (cf. Sp. capitan, It. capitano), LL. capitaneus, capitanus, fr. L. caput the head. See under Chief, and cf. Chieftain.]

senses.d: To act as captain of; to lead.
q: Men who captained or accompanied the exodus from existing forms. Lowell.

senses.d: Chief; superior.
q: captain jewes in the carcanet. Shak.

senses.d: A prisoner taken by force or stratagem, esp., by an enemy, in war; one kept in bondage or in the power of another.
q: Then, when I am thy captive, talk of chains. Milton.

senses.d: One charmed or subdued by beaty, excellence, or affection; one who is captivated.

Captive.etym: [L. captivus, fr. capere to take: cf. F. captif. See Caitiff.]

senses.d: Made prisoner, especially in war; held in bondage or in confinement.
q: A poor, miserable, captive thrall. Milton.

senses.d: Subdued by love; charmed; captivated.
q: Even in so short a space, my wonan's heart Grossly grew captive to his honey words. Shak.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to bondage or confinement; serving to confine; as, captive chains; captive hours.
To take prisoner; to capture.
q: Their inhabitans slaughtered and captived. Burke.

senses.d: The state of being a captive or a prisoner.
q: More celebrated in his captivity that in his greatest triumphs. Dryden.

senses.d: A state of being under control; subjection of the will or affections; bondage.
q: Sink in the soft captivity together. Addison.

Captivity.syn: Imprisonment; confinement; bondage; subjection; servitude; slavery; thralldom; serfdom.

senses.d: A small vehicle moved on wheels; usually, one having but two wheels and drawn by one horse; a cart.
A vehicle adapted to the rails of a railroad.
A chariot of war or of triumph; a vehicle of splendor, dignity, or solemnity.
q: The gilded car of day. Milton.
The towering car, the sable steeds. Tennyson.

senses.d: The stars also called Charles's Wain, the Great Bear, or the Dipper.
q: The Pleiads, Hyads, and the Northern Car. Dryden.

senses.d: The cage of a lift or elevator.
The basket, box, or cage suspended from a balloon to contain passengers, ballast, etc.
A floating perforated box for living fish.

Car.etym: [OF. car, char, F. cahr, fr. L. carrus, Wagon: a Celtic word; cf. W. car, Armor. karr, Ir. & Gael. carr. cf. Chariot.]

senses.d: A beautiful gem of a deep red color (with a mixture of scarlet) called by the Greeks anthrax; found in the East Indies. When held up to the sun, it loses its deep tinge, and becomes of the color of burning coal. The name belongs for the most part to ruby sapphire, though it has been also given to red spinel and garnet.

A very painful acute local inflammation of the subcutaneous tissue, esp. of the trunk or back of the neck, characterized by brawny hardness of the affected parts, sloughing of the skin and deeper tissues, and marked constitutional depression. It differs from a boil in size, tendency to spread, and the absence of a central core, and is frequently fatal. It is also called anthrax.
A charge or bearing supposed to represent the precious stone. It has eight scepters or staves radiating from a common center. Called also escarbuncle.

Carbuncle.etym: [L. carbunculus a little coal, a bright kind of precious stone, a kind of tumor, dim. of carbo coal: cf. F. carboncle. See Carbon.]

senses.d: A burdensome sense of responsibility; trouble caused by onerous duties; anxiety; concern; solicitude.
q: Care keeps his watch in every old man's eye, And where care lodges, sleep will never lie. Shak.

senses.d: Charge, oversight, or management, implying responsibility for safety and prosperity.
q: The care of all the churches. 2 Cor. xi. 28.
Him thy care must be to find. Milton.
Perplexed with a thousand cares. Shak.

senses.d: Attention or heed; caution; regard; heedfulness; watchfulness; as, take care; have a care.
q: I thank thee for thy care and honest pains. Shak.

senses.d: The object of watchful attention or anxiety.
q: Right sorrowfully mourning her bereaved cares. Spenser.

Care.syn: Anxiety; solicitude; concern; caution; regard; management; direction; oversight. — Care, Anxiety, Solicitude, Concern. These words express mental pain in different degress. Care belongs primarily to the intellect, and becomes painful from overburdened thought. Anxiety denotes a state of distressing uneasiness fron the dread of evil. Solicitude expresses the same feeling in a diminished degree. Concern is opposed to indifference, and implies exercise of anxious thought more or less intense. We are careful about the means, solicitous and anxious about the end; we are solicitous to obtain a good,
Care.etym: [AS. caru, cearu; akin to OS. kara sorrow, Goth. kara, OHG chara, lament, and perh. to Gr. γη̑ρυσ voice. Not akin to cure. Cf. Chary.]

senses.d: To be anxious or solicitous; to be concerned; to have regard or interest; — sometimes followed by an objective of measure.
q: I would not care a pin, if the other three were in. Shak.
Master, carest thou not that we perish? Mark. iv. 38.
He cared not for the affection of the house. Tennyson.

senses.d: Full of care; anxious; solicitous.
q: Be careful for nothing. Phil. iv. 6.
The careful plowman doubting stands. Milton.

senses.d: Filling with care or solicitude; exposing to concern, anxiety, or trouble; painful.
q: The careful cold beginneth for to creep. Spenser.
By Him that raised me to this careful height. Shak.

senses.d: Taking care; giving good heed; watchful; cautious; provident; not indifferent, heedless, or reckless; — often followed by of, for, or the infinitive; as, careful of money; careful to do right.
q: Thou hast been careful for us with all this care. 2. Kings iv, 13.
What could a careful father more have done? Dryden.

Careful.syn: Anxious; solicitous; provident; thoughtful; cautious; circumspect; heedful; watchful; vigilant.

senses.d: In a careful manner.
Quality or state of being careful.
Free from care or anxiety. hence, cheerful; light-hearted.
q: Sleep she as sound as careless infancy. Shak.

senses.d: Having no care; not taking ordinary or proper care; negligent; unconcerned; heedless; inattentive; unmindful; regardless.
q: My brother was too careless of his charge. Shak.
He grew careless of himself. Steele.

senses.d: Without thought or purpose; without due care; without attention to rule or system; unstudied; inconsiderate; spontaneous; rash; as, a careless throw; a careless expression.
q: He framed the careless rhyme. Beattie.

senses.d: Not receiving care; uncared for.
q: Their many wounds and careless harms. Spenser.

Careless.syn: Negligent; heedless; thoughtless; unthinking; inattentive; incautious; remiss; supine; forgetful; regardless; inconsiderate; listless.

senses.d: In a careless manner.
Of or pertaining to the order of Carmelites.
A friar of a mendicant order (the Order of Our Lady of Mount Carmel) established on Mount Carmel, in Syria, in the twelfth century; a White Friar.
A nun of the Order of Our lady of Mount Carmel.
Of or pertaining to the body or its appetites; animal; fleshly; sensual; given to sensual indulgence; lustful; human or worldly as opposed to spiritual.
q: For ye are yet carnal. 1 Cor. iii. 3.
Not sunk in carnal pleasure. Milton
Carnal desires after miracles. Trench.

senses.d: Flesh-devouring; cruel; ravenous; bloody.
q: This carnal cur Preys on the issue of his mother's body. Shak.

Carnal.etym: [L. carnalis, fr. caro, carnis, flesh; akin to Gr. �, Skr. kravya; cf. F. charnel, Of. also carnel. Cf. Charnel.]

senses.d: According to the flesh, to the world, or to human nature; in a manner to gratify animal appetites and lusts; sensually.
q: For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace. Rom. viii. 6.

senses.d: An artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses, ships, etc.

Carpenter.etym: [OF. carpentier, F. charpentier, LL. carpentarius, fr. L. carpentum wagon, carriage.]

senses.d: The wrist; the bones or cartilages between the forearm, or antibrachium, and the hand or forefoot; in man, consisting of eight short bones disposed in two rows.
That which is carried; burden; baggage.
q: David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage. 1. Sam. xvii. 22.
And after those days we took up our carriages and went up to Jerusalem. Acts. xxi. 15.

senses.d: The act of carrying, transporting, or conveying.
q: Nine days employed in carriage. Chapman.

senses.d: The price or expense of carrying.
That which carries of conveys,
The manner of carrying one's self; behavior; bearing; deportment; personal manners.
q: His gallant carriage all the rest did grace. Stirling.

senses.d: The act or manner of conducting measures or projects; management.
q: The passage and whole carriage of this action. Shak.

Carriage.etym: [OF. cariage luggage, carriage, chariage carriage, cart, baggage, F. charriage, cartage, wagoning, fr. OF. carier, charier, F. charrier, to cart. See Carry.]

senses.d: To convey or transport in any manner from one place to another; to bear; — often with away or off.
q: When he dieth he small carry nothing away. Ps. xiix. 17.
Devout men carried Stephen to his burial. Acts viii, 2.
Another carried the intelligence to Russell. Macaulay.
The sound will be carried, at the least, twenty miles. Bacon.

senses.d: To have or hold as a burden, while moving from place to place; to have upon or about one's person; to bear; as, to carry a wound; to carry an unborn child.
q: If the ideas . . . were carried along with us in our minds. Locke.

senses.d: To move; to convey by force; to impel; to conduct; to lead or guide.
q: Go, carry Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet. Shak.
He carried away all his cattle. Gen. xxxi. 18.
Passion and revenge will carry them too far. Locke.

senses.d: To transfer from one place (as a country, book, or column) to another; as, to carry the war from Greece into Asia; to carry an account to the ledger; to carry a number in adding figures.
To convey by extension or continuance; to extend; as, to carry the chimney through the roof; to carry a road ten miles farther.
To bear or uphold successfully through conflict, as a leader or principle; hence, to succeed in, as in a contest; to bring to a successful issue; to win; as, to carry an election.
q: The carrying of our main point. Addison.

senses.d: To get possession of by force; to capture.
q: The town would have been carried in the end. Bacon.

senses.d: To contain; to comprise; to bear the aspect of ; to show or exhibit; to imply.
q: He thought it carried something of argument in it. Watts.
It carries too great an imputation of ignorance. Lacke.

senses.d: To bear (one's self); to behave, to conduct or demean; — with the reflexive pronouns.
q: He carried himself so insolently in the house, and out of the house, to all persons, that he became odious. Clarendon.

senses.d: To bear the charges or burden of holding or having, as stocks, merchandise, etc., from one time to another; as, a merchant is carrying a large stock; a farm carries a mortgage; a broker carries stock for a customer; to carry a life insurance.

Carry.etym: [OF. carier, charier, F. carrier, to cart, from OF. car, char, F. car, car. See Car.]

senses.d: To act as a bearer; to convey anything; as, to fetch and carry.
To have propulsive power; to propel; as, a gun or mortar carries well.
To hold the head; — said of a horse; as, to carry well i. e., to hold the head high, with arching neck.
To have earth or frost stick to the feet when running, as a hare.
A tract of land, over which boats or goods are carried between two bodies of navigable water; a carrying place; a portage.
The act or business of transporting from one place to another.
q: We are rivals with them in . . . the carrying trade. Jay.

senses.d: A common name for various kinds of vehicles, as a Scythian dwelling on wheels, or a chariot.
A two-wheeled vehicle for the ordinary purposes of husbandry, or for transporting bulky and heavy articles.
q: Packing all his goods in one poor cart. Dryden.

senses.d: A light business wagon used by bakers, grocerymen, butchers, etc.
An open two-wheeled pleasure carriage.

Cart.etym: [AS. cræt; cf. W. cart, Ir. & Gael. cairt, or Icel. kartr. Cf. Car.]

senses.d: To carry or convey in a cart.
To expose in a cart by way of punishment.
q: She chuckled when a bawd was carted. Prior.

senses.d: To carry burdens in a cart; to follow the business of a carter.
To cut.
q: Or they will carven the shepherd's throat. Spenser.

senses.d: To cut, as wood, stone, or other material, in an artistic or decorative manner; to sculpture; to engrave.
q: Carved with figures strange and sweet. Coleridge.

senses.d: To make or shape by cutting, sculpturing, or engraving; to form; as, to carve a name on a tree.
q: An angel carved in stone. Tennyson.
We carved not a line, and we raised not a stone. C. Wolfe.

senses.d: To cut into small pieces or slices, as meat at table; to divide for distribution or apportionment; to apportion.
To cut: to hew; to mark as if by cutting.
q: My good blade carved the casques of men. Tennyson.
A million wrinkles carved his skin. Tennyson.

senses.d: To take or make, as by cutting; to provide.
q: Who could easily have carved themselves their own food. South.

senses.d: To lay out; to contrive; to design; to plan.
q: Lie ten nights awake carving the fashion of a new doublet. Shak.
Fortunes were carved out of the property of the crown. Macaulay.

Carve.etym: [AS. ceorfan to cut, carve; akin to D. kerven, G. kerben, Dan. karve, Sw. karfva, and to Gr. γράφειν to write, orig. to scratch, and E. -graphy. Cf. Graphic.]

senses.d: To exercise the trade of a sculptor or carver; to engrave or cut figures.
To cut up meat; as, to carve for all the guests.
A carucate.
The act or art of one who carves.
A piece of decorative work cut in stone, wood, or other material.
The whole body of decorative sculpture of any kind or epoch, or in any material; as, the Italian carving of the 15th century.
A box, sheath, or covering; as, a case for holding goods; a case for spectacles; the case of a watch; the case (capsule) of a cartridge; a case (cover) for a book.
A box and its contents; the quantity contained in a box; as, a case of goods; a case of instruments.
A shallow tray divided into compartments or “boxes” for holding type.
An inclosing frame; a casing; as, a door case; a window case.
A small fissure which admits water to the workings.

Case.etym: [OF. casse, F. caisse (cf. It. cassa), fr. L. capsa chest, box, case, fr. capere to take, hold. See Capacious, and cf. 4th Chase, Cash, Enchase, 3d Sash.]

senses.d: To cover or protect with, or as with, a case; to inclose.
q: The man who, cased in steel, had passed whole days and nights in the saddle. Prescott.

senses.d: To strip the skin from; as, to case a box.
Chance; accident; hap; opportunity.
q: By aventure, or sort, or cas. Chaucer.

senses.d: That which befalls, comes, or happens; an event; an instance; a circumstance, or all the circumstances; condition; state of things; affair; as, a strange case; a case of injustice; the case of the Indian tribes.
q: In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge. Deut. xxiv. 13.
If the case of the man be so with his wife. Matt. xix. 10.
And when a lady's in the case You know all other things give place. Gay.
You think this madness but a common case. Pope.
I am in case to justle a constable, Shak.

senses.d: A patient under treatment; an instance of sickness or injury; as, ten cases of fever; also, the history of a disease or injury.
q: A proper remedy in hypochondriacal cases. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: The matters of fact or conditions involved in a suit, as distinguished from the questions of law; a suit or action at law; a cause.
q: Let us consider the reason of the case, for nothing is law that is not reason. Sir John Powell.
Not one case in the reports of our courts. Steele.

senses.d: One of the forms, or the inflections or changes of form, of a noun, pronoun, or adjective, which indicate its relation to other words, and in the aggregate constitute its declension; the relation which a noun or pronoun sustains to some other word.
q: Case is properly a falling off from the nominative or first state of word; the name for which, however, is now, by extension of its signification, applied also to the nominative. J. W. Gibbs.

Case.syn: Situation, condition, state; circumstances; plight; predicament; occurrence; contingency; accident; event; conjuncture; cause; action; suit.
Case.etym: [F. cas, fr. L. casus, fr. cadere to fall, to happen. Cf. Chance.]

senses.d: To propose hypothetical cases.
A window sash opening on hinges affixed to the upright side of the frame into which it is fitted. (Poetically) A window.
q: A casement of the great chamber window. Shak.

Casement.etym: [Shortened fr. encasement. See Incase 1st Case, and cf. Incasement.]

senses.d: A genus of leguminous plants (herbs, shrubs, or trees) of many species, most of which have purgative qualities. The leaves of several species furnish the senna used in medicine.

The bark of several species of Cinnamomum grown in China, etc.; Chinese cinnamon. It is imported as cassia, but commonly sold as cinnamon, from which it differs more or less in strength and flavor, and the amount of outer bark attached.

Cassia.etym: [L. cassia and casia, Gr. κασσία and κασία; of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. qetsīāh, fr. qātsa' to cut off, to peel off.]

senses.d: To send or drive by force; to throw; to fling; to hurl; to impel.
q: Uzziah prepared . . . slings to cast stones. 2 Chron. xxvi. 14.
Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me. Acts. xii. 8.
We must be cast upon a certain island. Acts. xxvii. 26.

senses.d: To direct or turn, as the eyes.
q: How earnestly he cast his eyes upon me! Shak.

senses.d: To drop; to deposit; as, to cast a ballot.
To throw down, as in wrestling.
To throw up, as a mound, or rampart.
q: Thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee. Luke xix. 48.

senses.d: To throw off; to eject; to shed; to lose.
q: His filth within being cast. Shak.
Neither shall your vine cast her fruit. Mal. iii. 11
The creatures that cast the skin are the snake, the viper, etc. Bacon.

senses.d: To bring forth prematurely; to slink.
q: Thy she-goats have not cast their young. Gen. xxi. 38.

senses.d: To throw out or emit; to exhale.
q: This . . . casts a sulphureous smell. Woodward.

senses.d: To cause to fall; to shed; to reflect; to throw; as, to cast a ray upon a screen; to cast light upon a subject.
To impose; to bestow; to rest.
q: The government I cast upon my brother. Shak.
Cast thy burden upon the Lord. Ps. iv. 22.

senses.d: To dismiss; to discard; to cashier.
q: The state can not with safety cast him.

senses.d: To compute; to reckon; to calculate; as, to cast a horoscope.
q: You cast the event of war, my noble lord. Shak.

Cast.etym: [Cf. Dan. kaste, Icel. & Sw. kasta; perh. akin to L. gerere to bear, carry. E. jest.]

senses.d: To throw, as a line in angling, esp, with a fly hook.
To turn the head of a vessel around from the wind in getting under weigh.
q: Weigh anchor, cast to starboard. Totten.

senses.d: To consider; to turn or revolve in the mind; to plan; as, to cast about for reasons.
q: She . . . cast in her mind what manner of salution this should be. Luke. i. 29.

senses.d: To calculate; to compute.
q: Who would cast and balance at a desk. Tennyson.

senses.d: To receive form or shape in a mold.
q: It will not run thin, so as to cast and mold. Woodward.

senses.d: To warp; to become twisted out of shape.
q: Stuff is said to cast or warp when . . . it alters its flatness or straightness. Moxon.

senses.d: To vomit.
q: These verses . . . make me ready to cast. B. Jonson.

senses.d: The act of casting or throwing; a throw.
The thing thrown.
q: A cast of dreadful dust. Dryden.

senses.d: The distance to which a thing is or can be thrown.
A throw of dice; hence, a chance or venture.
q: An even cast whether the army should march this way or that way. Sowth.
I have set my life upon a cast, And I will stand the hazard of the die. Shak.

senses.d: That which is throw out or off, shed, or ejected; as, the skin of an insect, the refuse from a hawk's stomach, the excrement of a earthworm.
The act of casting in a mold.
q: And why such daily cast of brazen cannon. Shak.

senses.d: An impression or mold, taken from a thing or person; amold; a pattern.
That which is formed in a mild; esp. a reproduction or copy, as of a work of art, in bronze or plaster, etc.; a casting.
Form; appearence; mien; air; style; as, a peculiar cast of countenance.
q: An heroic poem, but in another cast and figure. Prior.
And thus the native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought. Shak.

senses.d: A tendency to any color; a tinge; a shade.
q: Gray with a cast of green. Woodward.

senses.d: A chance, opportunity, privilege, or advantage; specifically, an opportunity of riding; a lift.
q: We bargained with the driver to give us a cast to the next stage. Smollett.
If we had the cast o' a cart to bring it. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: The assignment of parts in a play to the actors.
One who, or that which, is cast away or shipwrecked.
One who is ruined; one who has made moral shipwreck; a reprobate.
q: Lest . . . when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. 1 Cor. ix. 27.

senses.d: Of no value; rejected; useless.
One of the hereditary classes into which the Hindoos are divided according to the laws of Brahmanism.
A separate and fixed order or class of persons in society who chiefly hold intercourse among themselves.
q: The tinkers then formed an hereditary caste. Macaulay.

Caste.etym: [Pg. casta race, lineage, fr. L. castus pure, chaste: cf. F. caste, of same origin.]

senses.d: The act of one who casts or throws, as in fishing.
The act or process of making casts or impressions, or of shaping metal or plaster in a mold; the act or the process of pouring molten metal into a mold.
That which is cast in a mold; esp. the mass of metal so cast; as, a casting in iron; bronze casting.
The warping of a board.
The act of casting off, or that which is cast off, as skin, feathers, excrement, etc.
A fortified residence, especially that of a prince or nobleman; a fortress.
q: The house of every one is to him castle and fortress, as well for his defense againts injury and violence, as for his repose. Coke.
Our castle's strength Will laugh a siege to scorn. Shak.

senses.d: Any strong, imposing, and stately mansion.
A small tower, as on a ship, or an elephant's back.
A piece, made to represent a castle, used in the game of chess; a rook.

Castle.syn: Fortress; fortification; citadel; stronghold. See Fortress.
Castle.etym: [AS. castel, fr. L. castellum, dim. of castrum a fortified place, castle.]

senses.d: To move the castle to the square next to king, and then the king around the castle to the square next beyond it, for the purpose of covering the king.
A genus of rodents, including the beaver. See Beaver.
Castoreum. See Castoreum.
A hat, esp. one made of beaver fur; a beaver.
q: I have always been known for the jaunty manner in which I wear my castor. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A heavy quality of broadcloth for overcoats.

Castor.etym: [L. castor the beaver, Gr. �; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: the northernmost of the two bright stars in the constellation Gemini, the other being Pollux.
A variety of the mineral called petalite, from Elba.

Castor.etym: [The minerals castor and pollux were so named because found together on the island of Elba. See Castor and Pollux.]

senses.d: To lay hold on; to seize, especially with the hand; to grasp (anything) in motion, with the effect of holding; as, to catch a ball.
To seize after pursuing; to arrest; as, to catch a thief.
To take captive, as in a snare or net, or on a hook; as, to catch a bird or fish.
Hence: To insnare; to entangle.
To seize with the senses or the mind; to apprehend; as, to catch a melody.
To communicate to; to fasten upon; as, the fire caught the adjoining building.
To engage and attach; to please; to charm.
q: The soothing arts that catch the fair. Dryden.

senses.d: To get possession of; to attain.
q: Torment myself to catch the English throne. Shak.

senses.d: To take or receive; esp. to take by sympathy, contagion, infection, or exposure; as, to catch the spirit of an occasion; to catch the measles or smallpox; to catch cold; the house caught fire.
To come upon unexpectedly or by surprise; to find; as, to catch one in the act of stealing.
To reach in time; to come up with; as, to catch a train.

Catch.etym: [OE. cacchen, OF. cachier, dialectic form of chacier to hunt, F. chasser, fr. (assumend) LL. captiare, for L. capture, V. intens. of capere to take, catch. See Capacious, and cf. Chase, Case a box.]

senses.d: To attain possession.
q: Have is have, however men do catch. Shak.

senses.d: To be held or impeded by entanglement or a light obstruction; as, a kite catches in a tree; a door catches so as not to open.
To take hold; as, the bolt does not catch.
To spread by, or as by, infecting; to communicate.
q: Does the sedition catch from man to man? Addison.

senses.d: Act of seizing; a grasp.
That by which anything is caught or temporarily fastened; as, the catch of a gate.
The posture of seizing; a state of preparation to lay hold of, or of watching he opportunity to seize; as, to lie on the catch.
q: The common and the canon law . . . lie at catch, and wait advantages one againt another. T. Fuller.

senses.d: That which is caught or taken; profit; gain; especially, the whole quantity caught or taken at one time; as, a good catch of fish.
q: Hector shall have a great catch if he knock out either of your brains. Shak.

senses.d: Something desirable to be caught, esp. a husband or wife in matrimony.
Passing opportunities seized; snatches.
q: It has been writ by catches with many intervals. Locke.

senses.d: A slight remembrance; a trace.
q: We retain a catch of those pretty stories. Glanvill.

senses.d: A humorous canon or round, so contrived that the singers catch up each other's words.
Quadrupeds of the Bovine family; sometimes, also, including all domestic quadrupeds, as sheep, goats, horses, mules, asses, and swine.

Cattle.etym: [OE. calet, chatel, goods, property, OF. catel, chatel, LL. captale, capitale, goods, property, esp. cattle, fr. L. capitals relating to the head, chief; because in early ages beasts constituted the chief part of a man's property. See Capital, and cf. Chattel.]

senses.d: A covering of network for the head, worn by women; also, a net.
The fold of membrane loaded with fat, which covers more or less of the intestines in mammals; the great omentum. See Omentum.
q: The caul serves for the warming of the lower belly. Ray.

senses.d: A part of the amnion, one of the membranes enveloping the fetus, which sometimes is round the head of a child at its birth.
q: It is deemed lucky to be with a caul or membrane over the face. This caul is esteemed an infallible preservative against drowning . . . According to Chysostom, the midwives frequently sold it for magic uses. Grose.
I was born with a caul, which was advertised for sale, in the newspapers, at the low price of fifteen guineas. Dickens.

Caul.etym: [OE. calle, kelle, prob. fr. F. cale; cf. Ir. calla a veil.]

senses.d: That which produces or effects a result; that from which anything proceeds, and without which it would not exist.
q: Cause is substance exerting its power into act, to make one thing begin to be. Locke.

senses.d: That which is the occasion of an action or state; ground; reason; motive; as, cause for rejoicing.
Sake; interest; advantage.
q: I did it not for his cause. 2 Cor. vii. 12.

senses.d: A suit or action in court; any legal process by which a party endeavors to obtain his claim, or what he regards as his right; case; ground of action.
Any subject of discussion or debate; matter; question; affair in general.
q: What counsel give you in this weighty cause! Shak.

senses.d: The side of a question, which is espoused, advocated, and upheld by a person or party; a principle which is advocated; that which a person or party seeks to attain.
q: God befriend us, as our cause is just. Shak.
The part they take against me is from zeal to the cause. Burke.

Cause.syn: Origin; source; mainspring; motive; reason; incitement; inducement; purpose; object; suit; action.
Cause.etym: [F. cause, fr. L. causa. Cf. Cause, v., Kickshaw.]

senses.d: To effect as an agent; to produce; to be the occasion of; to bring about; to bring into existence; to make; — usually followed by an infinitive, sometimes by that with a finite verb.
q: I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days. Gen. vii. 4.
Cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans. Col. iv. 16.

Cause.syn: To create; produce; beget; effect; occasion; originate; induce; bring about.
Cause.etym: [F. causer, fr. cause, fr. L. causa. See Cause, n., and cf. Acouse.]

senses.d: To assign or show cause; to give a reason; to make excuse.
Abbreviation of Because.
1. Self-originating; uncreated.
Without just or sufficient reason; groundless.
q: My fears are causeless and ungrounded. Denham.

senses.d: Without cause or reason.
A way or road raised above the natural level of the ground, serving as a dry passage over wet or marshy ground.
q: But that broad causeway will direct your way. Dryden.
The other way Satan went down The causey to Hell-gate. Milton.

Causeway.etym: [OE. cauci, cauchie, OF. cauchie, F. chaussée, from LL. (via) calciata, fr calciare to make a road, either fr. L. calx lime, hence, to pave with limestone (cf. E. chalk), or from L. calceus shoe, from calx heel, hence, to shoe, pave, or wear by treading.]

senses.d: A hollow place in the earth, either natural or artificial; a subterraneous cavity; a cavern; a den.
Any hollow place, or part; a cavity.

Cave.etym: [F. cave, L. cavus hollow, whence cavea cavity. Cf. Cage.]

senses.d: To make hollow; to scoop out.
q: The mouldred earth cav'd the banke. Spenser.

senses.d: To dwell in a cave.
To fall in or down; as, the sand bank caved. Hence (Slang), to retreat from a position; to give way; to yield in a disputed matter.
A coalition or group of seceders from a political party, as from the Liberal party in England in 1866. See Adullam, Cave of, in the Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.
To come to an end; to stop; to leave off or give over; to desist; as, the noise ceased.
To be wanting; to fail; to pass away.
q: The poor shall never cease out of the land. Deut. xv. 11.

Cease.syn: To intermit; desist; stop; abstain; quit; discontinue; refrain; leave off; pause; end.
Cease.etym: [OE. cessen, cesen, F. cesser, fr. L. cessare, v. intensive fr. cedere to withdraw. See Cede , and cf. Cessation.]

senses.d: To put a stop to; to bring to an end.
q: But he, her fears to cease Sent down the meek-eyed peace. Milton.
Cease, then, this impious rage. Milton

senses.d: Extinction.
The name of several evergreen trees. The wood is remarkable for its durability and fragrant odor.

Cedar.etym: [AS. ceder, fr. L. cedrus, Gr. κέδροσ.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to cedar.
To extol or honor in a solemn manner; as, to celebrate the name of the Most High.
To honor by solemn rites, by ceremonies of joy and respect, or by refraining from ordinary business; to observe duly; to keep; as, to celebrate a birthday.
q: From even unto even shall ye celebrate your Sabbath. Lev. xxiii. 32.

senses.d: To perform or participate in, as a sacrament or solemn rite; to solemnize; to perform with appropriate rites; as, to celebrate a marriage.
q: We are called upon to commemorate a revolution as surprising in its manner as happy in its consequences. Atterbury.
Earth, water, air, and fire, with feeling glee, Exult to celebrate thy festival. Thomson.

Celebrate.etym: [L. celebratus, p. p. of celebrare to frequent, to celebrate, fr. celeber famous.]

senses.d: Belonging to the aërial regions, or visible heavens.
Of or pertaining to the spiritual heaven; heavenly; divine.

Celestial.etym: [OF. celestial, celestied, fr. L. caelestic, fr. caelum heaved. See Cell.]

senses.d: An inhabitant of heaven.
A native of China.
Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of, the Chinese, or Celestial, Empire, of the Chinese people.
A Chinaman; a Chinese.
A room or rooms under a building, and usually below the surface of the ground, where provisions and other stores are kept.

Cellar.etym: [OE. celer, OF. celier, F. celier, fr. L. cellarium a receptacle for food, pantry, fr. cella storeroom. See Cell.]

senses.d: A census; — also, a public rate or tax.
Condition; rank.

Cense.etym: [OF. cense, F. cens, L. census. See Census.]

senses.d: To perfume with odors from burning gums and spices.
q: The Salii sing and cense his altars round. Dryden.

senses.d: To burn or scatter incense.
A vessel for perfumes; esp. one in which incense is burned.
q: Her thoughts are like the fume of frankincense Which from a golden censer forth doth rise. Spenser.

Censer.etym: [For incenser, fr. OF. encensier, F. encensoir, fr. LL. incensarium, incensorium, fr. L. incensum incense. See Incense, and cf. Incensory.]

senses.d: A military officer who commanded a minor division of the Roman army; a captain of a century.
q: A centurion of the hand called the Italian band. Acts x. 1.

Centurion.etym: [L. centurio, fr. centuria; cf. F. centurion. See Century.]

senses.d: Ar act or series of acts, often of a symbolical character, prescribed by law, custom, or authority, in the conduct of important matters, as in the performance of religious duties, the transaction of affairs of state, and the celebration of notable events; as, the ceremony of crowning a sovereign; the ceremonies observed in consecrating a church; marriage and baptismal ceremonies.
q: According to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof shall ye keep it . Numb. ix. 3
Bring her up the high altar, that she may The sacred ceremonies there partake. Spenser.
with awful ceremony And trumpet's sound, throughout the host proclaim A solemn council. Milton.

senses.d: Behavior regulated by strict etiquette; a formal method of performing acts of civility; forms of civility prescribed by custom or authority.
q: Ceremony was but devised at first To set a gloss on . . . hollow welcomes . . . But where there is true friendship there needs none. Shak.
Al ceremonies are in themselves very silly things; but yet a man of the world should know them. Chesterfield.

senses.d: A ceremonial symbols; an emblem, as a crown, scepter, garland, etc.
q: Disrobe the images, If you find them decked with ceremonies. . . . Let no images Be hung with Cæsar's trophies. Shak.

senses.d: A sign or prodigy; a portent.
q: Cæsar, I never stood on ceremonies, Yet, now they fright me. Shak.

Ceremony.etym: [F. cérémonie, L. caerimonia; perh. akin to E. create and from a root signifying to do or make.]

senses.d: Assured in mind; having no doubts; free from suspicions concerning.
q: To make her certain of the sad event. Dryden.
I myself am certain of you. Wyclif.

senses.d: Determined; resolved; — used with an infinitive.
q: However, I with thee have fixed my lot, Certain to undergo like doom. Milton.

senses.d: Not to be doubted or denied; established as a fact.
q: The dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure. Dan. ii. 45.

senses.d: Actually existing; sure to happen; inevitable.
q: Virtue that directs our ways Through certain dangers to uncertain praise. Dryden.
Death, as the Psalmist saith, is certain to all. Shak.

senses.d: Unfailing; infallible.
q: I have often wished that I knew as certain a remedy for any other distemper. Mead.

senses.d: Fixed or stated; regular; determinate.
q: The people go out and gather a certain rate every day. Ex. xvi. 4.

senses.d: Not specifically named; indeterminate; indefinite; one or some; — sometimes used independenty as a noun, and meaning certain persons.
q: It came to pass when he was in a certain city. Luke. v. 12.
About everything he wrote there was a certain natural grace und decorum. Macaulay.

Certain.syn: Bound; sure; true; undeniable; unquestionable; undoubted; plain; indubitable; indisputable; incontrovertible; unhesitating; undoubting; fixed; stated.
Certain.etym: [F. certain, fr. (assumed) LL. certanus, fr. L. certus determined, fixed, certain, orig. p. p. of cernere to perceive, decide, determine; akin to Gr. � to decide, separate, and to E. concern, critic, crime, riddle a sieve, rinse, v.]

senses.d: Certainty.
A certain number or quantity.
Certainly.
Without doubt or question; unquestionably.
The quality, state, or condition, of being certain.
q: The certainty of punishment is the truest security against crimes. Fisher Ames.

senses.d: A fact or truth unquestionable established.
q: Certainties are uninteresting and sating. Landor.

senses.d: Clearness; freedom from ambiguity; lucidity.
To give cetain information to; to assure; to make certain.
q: We certify the king, that . . . thou shalt have no portion on this side the river. Ezra iv. 16.

senses.d: To give certain information of; to make certain, as a fact; to verify.
q: The industry of science at once certifies and greatly extends our knowledge of the vastness of the creation. I. Taylor.

senses.d: To testify to in writing; to make a declaration concerning, in writing, under hand, or hand and seal.
q: The judges shall certify their opinion to the chancellor, and upon such certificate the decree is usually founded. Blackstone.

Certify.etym: [F. certifier, LL. certificare; L. certus certain + facere to make. See Certain, and cf. Certificate, v. t.]

senses.d: To excite heat in by friction; to rub in order to stimulate and make warm.
q: To rub her temples, and to chafe her skin. Spenser.

senses.d: To excite passion or anger in; to fret; to irritate.
q: Her intercession chafed him. Shak.

senses.d: To fret and wear by rubbing; as, to chafe a cable.
q: Two slips of parchment which she sewed round it to prevent its being chafed. Sir W. Scott.

Chafe.syn: To rub; fret; gall; vex; excite; inflame.
Chafe.etym: [OE. chaufen to warm, OF. chaufer, F. chauffer, fr. L. calefacere, calfacere, to make warm; calere to be warm + facere to make. See Caldron.]

senses.d: To rub; to come together so as to wear by rubbing; to wear by friction.
q: Made its great boughs chafe together. Longfellow.
The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores. Shak.

senses.d: To be worn by rubbing; as, a cable chafes.
To have a feeling of vexation; to be vexed; to fret; to be irritated.
q: He will chafe at the doctor's marrying my daughter. Shak.

senses.d: Heat excited by friction.
Injury or wear caused by friction.
Vexation; irritation of mind; rage.
q: The cardinal in a chafe sent for him to Whitehall. Camden.

senses.d: The glumes or husks of grains and grasses separated from the seed by threshing and winnowing, etc.
q: So take the corn and leave the chaff behind. Dryden.
Old birds are not caught with caff. Old Proverb.

senses.d: Anything of a comparatively light and worthless character; the refuse part of anything.
q: The chaff and ruin of the times. Shak.

senses.d: Straw or hay cut up fine for the food of cattle.
q: By adding chaff to his corn, the horse must take more time to eat it. In this way chaff is very useful. Ywatt.

senses.d: Light jesting talk; banter; raillery.
The scales or bracts on the receptacle, which subtend each flower in the heads of many Compositæ, as the sunflower.

Chaff.etym: [AC. ceaf; akin to D. kaf, G. kaff.]

senses.d: To use light, idle language by way of fun or ridicule; to banter.
To make fun of; to turn into ridicule by addressing in ironical or bantering language; to quiz.
q: Morgan saw that his master was chaffing him. Thackeray.
A dozen honest fellows . . . chaffed each other about their sweethearts. C. Kingsley.

senses.d: A series of links or rings, usually of metal, connected, or fitted into one another, used for various purposes, as of support, of restraint, of ornament, of the exertion and transmission of mechanical power, etc.
q: put a chain of gold about his neck. Dan. v. 29.

senses.d: That which confines, fetters, or secures, as a chain; a bond; as, the chains of habit.
q: Driven down To chains of darkness and the undying worm. Milton.

senses.d: A series of things linked together; or a series of things connected and following each other in succession; as, a chain of mountains; a chain of events or ideas.
An instrument which consists of links and is used in measuring land.
Iron links bolted to the side of a vessel to bold the dead-eyes connected with the shrouds; also, the channels.
The warp threads of a web.

Chain.etym: [F. chaîne, fr. L. catena. Cf. Catenate.]

senses.d: To fasten, bind, or connect with a chain; to fasten or bind securely, as with a chain; as, to chain a bulldog.
q: Chained behind the hostile car. Prior.

senses.d: To keep in slavery; to enslave.
q: And which more blest? who chained his country, say Or he whose virtue sighed to lose a day? Pope.

senses.d: To unite closely and strongly.
q: And in this vow do chain my soul to thine. Shak.

senses.d: To measure with the chain.
To protect by drawing a chain across, as a harbor.
A cryptocrystalline, translucent variety of quartz, having usually a whitish color, and a luster nearly like wax.

Chalcedony.etym: [ L. chalcedonius, fr. Gr. Χαλκηδών Chalcedon, a town in Asia Minor, opposite to Byzantium: cf. calcédoine, OE. calcidoine, casidoyne. Cf. Cassidony.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Chaldea.
A native or inhabitant of Chaldea.
Of or pertaining to Chaldea.
The language or dialect of the Chaldeans; eastern Aramaic, or the Aramaic used in Chaldea.
A mass of chalk.
q: As chalkstones . . . beaten in sunder. Isa. xxvii. 9.

senses.d: A chalklike concretion, consisting mainly of urate of sodium, found in and about the small joints, in the external ear, and in other situations, in those affected with gout; a tophus.
An invitation to engage in a contest or controversy of any kind; a defiance; specifically, a summons to fight a duel; also, the letter or message conveying the summons.
q: A challenge to controversy. Goldsmith.

senses.d: The act of a sentry in halting any one who appears at his post, and demanding the countersign.
A claim or demand.
q: There must be no challenge of superiority. Collier.

senses.d: The opening and crying of hounds at first finding the scent of their game.

An exception to a juror or to a member of a court martial, coupled with a demand that he should be held incompetent to act; the claim of a party that a certain person or persons shall not sit in trial upon him or his cause.
An exception to a person as not legally qualified to vote. The challenge must be made when the ballot is offered.

Challenge.etym: [OE. chalenge claim, accusation, challenge, OF. chalenge, chalonge, claim, accusation, contest, fr. L. calumnia false accusation, chicanery. See Calumny.]

senses.d: To call to a contest of any kind; to call to answer; to defy.
q: I challenge any man to make any pretense to power by right of fatherhood. Locke.

senses.d: To call, invite, or summon to answer for an offense by personal combat.
q: By this I challenge him to single fight. Shak.

senses.d: To claim as due; to demand as a right.
q: Challenge better terms. Addison.

senses.d: To censure; to blame.
q: He complained of the emperors . . . and challenged them for that he had no greater revenues . . . from them. Holland.

senses.d: To question or demand the countersign from (one who attempts to pass the lines); as, the sentinel challenged us, with “Who comes there?”
To take exception to; question; as, to challenge the accuracy of a statement or of a quotation.
To object to or take exception to, as to a juror, or member of a court.
To object to the reception of the vote of, as on the ground that the person in not qualified as a voter.

Challenge.etym: [OE. chalengen to accuse, claim, OF. chalengier, chalongier, to claim, accuse, dispute, fr. L. calumniar to attack with false accusations. See Challenge, n., and cf. Calumniate.]

senses.d: To assert a right; to claim a place.
q: Where nature doth with merit challenge. Shak.

senses.d: A retired room, esp. an upper room used for sleeping; a bedroom; as, the house had four chambers.
Apartments in a lodging house.
A hall, as where a king gives audience, or a deliberative body or assembly meets; as, presence chamber; senate chamber.
A legislative or judicial body; an assembly; a society or association; as, the Chamber of Deputies; the Chamber of Commerce.
A compartment or cell; an inclosed space or cavity; as, the chamber of a canal lock; the chamber of a furnace; the chamber of the eye.
A room or rooms where a lawyer transacts business; a room or rooms where a judge transacts such official business as may be done out of court.
A chamber pot.

That part of the bore of a piece of ordnance which holds the charge, esp. when of different diameter from the rest of the bore; — formerly, in guns, made smaller than the bore, but now larger, esp. in breech-loading guns.

Chamber.etym: [F. chambre, fr. L. camera vault, arched roof, in LL. chamber, fr. Gr. � anything with a vaulted roof or arched covering; cf. Skr. kmar to be crooked. Cf. Camber, Camera, Comrade.]

senses.d: To reside in or occupy a chamber or chambers.
To be lascivious.
To shut up, as in a chamber.
To furnish with a chamber; as, to chamber a gun.
Lewdness.
An officer or servant who has charge of a chamber or chambers.
An upper servant of an inn.
An officer having the direction and management of the private chambers of a nobleman or monarch; hence, in Europe, one of the high officers of a court.
A treasurer or receiver of public money; as, the chamberlain of London, of North Wales, etc.

Chamberlain.etym: [OF. chamberlain, chambrelencF. chambellon, OHG. chamerling, chamarlinc, G. kämmerling, kammer chamber (fr. L. camera) + -ling. See Chamber, and -ling.]

senses.d: A lizardlike reptile of the genus Chamæleo, of several species, found in Africa, Asia, and Europe. The skin is covered with fine granulations; the tail is prehensile, and the body is much compressed laterally, giving it a high back.

Chameleon.etym: [L. Chamaeleon, Gr. χαμαιλέων, lit., “ground lion;” χαμαί on the ground + λέων lion. See Humble, and Lion.]

senses.d: A small species of antelope (Rupicapra tragus), living on the loftiest mountain ridges of Europe, as the Alps, Pyrenees, etc. It possesses remarkable agility, and is a favorite object of chase.
A soft leather made from the skin of the chamois, or from sheepskin, etc.; — called also chamois leather, and chammy or shammy leather. See Shammy.

Chamois.etym: [F. chamois, prob. fr. OG. gamz, G. gemse.]

senses.d: A flat, open country.
q: Fair champaign, with less rivers interveined. Milton.
Through Apline vale or champaign wide. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Flat; open; level.
q: A wide, champaign country, filled with herds. Addison.

senses.d: One who engages in any contest; esp. one who in ancient times contended in single combat in behalf of another's honor or rights; or one who now acts or speaks in behalf of a person or a cause; a defender; an advocate; a hero.
q: A stouter champion never handled sword. Shak.
Champions of law and liberty. Fisher Ames.

senses.d: One who by defeating all rivals, has obtained an acknowledged supremacy in any branch of athletics or game of skill, and is ready to contend with any rival; as, the champion of England.

Champion.syn: Leader; chieftain; combatant; hero; warrior; defender; protector.
Champion.etym: [F. champion, fr. LL. campio, of German origin; cf. OHG. chempho, chemphio, fighter, champf, G. kampf, contest; perh. influenced by L. campus field, taken in the sense of “field of battle.”]

senses.d: To furnish with a champion; to attend or defend as champion; to support or maintain; to protect.
q: Championed or unchampioned, thou diest. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A supposed material or psychical agent or mode of activity other than a force, law, or purpose; fortune; fate; — in this sense often personified.
q: It is strictly and philosophically true in nature and reason that there is no such thing as chance or accident; it being evident that these words do not signify anything really existing, anything that is truly an agent or the cause of any event; but they signify merely men's ignorance of the real and immediate cause. Samuel Clark.
Any society into which chance might throw him. Macaulay.
That power Which erring men call Chance. Milton.

senses.d: The operation or activity of such agent.
q: By chance a priest came down that way. Luke x. 31.

senses.d: The supposed effect of such an agent; something that befalls, as the result of unknown or unconsidered forces; the issue of uncertain conditions; an event not calculated upon; an unexpected occurrence; a happening; accident; fortuity; casualty.
q: It was a chance that happened to us. 1 Sam. vi. 9.
The Knave of Diamonds tries his wily arts, And wins (O shameful chance!) the Queen of Hearts. Pope.
I spake of most disastrous chance. Shak.

senses.d: A possibility; a likelihood; an opportunity; — with reference to a doubtful result; as, a chance to escape; a chance for life; the chances are all against him.
q: So weary with disasters, tugged with fortune. That I would get my life on any chance, To mend it, or be rid on 't Shak.

senses.d: Probability.

Chance.etym: [F. chance, OF. cheance, fr. LL. cadentia a allusion to the falling of the dice), fr. L. cadere to fall; akin to Skr. çad to fall, L. cedere to yield, E. cede. Cf. Cadence.]

senses.d: To happen, come, or arrive, without design or expectation.
q: If a bird's nest chance to be before thee. Deut. xxii. 6.
I chanced on this letter. Shak.
How chance, thou art returned so soon? Shak.

senses.d: To take the chances of; to venture upon; — usually with it as object.
q: Come what will, I will chance it. W. D. Howells.

senses.d: To befall; to happen to.
Happening by chance; casual.
By chance; perchance.
A judicial court of chancery, which in England and in the United States is distinctively a court with equity jurisdiction.

Chancellor.etym: [OE. canceler, chaunceler, F. chancelier, LL. cancellarius chancellor, a director of chancery, fr. L. cancelli lattices, crossbars, which surrounded the seat of judgment. See Chancel.]

senses.d: To alter; to make different; to cause to pass from one state to another; as, to change the position, character, or appearance of a thing; to change the countenance.
q: Therefore will I change their glory into shame. Hosea. iv. 7.

senses.d: To alter by substituting something else for, or by giving up for something else; as, to change the clothes; to change one's occupation; to change one's intention.
q: They that do change old love for new, Pray gods, they change for worse! Peele.

senses.d: To give and take reciprocally; to exchange; — followed by with; as, to change place, or hats, or money, with another.
q: Look upon those thousands with whom thou wouldst not, for any interest, change thy fortune and condition. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Specifically: To give, or receive, smaller denominations of money (technically called change) for; as, to change a gold coin or a bank bill.
q: He pulled out a thirty-pound note and bid me change it. Goldsmith.

Change.syn: To alter; vary; deviate; substitute; innovate; diversify; shift; veer; turn. See Alter.
Change.etym: [F. changer, fr. LL. cambiare, to exchange, barter, L. cambire. Cf. Cambial.]

senses.d: To be altered; to undergo variation; as, men sometimes change for the better.
q: For I am Lord, I change not. Mal. iii. 6.

senses.d: To pass from one phase to another; as, the moon changes to-morrow night.
Any variation or alteration; a passing from one state or form to another; as, a change of countenance; a change of habits or principles.
q: Apprehensions of a change of dynasty. Hallam.
All the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. Job xiv. 14.

senses.d: A succesion or substitution of one thing in the place of another; a difference; novelty; variety; as, a change of seasons.
q: Our fathers did for change to France repair. Dryden.
The ringing grooves of change. Tennyson.

senses.d: A passing from one phase to another; as, a change of the moon.
Alteration in the order of a series; permutation.
That which makes a variety, or may be substituted for another.
q: Thirty change (R.V. changes) of garments. Judg. xiv. 12.

senses.d: Small money; the money by means of which the larger coins and bank bills are made available in small dealings; hence, the balance returned when payment is tendered by a coin or note exceeding the sum due.
A place where merchants and others meet to transact business; a building appropriated for mercantile transactions.
A public house; an alehouse.
q: They call an alehouse a change. Burt.

senses.d: Any order in which a number of bells are struck, other than that of the diatonic scale.
q: Four bells admit twenty-four changes in ringing. Holder.

Change.syn: Variety; variation; alteration; mutation; transition; vicissitude; innovation; novelty; transmutation; revolution; reverse.
Change.etym: [F. change, fr. changer. See Change. v. t.]

senses.d: Capable of change; subject to alteration; mutable; variable; fickle; inconstant; as, a changeable humor.
Appearing different, as in color, in different lights, or under different circumstances; as, changeable silk.

Changeable.syn: Mutable; alterable; variable; inconstant; fitful; vacillating; capricious; fickle; unstable; unsteady; unsettled; wavering; erratic; giddy; volatile.

senses.d: One who changes or alters the form of anything.
One who deals in or changes money.
One apt to change; an inconstant person.
The hollow bed where a stream of water runs or may run.
The deeper part of a river, harbor, strait, etc., where the main current flows, or which affords the best and safest passage for vessels.
A strait, or narrow sea, between two portions of lands; as, the British Channel.
That through which anything passes; means of passing, conveying, or transmitting; as, the news was conveyed to us by different channels.
q: The veins are converging channels. Dalton.
At best, he is but a channel to convey to the National assembly such matter as may import that body to know. Burke.

senses.d: A gutter; a groove, as in a fluted column.
Flat ledges of heavy plank bolted edgewise to the outside of a vessel, to increase the spread of the shrouds and carry them clear of the bulwarks.

Channel.etym: [OE. chanel, canel, OF. chanel, F. chenel, fr. L. canalis. See Canal.]

senses.d: To form a channel in; to cut or wear a channel or channels in; to groove.
q: No more shall trenching war channel her fields. Shak.

senses.d: To course through or over, as in a channel.
To utter with a melodious voice; to sing.
q: The cheerful birds . . . do chant sweet music. Spenser.

senses.d: To celebrate in song.
q: The poets chant in the theaters. Bramhall.

senses.d: To sing or recite after the manner of a chant, or to a tune called a chant.

Chant.etym: [F. chanter, fr. L. cantare, intens. of canere to sing. Cf. Cant affected speaking, and see Hen.]

senses.d: To make melody with the voice; to sing.
To sing, as in reciting a chant.
Song; melody.
A short and simple melody, divided into two parts by double bars, to which unmetrical psalms, etc., are sung or recited. It is the most ancient form of choral music.
A psalm, etc., arranged for chanting.
Twang; manner of speaking; a canting tone.
q: His strange face, his strange chant. Macaulay.

Chant.etym: [F. chant, fr. L. cantus singing, song, fr. canere to sing. See Chant, v. t.]

senses.d: A subordinate place of worship
A place of worship not connected with a church; as, the chapel of a palace, hospital, or prison.
In England, a place of worship used by dissenters from the Established Church; a meetinghouse.
A choir of singers, or an orchestra, attached to the court of a prince or nobleman.
A printing office, said to be so called because printing was first carried on in England in a chapel near Westminster Abbey.

Chapel.etym: [OF. chapele, F. chapelle, fr. LL. capella, orig., a short cloak, hood, or cowl; later, a reliquary, sacred vessel, chapel; dim. of cappa, capa, cloak, cape, cope; also, a covering for the head. The chapel where St. Martin's cloak was preserved as a precious relic, itself came to be called capella,

senses.d: To deposit or inter in a chapel; to enshrine.
To cause (a ship taken aback in a light breeze) so to turn or make a circuit as to recover, without bracing the yards, the same tack on which she had been sailing.
A capital See Chapital.
A summary in writing of such matters as are to be inquired of or presented before justices in eyre, or justices of assize, or of the peace, in their sessions; — also called articles.

Chapiter.etym: [OF. chapitel, F. chapiteau, from L. capitellum, dim. of caput head. Cf. Capital, Chapter.]

senses.d: To lay on or impose, as a load, tax, or burden; to load; to fill.
q: A carte that charged was with hay. Chaucer.
The charging of children's memories with rules. Locke.

senses.d: To lay on or impose, as a task, duty, or trust; to command, instruct, or exhort with authority; to enjoin; to urge earnestly; as, to charge a jury; to charge the clergy of a diocese; to charge an agent.
q: Moses . . . charged you to love the Lord your God. Josh. xxii. 5.
Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition. Shak.

senses.d: To lay on, impose, or make subject to or liable for.
q: When land shall be charged by any lien. Kent.

senses.d: To fix or demand as a price; as, he charges two dollars a barrel for apples.
To place something to the account of as a debt; to debit, as, to charge one with goods. Also, to enter upon the debit side of an account; as, to charge a sum to one.
To impute or ascribe; to lay to one's charge.
q: No more accuse thy pen, but charge the crime On native sloth and negligence of time. Dryden.

senses.d: To accuse; to make a charge or assertion against (a person or thing); to lay the responsibility (for something said or done) at the door of.
q: If he did that wrong you charge him with. Tennyson.

senses.d: To place within or upon any firearm, piece of apparatus or machinery, the quantity it is intended and fitted to hold or bear; to load; to fill; as, to charge a gun; to charge an electrical machine, etc.
q: Their battering cannon charged to the mouths. Shak.

senses.d: To ornament with or cause to bear; as, to charge an architectural member with a molding.
To assume as a bearing; as, he charges three roses or; to add to or represent on; as, he charges his shield with three roses or.
To call to account; to challenge.
q: To charge me to an answer. Shak.
