senses.d: To bear down upon; to rush upon; to attack.
q: Charged our main battle's front. Shak.

Charge.syn: To intrust; command; exhort; instruct; accuse; impeach; arraign. See Accuse.
Charge.etym: [OF. chargier, F. charger, fr. LL. carricare, fr. L. carrus wagon. Cf. Cargo, Caricature, Cark, and see Car.]

senses.d: To make an onset or rush; as, to charge with fixed bayonets.
q: Like your heroes of antiquity, he charges in iron. Glanvill.
“Charge for the guns!” he said. Tennyson.

senses.d: To demand a price; as, to charge high for goods.
To debit on an account; as, to charge for purchases.
To squat on its belly and be still; — a command given by a sportsman to a dog.
A load or burder laid upon a person or thing.
A person or thing commited or intrusted to the care, custody, or management of another; a trust.
Custody or care of any person, thing, or place; office; responsibility; oversight; obigation; duty.
q: 'Tis a great charge to come under one body's hand. Shak.

senses.d: Heed; care; anxiety; trouble.
Harm.
An order; a mandate or command; an injunction.
q: The king gave cherge concerning Absalom. 2. Sam. xviii. 5.

senses.d: An address (esp. an earnest or impressive address) containing instruction or exhortation; as, the charge of a judge to a jury; the charge of a bishop to his clergy.
An accusation of a wrong of offense; allegation; indictment; specification of something alleged.
q: The charge of confounding very different classes of phenomena. Whewell.

senses.d: Whatever constitutes a burden on property, as rents, taxes, lines, etc.; costs; expense incurred; — usually in the plural.
The price demanded for a thing or service.
An entry or a account of that which is due from one party to another; that which is debited in a business transaction; as, a charge in an account book.

That quantity, as of ammunition, electricity, ore, fuel, etc., which any apparatus, as a gun, battery, furnace, machine, etc., is intended to receive and fitted to hold, or which is actually in it at one time

Charge.syn: Care; custody; trust; management; office; expense; cost; price; assault; attack; onset; injunction; command; order; mandate; instruction; accusation; indictment.
Charge.etym: [F. charge, fr. charger to load. See Charge, v. t., and cf. Cargo, Caricature.]

senses.d: That may be charged, laid, imposed, or imputes; as, a duty chargeable on iron; a fault chargeable on a man.
Subject to be charge or accused; liable or responsible; as, revenues chargeable with a claim; a man chargeable with murder.
Serving to create expense; costly; burdensome.
q: That we might not be chargeable to any of you. 2. Thess. iii. 8.
For the sculptures, which are elegant, were very chargeable. Evelyn.

senses.d: One who, or that which charges.
An instrument for measuring or inserting a charge.
A large dish.
q: Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger. Matt. xiv. 8.

senses.d: A horse for battle or parade.
q: And furious every charger neighed. Campbell.

senses.d: A two-wheeled car or vehicle for war, racing, state processions, etc.
q: First moved the chariots, after whom the foot. Cowper.

senses.d: A four-wheeled pleasure or state carriage, having one seat.

Chariot.etym: [F. Chariot, from char car. See Car.]

senses.d: To convey in a chariot.
In a charitable manner.
Love; universal benevolence; good will.
q: Now abideth faith, hope, charity, three; but the greatest of these is charity. 1. Cor. xiii. 13.
They, at least, are little to be envied, in whose hearts the great charities . . . lie dead. Ruskin.
With malice towards none, with charity for all. Lincoln.

senses.d: Liberality in judging of men and their actions; a disposition which inclines men to put the best construction on the words and actions of others.
q: The highest exercise of charity is charity towards the uncharitable. Buckminster.

senses.d: Liberality to the poor and the suffering, to benevolent institutions, or to worthy causes; generosity.
q: The heathen poet, in commending the charity of Dido to the Trojans, spake like a Christian. Dryden.

senses.d: Whatever is bestowed gratuitously on the needy or suffering for their relief; alms; any act of kindness.
q: She did ill then to refuse her a charity. L'Estrange.

senses.d: A charitable institution, or a gift to create and support such an institution; as, Lady Margaret's charity.
Eleemosynary appointments including relief of the poor or friendless, education, religious culture, and public institutions.
q: The charities that soothe, and heal, and bless, Are scattered at the feet of man like flowers. Wordsworth.

Charity.syn: Love; benevolence; good will; affection; tenderness; beneficence; liberality; almsgiving.
Charity.etym: [F. charité fr. L. caritas dearness, high regard, love, from carus dear, costly, loved; asin to Skr. kam to wish, love, cf. Ir. cara a friend, W. caru to love. Cf. Caress.]

senses.d: A melody; a song.
q: With charm of earliest birds. Milton.
Free liberty to chant our charms at will. Spenser.

senses.d: A word or combination of words sung or spoken in the practice of magic; a magical combination of words, characters, etc.; an incantation.
q: My high charms work. Shak.

senses.d: That which exerts an irresistible power to please and attract; that which fascinates; any alluring quality.
q: Charms strike the sight, but merit wins the soul. Pope.
The charm of beauty's powerful glance. Milton.

senses.d: Anything worn for its supposed efficacy to the wearer in averting ill or securing good fortune.
Any small decorative object worn on the person, as a seal, a key, a silver whistle, or the like. Bunches of charms are often worn at the watch chain.

Charm.syn: Spell; incantation; conjuration; enchantment; fascination; attraction.
Charm.etym: [F. charme, fr. L. carmen song, verse, incantation, for casmen, akin to Skr. çasman, çasā, a laudatory song, from a root signifying to praise, to sing.]

senses.d: To make music upon; to tune.
q: Here we our slender pipes may safely charm. Spenser.

senses.d: To subdue, control, or summon by incantation or supernatural influence; to affect by magic.
q: No witchcraft charm thee! Shak.

senses.d: To subdue or overcome by some secret power, or by that which gives pleasure; to allay; to soothe.
q: Music the fiercest grief can charm. Pope.

senses.d: To attract irresistibly; to delight exceedingly; to enchant; to fascinate.
q: They, on their mirth and dance Intent, with jocund music charm his ear. Milton.

senses.d: To protect with, or make invulnerable by, spells, charms, or supernatural influences; as, a charmed life.
q: I, in my own woe charmed, Could not find death. Shak.

Charm.syn: To fascinate; enchant; enrapture; captivate; bewitch; allure; subdue; delight; entice; transport.

senses.d: To use magic arts or occult power; to make use of charms.
q: The voice of charmers, charming never so wisely. Ps. lviii. 5.

senses.d: To act as, or produce the effect of, a charm; to please greatly; to be fascinating.
To make a musical sound.
One who charms, or has power to charm; one who uses the power of enchantment; a magician.
One who delights and attracts the affections.
Pleasing the mind or senses in a high degree; delighting; fascinating; attractive.
q: How charming is divine philosophy. Milton.

Charming.syn: Enchanting; bewitching; captivating; enrapturing; alluring; fascinating; delightful; pleasurable; graceful; lovely; amiable; pleasing; winning.

senses.d: To pursue for the purpose of killing or taking, as an enemy, or game; to hunt.
q: We are those which chased you from the field. Shak.
Philologists, who chase A panting syllable through time and place. Cowper.

senses.d: To follow as if to catch; to pursue; to compel to move on; to drive by following; to cause to fly; — often with away or off; as, to chase the hens away.
q: Chased by their brother's endless malice from prince to prince and from place to place. Knolles.

senses.d: To pursue eagerly, as hunters pursue game.
q: Chasing each other merrily. Tennyson.

Chase.etym: [OF. chacier, F. chasser, fr. (assumed) LL. captiare, fr. L. captare to strive to seize. See Catch.]

senses.d: To give chase; to hunt; as, to chase around after a doctor.
Vehement pursuit for the purpose of killing or capturing, as of an enemy, or game; an earnest seeking after any object greatly desired; the act or habit of hunting; a hunt.
q: You see this chase is hotly followed. Shak.

senses.d: That which is pursued or hunted.
q: Nay, Warwick, seek thee out some other chase, For I myself must hunt this deer to death. Shak.

senses.d: An open hunting ground to which game resorts, and which is private property, thus differing from a forest, which is not private property, and from a park, which is inclosed. Sometimes written chace.
A division of the floor of a gallery, marked by a figure or otherwise; the spot where a ball falls, and between which and the dedans the adversary must drive his ball in order to gain a point.

Chase.etym: [Cf. F. chasse, fr. chasser. See Chase, v.]

senses.d: A rectangular iron frame in which pages or columns of type are imposed.
The part of a cannon from the reënforce or the trunnions to the swell of the muzzle. See Cannon.
A groove, or channel, as in the face of a wall; a trench, as for the reception of drain tile.
A kind of joint by which an overlap joint is changed to a flush joint, by means of a gradually deepening rabbet, as at the ends of clinker-built boats.

Chase.etym: [F. cháse, fr. L. capsa box, case. See Case a box.]

senses.d: To ornament (a surface of metal) by embossing, cutting away parts, and the like.
To cut, so as to make a screw thread.
The art of ornamenting metal by means of chasing tools; also, a piece of ornamental work produced in this way.
Pure from unlawful sexual intercourse; virtuous; continent.
q: Whose bed is undefiled and chaste pronounced. Milton.

senses.d: Pure in thought and act; innocent; free from lewdness and obscenity, or indecency in act or speech; modest; as, a chaste mind; chaste eyes.
Pure in design and expression; correct; free from barbarisms or vulgarisms; refined; simple; as, a chaste style in composition or art.
q: That great model of chaste, lofty, and eloquence, the Book of Common Prayer. Macaulay.

senses.d: Unmarried.

Chaste.syn: Undefiled; pure; virtuous; continent; immaculate; spotless.
Chaste.etym: [F. chaste, from L. castus pure, chaste; cf. Gr. καθαρόσ pure, Skr. çudth to purify.]

senses.d: To correct by punishment; to inflict pain upon the purpose of reclaiming; to discipline; as, to chasten a son with a rod.
q: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth. Heb. xii. 6.

senses.d: To purify from errors or faults; to refine.
q: They chasten and enlarge the mind, and excite to noble actions. Layard.

Chasten.syn: To chastise; punish; correct; discipline; castigate; afflict; subdue; purify.
Chasten.etym: [OE. chastien, OF. Chastier, F. Ch�tier, fr. L. castigare to punish, chastise; castus pure + agere to lead, drive. See Chaste, Act, and cf. Castigate, Chastise.]

senses.d: Corrected; disciplined; refined; purified; toned down.
q: Of such a finished chastened purity. Tennyson.

senses.d: To inflict pain upon, by means of stripes, or in any other manner, for the purpose of punishment or reformation; to punish, as with stripes.
q: How fine my master is! I am afraid He will chastise me. Shak.
I am glad to see the vanity or envy of the canting chemists thus discovered and chastised. Boyle.

senses.d: To reduce to order or obedience; to correct or purify; to free from faults or excesses.
q: The gay, social sense, by decency chastised. Thomson.

Chastise.etym: [OE. chastisen; chastien + ending -isen + modern -ise, -ize, L. -izare, Gr. -ίζειν. See Chasten.]

senses.d: The act of chastising; pain inflicted for punishment and correction; discipline; punishment.
q: Shall I so much dishonor my fair stars, On equal terms to give him chastesement! Shak.
I have borne chastisement; I will not offend any more. Job xxxiv. 31.

senses.d: To talk in a light and familiar manner; to converse without form or ceremony; to gossip.
q: To chat a while on their adventures. Dryden.

senses.d: To talk of.
Light, familiar talk; conversation; gossip.
q: Snuff, or fan, supply each pause of chat, With singing, laughing, ogling, and all that. Pope.

senses.d: A bird of the genus Icteria, allied to the warblers, in America. The best known species are the yellow-breasted chat (I. viridis), and the long-tailed chat (I. longicauda). In Europe the name is given to several birds of the family Saxicolidæ, as the stonechat, and whinchat.
A twig, cone, or little branch. See Chit.
Small stones with ore.
To utter sounds which somewhat resemble language, but are inarticulate and indistinct.
q: The jaw makes answer, as the magpie chatters. Wordsworth.

senses.d: To talk idly, carelessly, or with undue rapidity; to jabber; to prate.
q: To tame a shrew, and charm her chattering tongue. Shak.

senses.d: To make a noise by rapid collisions.
q: With chattering teeth, and bristling hair upright. Dryden.

Chatter.etym: [Of imitative origin. Cf. Chat, v. i. Chitter.]

senses.d: To utter rapidly, idly, or indistinctly.
q: Begin his witless note apace to chatter. Spenser.

senses.d: Sounds like those of a magpie or monkey; idle talk; rapid, thoughtless talk; jabber; prattle.
q: Your words are but idle and empty chatter. Longfellow.

senses.d: Noise made by collision of the teeth, as in shivering.

A word of warning denoting that the king is in danger; such a menace of a player's king by an adversary's move as would, if it were any other piece, expose it to immediate capture. A king so menaced is said to be in check, and must be made safe at the next move.
A condition of interrupted or impeded progress; arrest; stop; delay; as, to hold an enemy in check.
q: Which gave a remarkable check to the first progress of Christianity. Addison.
No check, no stay, this streamlet fears. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Whatever arrests progress, or limits action; an obstacle, guard, restraint, or rebuff.
q: Useful check upon the administration of government. Washington.
A man whom no check could abash. Macaulay.

senses.d: A mark, certificate, or token, by which, errors may be prevented, or a thing or person may be identified; as, checks placed against items in an account; a check given for baggage; a return check on a railroad.
A written order directing a bank or banker to pay money as therein stated. See Bank check, below.
A woven or painted design in squares resembling the patten of a checkerboard; one of the squares of such a design; also, cloth having such a figure.
The forsaking by a hawk of its proper game to follow other birds.
Small chick or crack.

Check.syn: Hindrance; setback; interruption; obstruction; reprimand; censure; rebuke; reproof; repulse; rebuff; tally; counterfoil; counterbalance; ticket; draft.
Check.etym: [OE. chek, OF. eschec, F. échec, a stop, hindrance, orig. check in the game of chess, pl. échecs chess, through Ar., fr. Pers. shāh king. See Shah, and cf. Checkmate, Chess, Checker.]

senses.d: To make a move which puts an adversary's piece, esp. his king, in check; to put in check.
To put a sudden restraint upon; to stop temporarily; to hinder; to repress; to curb.
q: So many clogs to check and retard the headlong course of violence and oppression. Burke.

senses.d: To verify, to guard, to make secure, by means of a mark, token, or other check; to distinguish by a check; to put a mark against (an item) after comparing with an original or a counterpart in order to secure accuracy; as, to check an account; to check baggage.
To chide, rebuke, or reprove.
q: The good king, his master, will check him for it. Shak.

senses.d: To slack or ease off, as a brace which is too stiffly extended.
To make checks or chinks in; to cause to crack; as, the sun checks timber.

Check.syn: To restrain; curb; bridle; repress; control; hinder; impede; obstruct; interrupt; tally; rebuke; reprove; rebuff.

senses.d: To make a stop; to pause; — with at.
q: The mind, once jaded by an attempt above its power, either is disabled for the future, or else checks at any vigorous undertaking ever after. Locke.

senses.d: To clash or interfere.
To act as a curb or restraint.
q: It checks too strong upon me. Dryden.

senses.d: To crack or gape open, as wood in drying; or to crack in small checks, as varnish, paint, etc.
To turn, when in pursuit of proper game, and fly after other birds.
q: And like the haggard, check at every feather That comes before his eye. Shak.

senses.d: Checkered; designed in checks.
One who checks.
To mark with small squares like a checkerboard, as by crossing stripes of different colors.
To variegate or diversify with different qualities, colors, scenes, or events; esp., to subject to frequent alternations of prosperity and adversity.
q: Our minds are, as it were, checkered with truth and falsehood. Addison.

Checker.etym: [From OF. eschequier a chessboard, F. échiquier. See Check, n., and cf. 3d Checker.]

senses.d: A piece in the game of draughts or checkers.
A pattern in checks; a single check.
Checkerwork.
The side of the face below the eye.
The cheek bone.
Those pieces of a machine, or of any timber, or stone work, which form corresponding sides, or which are similar and in pair; as, the cheeks (jaws) of a vise; the cheeks of a gun carriage, etc.
The branches of a bridle bit.
A section of a flask, so made that it can be moved laterally, to permit the removal of the pattern from the mold; the middle part of a flask.
Cool confidence; assurance; impudence.

Cheek.etym: [OE. cheke, cheoke, AS. ceàce, ceòce; cf. Goth. kukjan to kiss, D. kaak cheek; perh. akin to E. chew, jaw.]

senses.d: To be impudent or saucy to.
The face; the countenance or its expression.
Feeling; spirit; state of mind or heart.
q: Be of good cheer. Matt. ix. 2.
The parents . . . fled away with heavy cheer. Holland.

senses.d: Gayety; mirth; cheerfulness; animation.
q: I have not that alacrity of spirit, Nor cheer of mind, that I was wont to have. Shak.

senses.d: That which promotes good spirits or cheerfulness; provisions prepared for a feast; entertainment; as, a table loaded with good cheer.
A shout, hurrah, or acclamation, expressing joy enthusiasm, applause, favor, etc.
q: Welcome her, thundering cheer of the street. Tennyson.

Cheer.etym: [OE. chere face, welcome, cheer, OF. chiere, F. chère, fr. LL. cara face, Gr. κάρα head; akin to Skr. çiras, L. cerebrum brain, G. hirn, and E. cranium.]

senses.d: To cause to rejoice; to gladden; to make cheerful; — often with up.
To infuse life, courage, animation, or hope, into; to inspirit; to solace or comfort.
q: The proud he tamed, the penitent he cheered. Dryden.

senses.d: To salute or applaud with cheers; to urge on by cheers; as, to cheer hounds in a chase.

Cheer.syn: To gladden; encourage; inspirit; comfort; console; enliven; refresh; exhilarate; animate; applaud.

senses.d: To grow cheerful; to become gladsome or joyous; — usually with up.
q: At sight of thee my gloomy soul cheers up. A. Philips.

senses.d: To be in any state or temper of mind.
q: How cheer'st thou, Jessica? Shak.

senses.d: To utter a shout or shouts of applause, triumph, etc.
q: And even the ranks of Tusculum Could scare forbear to cheer. Macaulay.

senses.d: Having or showing good spirits or joy; cheering; cheery; contented; happy; joyful; lively; animated; willing.
q: To entertain a cheerful disposition. Shak.
The cheerful birds of sundry kind Do chant sweet music. Spenser.
A cheerful confidence in the mercy of God. Macaulay.
This general applause and cheerful shout. Shak.

Cheerful.syn: Lively; animated; gay; joyful; lightsome; gleeful; blithe; airy; sprightly; jocund; jolly; joyous; vivacious; buoyant; sunny; happy; hopeful.

senses.d: In a cheerful manner, gladly.
Good spirits; a state of moderate joy or gayety; alacrity.
The curd of milk, coagulated usually with rennet, separated from the whey, and pressed into a solid mass in a hoop or mold.
A mass of pomace, or ground apples, pressed together in the form of a cheese.
The flat, circular, mucilaginous fruit of the dwarf mallow (Malva rotundifolia).
A low courtesy; — so called on account of the cheese form assumed by a woman's dress when she stoops after extending the skirts by a rapid gyration.

Cheese.etym: [OE. chese, AS. cēse, fr. L. caseus, LL. casius. Cf. Casein.]

senses.d: To treat with tenderness and affection; to nurture with care; to protect and aid.
q: We were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children. 1 Thess. ii. 7.

senses.d: To hold dear; to embrace with interest; to indulge; to encourage; to foster; to promote; as, to cherish religious principle.
q: To cherish virtue and humanity. Burke.

Cherish.syn: To nourish; foster; nurse; nurture; entertain; encourage; comfort; protect; support; See Nurture.
Cherish.etym: [F. chérir, fr. cher dear, fr. L. carus. See Caress, Finish.]

senses.d: A mysterious composite being, the winged footstool and chariot of the Almighty, described in Ezekiel i. and x.
q: I knew that they were the cherubim. Ezek. x. 20.
He rode upon a cherub and did fly. Ps. xviii. 10.

senses.d: A symbolical winged figure of unknown form used in connection with the mercy seat of the Jewish Ark and Temple.

One of a order of angels, variously represented in art. In European painting the cherubim have been shown as blue, to denote knowledge, as distinguished from the seraphim (see Seraph), and in later art the children's heads with wings are generally called cherubs.
A beautiful child; — so called because artists have represented cherubs as beautiful children.
The Hebrew plural of Cherub.. Cf. Seraphim.
pret. of Chese.
To choose
A large box of wood, or other material, having, like a trunk, a lid, but no covering of skin, leather, or cloth.
q: Heaps of money crowded in the chest. Dryden.

senses.d: A coffin.
q: He is now dead and mailed in his cheste. Chaucer.

senses.d: The part of the body inclosed by the ribs and breastbone; the thorax.
A case in which certain goods, as tea, opium, etc., are transported; hence, the quantity which such a case contains.
A tight receptacle or box, usually for holding gas, steam, liquids, etc.; as, the steam chest of an engine; the wind chest of an organ.

Chest.etym: [OE. chest, chist, AS. cest, cist, cyst, L. cista, fr. Gr. κίστη. Cf. Cist, Cistern.]

senses.d: To deposit in a chest; to hoard.
To place in a coffin.
q: He dieth and is chested. Gen. 1. 26 (heading).

senses.d: Strife; contention; controversy.
To bite and grind with the teeth; to masticate.
To ruminate mentally; to meditate on.
q: He chews revenge, abjuring his offense. Prior.
Every beast the parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat. Deut. xxiv. 6.

Chew.etym: [As ceówan, akin to D. kauwen, G. kauen. Cf. Chaw, Jaw.]

senses.d: To perform the action of biting and grinding with the teeth; to ruminate; to meditate.
q: old politicians chew wisdom past. Pope.

senses.d: That which is chewed; that which is held in the mouth at once; a cud.
A young bird or fowl, esp. a young barnyard fowl.
A young person; a child; esp. a young woman; a maiden.

Chicken.etym: [AS. cicen, cyceun, dim. of coc cock; akin to LG. kiken, küken, D. Kieken, kuiken, G. küchkein. See Cock the animal.]

senses.d: To rebuke; to reprove; to scold; to find fault with.
q: Upbraided, chid, and rated at. Shak.

senses.d: Fig.: To be noisy about; to chafe against.
q: The sea that chides the banks of England. Shak.

Chide.syn: To blame; rebuke; reprove; scold; censure; reproach; reprehend; reprimand.
Chide.etym: [imp. Chid (chĭd), or Chode (chīd Obs.); p. p. Chidden (?), Chid; p. pr. & vb. n. Chiding.]

senses.d: To utter words of disapprobation and displeasure; to find fault; to contend angrily.
q: Wherefore the people did chide with Moses. Ex. xvii. 2.

senses.d: To make a clamorous noise; to chafe.
q: As doth a rock againts the chiding flood. Shak.

senses.d: A continuous noise or murmur.
q: The chide of streams. Thomson.

senses.d: The head or leader of any body of men; a commander, as of an army; a head man, as of a tribe, clan, or family; a person in authority who directs the work of others; the principal actor or agent.
The principal part; the most valuable portion.
q: The chief of the things which should be utterly destroyed. 1 Sam. xv. 21

senses.d: The upper third part of the field. It is supposed to be composed of the dexter, sinister, and middle chiefs.

Chief.syn: Chieftain; captain; general; commander; leader; head; principal; sachem; sagamore; sheik.
Chief.etym: [OE. chief, chef, OF. chief, F. chef, fr. L. caput head, possibly akin to E. head. Cf. Captain, Chapter]

senses.d: Highest in office or rank; principal; head.
Principal or most eminent in any quality or action; most distinguished; having most influence; taking the lead; most important; as, the chief topic of conversation; the chief interest of man.
Very intimate, near, or close.
q: A whisperer separateth chief friends. Prov. xvi. 28.

Chief.syn: Principal; head; leading; main; paramount; supreme; prime; vital; especial; great; grand; eminent; master.

senses.d: First or foremost; chief; principal.
q: The chiefest among ten thousand. Canticles v. 10.

senses.d: In the first place; principally; preëminently; above; especially.
q: Search through this garden; leave unsearched no nook; But chiefly where those two fair creatures lodge. Milton.

senses.d: For the most part; mostly.
q: Those parts of the kingdom where the . . . estates of the dissenters chiefly lay. Swift.

senses.d: A son or a daughter; a male or female descendant, in the first degree; the immediate progeny of human parents; — in law, legitimate offspring. Used also of animals and plants.
A descendant, however remote; — used esp. in the plural; as, the children of Israel; the children of Edom.

One who, by character of practice, shows signs of relationship to, or of the influence of, another; one closely connected with a place, occupation, character, etc.; as, a child of God; a child of the devil; a child of disobedience; a child of toil; a child of the people.
A noble youth. See Childe.

A young person of either sex. esp. one between infancy and youth; hence, one who exhibits the characteristics of a very young person, as innocence, obedience, trustfulness, limited understanding, etc.
q: When I was child. I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. 1. Cor. xii. 11.

senses.d: A female infant.
q: A boy or a child, I wonder? Shak.

Child.etym: [AS. cild, pl. cildru; cf. Goth. kilþei womb, in-kilþō with child.]

senses.d: To give birth; to produce young.
q: This queen Genissa childing died. Warner.
It chanced within two days they childed both. Latimer.

senses.d: The act of producing or bringing forth children; parturition.
The state of being a child; the time in which persons are children; the condition or time from infancy to puberty.
q: I have walked before you from my childhood. 1. Sam. xii. 2.

senses.d: Children, taken collectively.
q: The well-governed childhood of this realm. Sir. W. Scott.

senses.d: The commencement; the first period.
q: The childhood of our joy. Shak.

Childhood.etym: [AS. cildhād; cild child + -hād. See Child, and -hood.]

senses.d: Of, pertaining to, befitting, or resembling, a child.
Puerile; trifling; weak.
q: Methinks that simplicity in her countenance is rather childish than innocent. Addison.

senses.d: pl. of Child.
A fireplace or hearth.

That part of a building which contains the smoke flues; esp. an upright tube or flue of brick or stone, in most cases extending through or above the roof of the building. Often used instead of chimney shaft.
q: Hard by a cottage chimney smokes. Milton.

senses.d: A tube usually of glass, placed around a flame, as of a lamp, to create a draft, and promote combustion.
A body of ore, usually of elongated form, extending downward in a vein.

Chimney.etym: [F. cheminée, LL. caminata, fr. L. caminus furnace, fireplace, Gr. � furnace, oven.]

senses.d: The ninth month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of November with a part of December.
the old imp. of chide. See Chide.
Act of choosing; the voluntary act of selecting or separating from two or more things that which is preferred; the determination of the mind in preferring one thing to another; election.
The power or opportunity of choosing; option.
q: Choice there is not, unless the thing which we take be so in our power that we might have refused it. Hooker.

senses.d: Care in selecting; judgment or skill in distinguishing what is to be preferred, and in giving a preference; discrimination.
q: I imagine they were collected with judgment and choice. Bacon.

senses.d: A sufficient number to choose among.
The thing or person chosen; that which is approved and selected in preference to others; selection.
q: The common wealth is sick of their own choice. Shak.

senses.d: The best part; that which is preferable.
q: The flower and choice Of many provinces from bound to bound. Milton.

Choice.etym: [OE. chois, OF. chois, F. choix, fr. choisir to choose; of German origin; cf. Goth. kausjan to examine, kiusan to choose, examine, G. kiesen. √46. Cf. Choose.]

senses.d: Worthly of being chosen or preferred; select; superior; precious; valuable.
q: My choicest hours of life are lost. Swift.

senses.d: Preserving or using with care, as valuable; frugal; — used with of; as, to be choice of time, or of money.
Selected with care, and due attention to preference; deliberately chosen.
q: Choice word measured phrase. Wordsworth.

Choice.syn: Select; precious; exquisite; uncommon; rare; chary; careful/

senses.d: To render unable to breathe by filling, pressing upon, or squeezing the windpipe; to stifle; to suffocate; to strangle.
q: With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder. Shak.

senses.d: To obstruct by filling up or clogging any passage; to block up.
To hinder or check, as growth, expansion, progress, etc.; to stifle.
q: Oats and darnel choke the rising corn. Dryden.

senses.d: To affect with a sense of strangulation by passion or strong feeling.
To make a choke, as in a cartridge, or in the bore of the barrel of a shotgun.

Choke.etym: [OE. cheken, choken; cf. AS. āceocian to suffocate, Icel. koka to gulp, E. chincough, cough.]

senses.d: To have the windpipe stopped; to have a spasm of the throat, caused by stoppage or irritation of the windpipe; to be strangled.
To be checked, as if by choking; to stick.
q: The words choked in his throat. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A stoppage or irritation of the windpipe, producing the feeling of strangulation.
The tied end of a cartridge.
The bile; — formerly supposed to be the seat and cause of irascibility.
q: His complexion . . . was sanguine, with a mixture of choler; and yet his motion was slow. I. Warton.

senses.d: Irritation of the passions; anger; wrath.
q: He is rash and very sudden in choler. Shak.

Choler.etym: [OE. coler, F. colère anger, L. cholera a bilious complaint, fr. Gr. � cholera, fr. �, χολή, bile. See Gall, and cf. Cholera.]

senses.d: To make choice of; to select; to take by way of preference from two or more objects offered; to elect; as, to choose the least of two evils.
q: Choose me for a humble friend. Pope.

senses.d: To wish; to desire; to prefer.
q: The landlady now returned to know if we did not choose a more genteel apartment. Goldsmith.

Choose.syn: To select; prefer; elect; adopt; follow.
Choose.etym: [OE. chesen, cheosen, AS. ceósan; akin to OS. kiosan, D. kiezen, G. kiesen, Icel. kjōsa, Goth. kiusan, L. gustare to taste, Gr. �, Skr. jush to enjoy. √46. Cf. Choice, 2d Gust.]

senses.d: To make a selection; to decide.
q: They had only to choose between implicit obedience and open rebellion. Prescott.

senses.d: To do otherwise.
q: Thou canst not choose but know who I am. Shak.

senses.d: To cut by striking repeatedly with a sharp instrument; to cut into pieces; to mince; — often with up.
To sever or separate by one more blows of a sharp instrument; to divide; — usually with off or down.
q: Chop off your hand, and it to the king. Shak.

senses.d: To seize or devour greedily; — with up.
q: Upon the opening of his mouth he drops his breakfast, which the fox presently chopped up. L'estrange.

Chop.etym: [Cf. LG. & D. kappen, Dan. kappe, Sw. kappa. Cf. Chap to crack.]

senses.d: To make a quick strike, or repeated strokes, with an ax or other sharp instrument.
To do something suddenly with an unexpected motion; to catch or attempt to seize.
q: Out of greediness to get both, he chops at the shadow, and loses the substance. L'Estrange.

senses.d: To interrupt; — with in or out.
q: This fellow interrupted the sermon, even suddenly chopping in. Latimer.

senses.d: To barter or truck.
To exchange; substitute one thing for another.
q: We go on chopping and changing our friends. L'Estrange.

Chop.etym: [Cf. D. koopen to buy. See Cheapen, v. t., and cf. Chap, v. i., to buy.]

senses.d: To purchase by way of truck.
To vary or shift suddenly; as, the wind chops about.
To wrangle; to altercate; to bandy words.
q: Let not the counsel at the bar chop with the judge. Bacon.

senses.d: A change; a vicissitude.
To crack. See Chap, v. t. & i.
The act of chopping; a stroke.
A piece chopped off; a slice or small piece, especially of meat; as, a mutton chop.
A crack or cleft. See Chap.
A jaw of an animal; — commonly in the pl. See Chops.
A movable jaw or cheek, as of a wooden vise.
The land at each side of the mouth of a river, harbor, or channel; as, East Chop or West Chop. See Chops.
Quality; brand; as, silk of the first chop.
A permit or clearance.
A thing; personal property.

Chose.etym: [F., fr. L. causa cause, reason. See Cause.]

senses.d: Selected from a number; picked out; choice.
q: Seven hundred chosen men left-handed. Judg. xx. 16.

senses.d: One who, or that which is the object of choice or special favor.
The Anointed; an appellation given to Jesus, the Savior. It is synonymous with the Hebrew Messiah.

Christ.etym: [L. Christus, Gr. �, fr. � anointed, fr. χρίειν to anoint. See Chrism.]

senses.d: One who believes, or professes or is assumed to believe, in Jesus Christ, and the truth as taught by Him; especially, one whose inward and outward life is conformed to the doctrines of Christ.
q: The disciples were called Christians first in Antioch. Acts xi. 26.

senses.d: One born in a Christian country or of Christian parents, and who has not definitely becomes an adherent of an opposing system.

One of a Christian denomination which rejects human creeds as bases of fellowship, and sectarian names. They are congregational in church government, and baptize by immersion. They are also called Disciples of Christ, and Campbellites.

Christian.etym: [L. christianus, Gr. �; cf. AS. cristen. See Christ.]

senses.d: Pertaining to Christ or his religion; as, Christian people.
Pertaining to the church; ecclesiastical; as, a Christian court.
Characteristic of Christian people; civilized; kind; kindly; gentle; beneficent.
q: The graceful tact; the Christian art. Tennyson.

senses.d: In various Protestant churches, a society of young people organized in each individual church to do Christian work; also, the whole body of such organizations, which are united in a corporation called the United Society of Christian Endeavor, organized in 1885. The parent society was founded in 1881 at Portland, Maine, by Rev. Francis E. Clark, a Congregational minister.
An historical register or account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
A narrative of events; a history; a record.
The two canonical books of the Old Testament in which immediately follow 2 Kings.

Chronicle.etym: [OE. cronicle, fr. cronique, OF. cronique, F. chronique, L. chronica, fr. Gr. �, neut. pl. of �. See Chronic.]

senses.d: To record in a history or chronicle; to record; to register.

A mineral, composed of silica, magnesia, and iron, of a yellow to green color. It is common in certain volcanic rocks; — called also olivine and peridot. Sometimes used as a gem. The name was also early used for yellow varieties of tourmaline and topaz.

Chrysolite.etym: [L. chrysolithos, Gr. �; χρυσόσ gold + � stone: cf. F. chrysolithe.]

senses.d: A species to fresh-water fish of the Cyprinidæ or Carp family. The common European species is Leuciscus cephalus; the cheven. In America the name is applied to various fishes of the same family, of the genera Semotilus, Squalius, Ceratichthys, etc., and locally to several very different fishes, as the tautog, black bass, etc.

Chub.etym: [This word seems to signify a large or thick fish. Cf. Sw. kubb a short and thick piece of wood, and perh. F. chabot chub.]

senses.d: A building set apart for Christian worship.
A Jewish or heathen temple.
A formally organized body of Christian believers worshiping together.

A body of Christian believers, holding the same creed, observing the same rites, and acknowledging the same ecclesiastical authority; a denomination; as, the Roman Catholic church; the Presbyterian church.
The collective body of Christians.
Any body of worshipers; as, the Jewish church; the church of Brahm.
The aggregate of religious influences in a community; ecclesiastical influence, authority, etc.; as, to array the power of the church against some moral evil.
q: Remember that both church and state are properly the rulers of the people, only because they are their benefactors. Bulwer.

Church.etym: [OE. chirche, chireche, cherche, Scot. kirk, from AS. circe, cyrice; akin to D. kerk, Icel. kirkja, Sw. kyrka, Dan. kirke, G. kirche, OHG. chirihha; all fr. Gr. κυριακόν the Lord's house, fr. κυριακόσ concerning a master or lord, fr. κύριοσ master, lord, fr. κυ̑ροσ power, might; akin to Skr. çūra he

senses.d: To bless according to a prescribed form, or to unite with in publicly returning thanks in church, as after deliverance from the dangers of childbirth; as, the churching of women.
A rustic; a countryman or laborer.
q: Your rank is all reversed; let men of cloth Bow to the stalwart churls in overalls. Emerson.

senses.d: A rough, surly, ill-bred man; a boor.
q: A churl's courtesy rarely comes, but either for gain or falsehood. Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: A selfish miser; an illiberal person; a niggard.
q: Like to some rich churl hoarding up his pelf. Drayton.

Churl.etym: [AS. ceorl a freeman of the lowest rank, man, husband; akin to D. karel, kerel, G. kerl, Dan. & Sw. karl, Icel. karl, and to the E. proper name Charles (orig., man, male), and perh. to Skr. jāra lover. Cf. Carl, Charles's Wain.]

senses.d: Churlish; rough; selfish.
Like a churl; rude; cross-grained; ungracious; surly; illiberal; niggardly.
q: Half mankind maintain a churlish strife. Cowper.

senses.d: Wanting pliancy; unmanageable; unyielding; not easily wrought; as, a churlish soil; the churlish and intractable nature of some minerals.
A vessel in which milk or cream is stirred, beaten, or otherwise agitated (as by a plunging or revolving dasher) in order to separate the oily globules from the other parts, and obtain butter.

Churn.etym: [OE. chirne, cherne, AS. ceren, cyrin; akin to D. karn, Dan. kierne. See Churn, v. t.]

senses.d: To stir, beat, or agitate, as milk or cream in a churn, in order to make butter.
To shake or agitate with violence.
q: Churned in his teeth, the foamy venom rose. Addison.

Churn.etym: [OE. chernen, AS. cernan; akin to LG. karnen, G. kernen, D. karnen, Dan. kierne, Sw. kärna, and also to E. corn, kernel, the meaning coming from the idea of extracting the kernel or marrow. See Kernel.]

senses.d: To perform the operation of churning.
The act of one who churns.
The quantity of butter made at one operation.
The inner bark of the shoots of Cinnamomum Zeylanicum, a tree growing in Ceylon. It is aromatic, of a moderately pungent taste, and is one of the best cordial, carminative, and restorative spices.
Cassia.

Cinnamon.etym: [Heb. qinnāmōn; cf. Gr. �, �, cinnamomum, cinnamon. The Heb. word itself seems to have been borrowed from some other language; cf. Malay kājū mānis sweet wood.]

senses.d: A plane figure, bounded by a single curve line called its circumference, every part of which is equally distant from a point within it, called the center.
The line that bounds such a figure; a circumference; a ring.
An instrument of observation, the graduated limb of which consists of an entire circle.
A round body; a sphere; an orb.
q: It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth. Is. xi. 22.

senses.d: Compass; circuit; inclosure.
q: In the circle of this forest. Shak.

senses.d: A company assembled, or conceived to assemble, about a central point of interest, or bound by a common tie; a class or division of society; a coterie; a set.
q: As his name gradually became known, the circle of his acquaintance widened. Macaulay.

senses.d: A circular group of persons; a ring.
A series ending where it begins, and repeating itself.
q: Thus in a circle runs the peasant's pain. Dryden.

senses.d: A form of argument in which two or more unproved statements are used to prove each other; inconclusive reasoning.
q: That heavy bodies descend by gravity; and, again, that gravity is a quality whereby a heavy body descends, is an impertinent circle and teaches nothing. Glanvill.

senses.d: Indirect form of words; circumlocution.
q: Has he given the lie, In circle, or oblique, or semicircle. J. Fletcher.

senses.d: A territorial division or district.

Circle.etym: [OE. cercle, F. cercle, fr. L. circulus (Whence also AS. circul), dim. of circus circle, akin to Gr. κρίκοσ, κίρκοσ, circle, ring. Cf. Circus, Circum-.]

senses.d: To move around; to revolve around.
q: Other planets circle other suns. Pope.

senses.d: To encompass, as by a circle; to surround; to inclose; to encircle.
q: Their heads are circled with a short turban. Dampier.
So he lies, circled with evil. Coleridge.

Circle.etym: [OE. cerclen, F. cercler, fr. L. circulare to make round. See Circle, n., and cf. Circulate.]

senses.d: To move circularly; to form a circle; to circulate.
q: Thy name shall circle round the gaping through. Byron.

senses.d: The act of moving or revolving around, or as in a circle or orbit; a revolution; as, the periodical circuit of the earth round the sun.
The circumference of, or distance round, any space; the measure of a line round an area.
q: The circuit or compass of Ireland is 1,800 miles. J. Stow.

senses.d: That which encircles anything, as a ring or crown.
q: The golden circuit on my head. Shak.

senses.d: The space inclosed within a circle, or within limits.
q: A circuit wide inclosed with goodliest trees. Milton.

senses.d: A regular or appointed journeying from place to place in the exercise of one's calling, as of a judge, or a preacher.
A certain division of a state or country, established by law for a judge or judges to visit, for the administration of justice.
Circumlocution.

Circuit.etym: [F. circuit, fr. L. circuitus, fr. circuire or circumire to go around; circum around + ire to go.]

senses.d: To move in a circle; to go round; to circulate.
To travel around.
To cut off the prepuce of foreskin of, in the case of males, and the internal labia of, in the case of females.
To purify spiritually.

Circumcise.etym: [L. circumcisus, p. p. of circumcidere to cut around, to circumcise; circum + caedere to cut; akin to E. cæsura, homicide, concise, and prob. to shed, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of cutting off the prepuce or foreskin of males, or the internal labia of females.
The Jews, as a circumcised people.
Attentive to all the circumstances of a case or the probable consequences of an action; cautious; prudent; wary.

Circumspect.etym: [L. circumspectus, p. p. of circumspicere to look about one's self, to observe; circum + spicere, specere, to look. See Spy.]

senses.d: In a circumspect manner; cautiously; warily.
An artificial reservoir or tank for holding water, beer, or other liquids.
A natural reservoir; a hollow place containing water.

Cistern.etym: [OE. cisterne, OF. cisterne, F. cisterne, fr. L. cisterna, fr. cista box, chest. See Cist, and cf. chest.]

senses.d: One who enjoys the freedom and privileges of a city; a freeman of a city, as distinguished from a foreigner, or one not entitled to its franchises.
q: That large body of the working men who were not counted as citizens and had not so much as a vote to serve as an anodyne to their stomachs. G. Eliot.

senses.d: An inhabitant of a city; a townsman.
A person, native or naturalized, of either sex, who owes allegiance to a government, and is entitled to reciprocal protection from it.
One who is domiciled in a country, and who is a citizen, though neither native nor naturalized, in such a sense that he takes his legal status from such country.

Citizen.etym: [OE. citisein, OF. citeain, F. citoyen, fr. cité city. See City, and cf. Cit.]

senses.d: Having the condition or qualities of a citizen, or of citizens; as, a citizen soldiery.
Of or pertaining to the inhabitants of a city; characteristic of citizens; effeminate; luxurious.
q: I am not well, But not so citizen a wanton as To seem to die ere sick. Shak.

senses.d: A large town.

A corporate town; in the United States, a town or collective body of inhabitants, incorporated and governed by a mayor and aldermen or a city council consisting of a board of aldermen and a common council; in Great Britain, a town corporate, which is or has been the seat of a bishop, or the capital of his see.
q: A city is a town incorporated; which is, or has been, the see of a bishop; and though the bishopric has been dissolved, as at Westminster, it yet remaineth a city. Blackstone
When Gorges constituted York a city, he of course meant it to be the seat of a bishop, for the word city has no other meaning in English law. Palfrey

senses.d: The collective body of citizens, or inhabitants of a city.

City.etym: [OE. cite, F. cité, fr. L. civitas citizenship, state, city, fr. civis citizen; akin to Goth. heiwa (in heiwafrauja man of the house), AS. hīwan, pl., members of a family, servants, hīred family, G. heirath marriage, prop., providing a house, E. hind a peasant.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a city.
To clothe.
Speaking and repeating loud words; full of clamor; calling or demanding loudly or urgently; vociferous; noisy; bawling; loud; turbulent.

Clamorous.etym: [LL. clamorosus, for L. Clamosus: cf. OF. clamoreux.]

senses.d: To strike; to slap; to strike, or strike together, with a quick motion, so, as to make a sharp noise; as, to clap one's hands; a clapping of wings.
q: Then like a bird it sits and sings, And whets and claps its silver wings. Marvell.

senses.d: To thrust, drive, put, or close, in a hasty or abrupt manner; — often followed by to, into, on, or upon.
q: He had just time to get in and clap to the door. Locke
Clap an extinguaisher upon your irony. Lamb.

senses.d: To manifest approbation of, by striking the hands together; to applaud; as, to clap a performance.

Clap.etym: [AS. clappan; akin to Icel. & Sw. klappa, D, klappen, to clap, prate, G. klaffen, v. i., to split open, yelp, klopfen, v. t. & i., to knock.]

senses.d: To knock, as at a door.
To strike the hands together in applause.
q: Their ladies bid them clap. Shak.

senses.d: To come together suddenly with noise.
q: The doors around me clapped. Dryden.

senses.d: To enter with alacrity and briskness; — with to or into.
To talk noisily; to chatter loudly.
A loud noise made by sudden collision; a bang.
A burst of sound; a sudden explosion.
q: Horrible claps of thunder. Hakewill.

senses.d: A single, sudden act or motion; a stroke; a blow.
q: What, fifty of my followers at a clap! Shak.

senses.d: A striking of hands to express approbation.
q: Unextrected claps or hisses. Addison.

senses.d: Noisy talk; chatter.
The nether part of the beak of a hawk.
Gonorrhea.
A sharp, hooked nail, as of a beast or bird.
The whole foot of an animal armed with hooked nails; the pinchers of a lobster, crab, etc.
Anything resembling the claw of an animal, as the curved and forked end of a hammer for drawing nails.
A slender appendage or process, formed like a claw, as the base of petals of the pink.

Claw.etym: [AS. clawu, clā, cleó; akin to D. klaauw, G. klaue, Icel. klō, Sw. & Dan. klo, and perh. to E. clew.]

senses.d: To pull, tear, or scratch with, or as with, claws or nails.
To relieve from some uneasy sensation, as by scratching; to tickle; hence, to flatter; to court.
q: Rich men they claw, soothe up, and flatter; the poor they contemn and despise. Holland.

senses.d: To rail at; to scold.
q: In the aforesaid preamble, the king fairly claweth the great monasteries, wherein, saith he, religion, thanks be to God, is right well kept and observed; though he claweth them soon after in another acceptation. T. Fuller

senses.d: To scrape, scratch, or dig with a claw, or with the hand as a claw.

A soft earth, which is plastic, or may be molded with the hands, consisting of hydrous silicate of aluminium. It is the result of the wearing down and decomposition, in part, of rocks containing aluminous minerals, as granite. Lime, magnesia, oxide of iron, and other ingredients, are often present as impurities.
Earth in general, as representing the elementary particles of the human body; hence, the human body as formed from such particles.
q: I also am formed out of the clay. Job xxxiii. 6.
The earth is covered thick with other clay, Which her own clay shall cover. Byron.

Clay.etym: [AS. clǣg; akin to LG. klei, D. klei, and perh. to AS. clām clay, L. glus, gluten glue, Gr. γλοιόσ glutinous substance, E. glue. Cf. Clog.]

senses.d: To cover or manure with clay.
To clarify by filtering through clay, as sugar.
Free from dirt or filth; as, clean clothes.
Free from that which is useless or injurious; without defects; as, clean land; clean timber.
Free from awkwardness; not bungling; adroit; dexterous; as, a clean trick; a clean leap over a fence.
Free from errors and vulgarisms; as, a clean style.
Free from restraint or neglect; complete; entire.
q: When ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not make clean riddance of corners of thy field. Lev. xxiii. 22.

senses.d: Free from moral defilement; sinless; pure.
q: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Ps. li. 10
That I am whole, and clean, and meet for Heaven Tennyson.

senses.d: Free from ceremonial defilement.
Free from that which is corrupting to the morals; pure in tone; healthy.
Well-proportioned; shapely; as, clean limbs.

Clean.etym: [OE. clene, AS. clǣne; akin to OHG. chleini pure, neat, graceful, small, G. klein small, and perh. to W. glan clean, pure, bright; all perh. from a primitive, meaning bright, shining. Cf. Glair.]

senses.d: Without limitation or remainder; quite; perfectly; wholly; entirely.
q: All the people were passed clean over Jordan. Josh. iii. 17.

senses.d: Without miscarriage; not bunglingly; dexterously.
To render clean; to free from whatever is foul, offensive, or extraneous; to purify; to cleanse.
The state or quality of being clean.
Purity of life or language; freedom from licentious courses.
To render clean; to free from fith, pollution, infection, guilt, etc.; to clean.
q: If we walk in the light . . . the blood of Jesus Christ his son cleanseth us from all sin. 1 John i. 7.
Can'st thou not minister to a mind diseased, And with some sweet oblivious antidote Cleanse the suffed bosom of that perilous stuff Which weighs upon the heart? Shak.

Cleanse.etym: [AS. clǣnsian, fr. clǣne clean. See Clean.]

senses.d: Free from opaqueness; transparent; bright; light; luminous; unclouded.
q: The stream is so transparent, pure, and clear. Denham.
Fair as the moon, clear as the sun. Canticles vi. 10.

senses.d: Free from ambiguity or indistinctness; lucid; perspicuous; plain; evident; manifest; indubitable.
q: One truth is clear; whatever is, is right. Pope.

senses.d: Able to perceive clearly; keen; acute; penetrating; discriminating; as, a clear intellect; a clear head.
q: Mother of science! now I feel thy power Within me clear, not only to discern Things in their causes, but to trace the ways Of highest agents. Milton.

senses.d: Not clouded with passion; serene; cheerful.
q: With a countenance as clear As friendship wears at feasts. Shak.

senses.d: Easily or distinctly heard; audible; canorous.
q: Hark! the numbers soft and clear Gently steal upon the ear. Pope.

senses.d: Without mixture; entirely pure; as, clear sand.
Without defect or blemish, such as freckles or knots; as, a clear complexion; clear lumber.
Free from guilt or stain; unblemished.
q: Statesman, yet friend to truth! in soul sincere, In action faithful, and in honor clear. Pope.

senses.d: Without diminution; in full; net; as, clear profit.
q: I often wished that I had clear, For life, six hundred pounds a-year. Swift.

senses.d: Free from impediment or obstruction; unobstructed; as, a clear view; to keep clear of debt.
q: My companion . . . left the way clear for him. Addison.

senses.d: Free from embarrassment; detention, etc.
q: The cruel corporal whispered in my ear, Five pounds, if rightly tipped, would set me clear. Gay.

Clear.syn: Manifest; pure; unmixed; pellucid; transparent; luminous; obvious; visible; plain; evident; apparent; distinct; perspicuous. See Manifest.
Clear.etym: [OE. cler, cleer, OF. cler, F. clair, fr.L. clarus, clear, bright, loud, distinct, renowned; perh. akin to L. clamare to call, E. claim. Cf. Chanticleer, Clairvoyant, Claret, Clarify.]

senses.d: Full extent; distance between extreme limits; especially; the distance between the nearest surfaces of two bodies, or the space between walls; as, a room ten feet square in the clear.
In a clear manner; plainly.
q: Now clear I understand What oft . . . thoughts have searched in vain. Milton.

senses.d: Without limitation; wholly; quite; entirely; as, to cut a piece clear off.
To render bright, transparent, or undimmed; to free from clouds.
q: He sweeps the skies and clears the cloudy north. Dryden.

senses.d: To free from impurities; to clarify; to cleanse.
To free from obscurity or ambiguity; to relive of perplexity; to make perspicuous.
q: Many knotty points there are Which all discuss, but few can clear. Prior.

senses.d: To render more quick or acute, as the understanding; to make perspicacious.
q: Our common prints would clear up their understandings. Addison

senses.d: To free from impediment or incumbrance, from defilement, or from anything injurious, useless, or offensive; as, to clear land of trees or brushwood, or from stones; to clear the sight or the voice; to clear one's self from debt; — often used with of, off, away, or out.
q: Clear your mind of cant. Dr. Johnson.
A statue lies hid in a block of marble; and the art of the statuary only clears away the superfluous matter. Addison.

senses.d: To free from the imputation of guilt; to justify, vindicate, or acquit; — often used with from before the thing imputed.
q: I . . . am sure he will clear me from partiality. Dryden.
How! wouldst thou clear rebellion? Addison.

senses.d: To leap or pass by, or over, without touching or failure; as, to clear a hedge; to clear a reef.
To gain without deduction; to net.
q: The profit which she cleared on the cargo. Macaulay.

senses.d: To become free from clouds or fog; to become fair; — often followed by up, off, or away.
q: So foul a sky clears not without a storm. Shak.
Advise him to stay till the weather clears up. Swift.

senses.d: To disengage one's self from incumbrances, distress, or entanglements; to become free.
q: He that clears at once will relapse; for finding himself out of straits, he will revert to his customs; but he that cleareth by degrees induceth a habit of frugality. Bacon.

senses.d: To make exchanges of checks and bills, and settle balances, as is done in a clearing house.
To obtain a clearance; as, the steamer cleared for Liverpool to-day.
One who, or that which, clears.
q: Gold is a wonderful clearer of the understanding. Addison.

senses.d: A tool of which the hemp for lines and twines, used by sailmakers, is finished.
The act or process of making clear.
q: The better clearing of this point. South.

senses.d: A tract of land cleared of wood for cultivation.
q: A lonely clearing on the shores of Moxie Lake. J. Burroughs.

senses.d: A method adopted by banks and bankers for making an exchange of checks held by each against the others, and settling differences of accounts.
The gross amount of the balances adjusted in the clearing house.
In a clear manner.
The quality or state of being clear.
To adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast; to cling.
q: My bones cleave to my skin. Ps. cii. 5.
The diseases of Egypt . . . shall cleave unto thee. Deut. xxviii. 60.
Sophistry cleaves close to and protects Sin's rotten trunk, concealing its defects. Cowper.

senses.d: To unite or be united closely in interest or affection; to adhere with strong attachment.
q: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife. Gen. ii. 24.
Cleave unto the Lord your God. Josh. xxiii. 8.

senses.d: To fit; to be adapted; to assimilate.
q: New honors come upon him, Like our strange garments, cleave not to their mold But with the aid of use. Shak.

Cleave.etym: [OE. cleovien, clivien, cliven, AS. cleofian, clifian; akin to OS. klibōn, G. kleben, LG. kliven, D. kleven, Dan. klæbe, Sw. klibba, and also to G. kleiben to cleve, paste, Icel. klīfa to climb. Cf. Climb.]

senses.d: To part or divide by force; to split or rive; to cut.
q: O Hamlet, thou hast cleft my heart in twain. Shak.

senses.d: To part or open naturally; to divide.
q: Every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws. Deut. xiv. 6.

Cleave.etym: [OE. cleoven, cleven, AS. cleófan; akin to OS. klioban, D. klooven, G. klieben, Icel. kljūfa, Sw. klyfva, Dan. klöve and prob. to Gr. γλύφειν to carve, L. glubere to peel. Cf. Cleft.]

senses.d: To part; to open; to crack; to separate; as parts of bodies; as, the ground cleaves by frost.
q: The Mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst. Zech. xiv. 4.

senses.d: Divided; split; partly divided or split.
Incised nearly to the midrib; as, a cleft leaf.
A space or opening made by splitting; a crack; a crevice; as, the cleft of a rock.
A piece made by splitting; as, a cleft of wood.
A disease in horses; a crack on the band of the pastern.

Cleft.etym: [OE. clift; cf. Sw. klyft cave, den, Icel. kluft cleft, Dan. klöft, G. kluft. See Cleave to split and cf. 2d Clift, 1st Clough.]

senses.d: Disposition to forgive and spare, as offenders; mildness of temper; gentleness; tenderness; mercy.
q: Great clemency and tender zeal toward their subjects. Stowe.
They had applied for the royal clemency. Macaulay.

senses.d: Mildness or softness of the elements; as, the clemency of the season.

Clemency.syn: Mildness; tenderness; indulgence; lenity; mercy; gentleness; compassion; kindness.

senses.d: Mild in temper and disposition; merciful; compassionate.
A high, steep rock; a precipice.

Cliff.etym: [AS. clif, cloef; akin to OS. klif, D. klif, klip, Icel. klif, Dan. & G. klippe, Sw. klippa; perh. orig. a climbing place. See Climb.]

senses.d: A cliff.
q: That gainst the craggy clifts did loudly roar. Spenser.

senses.d: A cleft of crack; a narrow opening.
The fork of the legs; the crotch.
To ascend or mount laboriously, esp. by use of the hands and feet.
To ascend as if with effort; to rise to a higher point.
q: Black vapors climb aloft, and cloud the day. Dryden.

senses.d: To ascend or creep upward by twining about a support, or by attaching itself by tendrils, rootlets, etc., to a support or upright surface.

Climb.etym: [AS. climban; akin to OHG. chlimban, G. & D. klimmen, Icel. klīfa, and E. cleave to adhere.]

senses.d: To ascend, as by means of the hands and feet, or laboriously or slowly; to mount.
The act of one who climbs; ascent by climbing.
To embrace, hence; to encompass.
q: O . . . that Neptune's arms, who clippeth thee about, Would bear thee from the knowledge of thyself. Shak.

senses.d: To cut off; as with shears or scissors; as, to clip the hair; to clip coin.
q: Sentenced to have his ears clipped. Macaulay.

senses.d: To curtail; to cut short.
q: All my reports go with the modest truth; No more nor clipped, but so. Shak.
In London they clip their words after one manner about the court, another in the city, and a third in the suburbs. Swift.

Clip.etym: [OE. cluppen, clippen, to embrace, AS. clyran to embrace, clasp; cf. OHG. kluft tongs, shears, Icel, klȳpa to pinch, squeeze, also OE. clippen to cut, shear, Dan. klippe to clip, cut, SW. & Icel. klippa.]

senses.d: To move swiftly; — usually with indefinite it.
q: Straight flies as chek, and clips it down the wind. Dryden.

senses.d: An embrace.
A cutting; a shearing.
The product of a single shearing of sheep; a season's crop of wool.
A clasp or holder for letters, papers, etc.
An embracing strap for holding parts together; the iron strap, with loop, at the ends of a whiffletree.
A projecting flange on the upper edge of a horseshoe, turned up so as to embrace the lower part of the hoof; — called also toe clip and beak.
A blow or stroke with the hand; as, he hit him a clip.
A part, attachment, or appendage, for seizing, clasping, or holding, an object, as a cable, etc.
A gaff or hook for landing the fish, as in salmon fishing.
A rapid gait.
A lump or mass, especially of earth, turf, or clay.
q: The earth that casteth up from the plow a great clod, is not so good as that which casteth up a smaller clod. Bacon.

senses.d: The ground; the earth; a spot of earth or turf.
q: The clod Where once their sultan's horse has trod. Swift.

senses.d: That which is earthy and of little relative value, as the body of man in comparison with the soul.
q: This cold clod of clay which we carry about with us. T. Burnet.

senses.d: A dull, gross, stupid fellow; a dolt
A part of the shoulder of a beef creature, or of the neck piece near the shoulder. See Illust. of Beef.

Clod.etym: [OE. clodde, latter form of clot. See Clot.]

senses.d: To collect into clods, or into a thick mass; to coagulate; to clot; as, clodded gore. See Clot.
q: Clodded in lumps of clay. G. Fletcher.

senses.d: To pelt with clods.
To throw violently; to hurl.
To stop, or fill up, as an opening; to shut; as, to close the eyes; to close a door.
To bring together the parts of; to consolidate; as, to close the ranks of an army; — often used with up.
To bring to an end or period; to conclude; to complete; to finish; to end; to consummate; as, to close a bargain; to close a course of instruction.
q: One frugal supper did our studies close. Dryden.

senses.d: To come or gather around; to inclose; to encompass; to confine.
q: The depth closed me round about. Jonah ii. 5.
But now thou dost thyself immure and close In some one corner of a feeble heart. Herbert.

Close.etym: [From OF. & F. clos, p. p. of clore to close, fr. L. claudere; akin to G. schliessen to shut, and to E. clot, cloister, clavicle, conclude, sluice. Cf. Clause, n.]

senses.d: To come together; to unite or coalesce, as the parts of a wound, or parts separated.
q: What deep wounds ever closed without a scar? Byron.

senses.d: To end, terminate, or come to a period; as, the debate closed at six o'clock.
To grapple; to engage in hand-to-hand fight.
q: They boldly closed in a hand-to-hand contest. Prescott.

senses.d: The manner of shutting; the union of parts; junction.
q: The doors of plank were; their close exquisite. Chapman.

senses.d: Conclusion; cessation; ending; end.
q: His long and troubled life was drawing to a close. Macaulay.

senses.d: A grapple in wrestling.
The conclusion of a strain of music; cadence.
q: At every close she made, the attending throng Replied, and bore the burden of the song. Dryden.

Close.syn: Conclusion; termination; cessation; end; ending; extremity; extreme.

senses.d: An inclosed place; especially, a small field or piece of land surrounded by a wall, hedge, or fence of any kind; — specifically, the precinct of a cathedral or abbey.
q: Closes surrounded by the venerable abodes of deans and canons. Macaulay.

senses.d: A narrow passage leading from a street to a court, and the houses within.
The interest which one may have in a piece of ground, even though it is not inclosed.

Close.etym: [OF. & F. clos an inclosure, fr. clos, p. p. of clore. See Close, v. t.]

senses.d: Shut fast; closed; tight; as, a close box.
q: From a close bower this dainty music flowed. Dryden.

senses.d: Narrow; confined; as, a close alley; close quarters.
Oppressive; without motion or ventilation; causing a feeling of lassitude; — said of the air, weather, etc.
q: If the rooms be low-roofed, or full of windows and doors, the one maketh the air close, . . . and the other maketh it exceeding unequal. Bacon.

senses.d: Strictly confined; carefully quarded; as, a close prisoner.
Out of the way observation; secluded; secret; hidden.
q: “Her close intent.” Spenser.

senses.d: Disposed to keep secrets; secretive; reticent.
Having the parts near each other; dense; solid; compact; as applied to bodies; viscous; tenacious; not volatile, as applied to liquids.
q: The golden globe being put into a press, . . . the water made itself way through the pores of that very close metal. Locke.

senses.d: Concise; to the point; as, close reasoning.
Adjoining; near; either in space; time, or thought; — often followed by to.
q: Plant the spring crocuses close to a wall. Mortimer.
The thought of the Man of sorrows seemed a very close thing — not a faint hearsay. G. Eliot.

senses.d: Short; as, to cut grass or hair close.
Intimate; familiar; confidential.
q: League with you I seek And mutual amity, so strait, so close, That I with you must dwell, or you with me. Milton.

senses.d: Nearly equal; almost evenly balanced; as, a close vote.

Close.etym: [Of. & F. clos, p. p. of clore. See Close, v. t.]

senses.d: In a close manner.
Secretly; darkly.
q: A wondrous vision which did close imply The course of all her fortune and posterity. Spenser.

senses.d: One who, or that which, closes; specifically, a boot closer. See under Boot.
A finisher; that which finishes or terminates.
The last stone in a horizontal course, if of a less size than the others, or a piece of brick finishing a course.
A small room or apartment for retirement; a room for privacy.
q: A chair-lumbered closet, just twelve feet by nine. Goldsmith.
When thou prayest, enter into thy closet. Matt. vi. 6.

senses.d: A small apartment, or recess in the side of a room, for household utensils, clothing, etc.

Closet.etym: [OF. closet little inclosure, dim. of clos. See Close an inclosure.]

senses.d: To shut up in, or as in, a closet; to conceal.
q: Bedlam's closeted and handcuffed charge. Cowper.

senses.d: To make into a closet for a secret interview.
q: He was to call a new legislature, to closet its members. Bancroft.
He had been closeted with De Quadra. Froude.

senses.d: A fabric made of fibrous material (or sometimes of wire, as in wire cloth); commonly, a woven fabric of cotton, woolen, or linen, adapted to be made into garments; specifically, woolen fabrics, as distinguished from all others.
The dress; raiment. See Clothes.
q: I'll ne'er distrust my God for cloth and bread. Quarles.

senses.d: The distinctive dress of any profession, especially of the clergy; hence, the clerical profession.
q: Appeals were made to the priesthood. Would they tamely permit so gross an insult to be offered to their cloth? Macaulay.
The cloth, the clergy, are constituted for administering and for giving the best possible effect to . . . every axiom. I. Taylor.

Cloth.etym: [OE. clath cloth, AS. clāþ cloth, garment; akin to D. kleed, Icel. klæði, Dan. klæde, cloth, Sw. kläde, G. kleid garment, dress.]

senses.d: To put garments on; to cover with clothing; to dress.
q: Go with me, to clothe you as becomes you. Shak.

senses.d: To provide with clothes; as, to feed and clothe a family; to clothe one's self extravagantly.
q: Drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags. Prov. xxiii. 21.
The naked every day he clad, When he put on his clothes. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Fig.: To cover or invest, as with a garment; as, to clothe one with authority or power.
q: Language in which they can clothe their thoughts. Watts.
His sides are clothed with waving wood. J. Dyer.
Thus Belial, with with words clothed in reason's garb. Milton.

Clothe.etym: [OE. clathen, clothen, clethen, AS. clāðian, clæðan. See Cloth.]

senses.d: To wear clothes.
q: Care no more to clothe eat. Shak.

senses.d: Covering for the human body; dress; vestments; vesture; — a general term for whatever covering is worn, or is made to be worn, for decency or comfort.
q: She . . . speaks well, and has excellent good clothes. Shak.
If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole. Mark. v. 28.

senses.d: The covering of a bed; bedclothes.
q: She turned each way her frighted head, Then sunk it deep beneath the clothes. Prior.

Clothes.syn: Garments; dress; clothing; apparel; attire; vesture; raiment; garb; costume; habit; habiliments.

senses.d: Garments in general; clothes; dress; raiment; covering.
q: From others he shall stand in need of nothing, Yet on his brothers shall depend for clothing. Milton.
As for me, . . . my clothing was sackloth. Ps. xxxv. 13

senses.d: The art of process of making cloth.
q: Instructing in the art of clothing. Ray.

senses.d: A covering of non-conducting material on the outside of a boiler, or steam chamber, to prevent radiation of heat.
A collection of visible vapor, or watery particles, suspended in the upper atmosphere.
q: I do set my bow in the cloud. Gen. ix. 13.

senses.d: A mass or volume of smoke, or flying dust, resembling vapor.
A dark vein or spot on a lighter material, as in marble; hence, a blemish or defect; as, a cloud upon one's reputation; a cloud on a title.
That which has a dark, lowering, or threatening aspect; that which temporarily overshadows, obscures, or depresses; as, a cloud of sorrow; a cloud of war; a cloud upon the intellect.
A great crowd or multitude; a vast collection.
A large, loosely-knitted scarf, worn by women about the head.

Cloud.etym: [Prob. fr. AS. clūd a rock or hillock, the application arising from the frequent resemblance of clouds to rocks or hillocks in the sky or air.]

senses.d: To overspread or hide with a cloud or clouds; as, the sky is clouded.
To darken or obscure, as if by hiding or enveloping with a cloud; hence, to render gloomy or sullen.
q: One day too late, I fear me, noble lord, Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth. Shak.
Be not disheartened, then, nor cloud those looks. Milton.
Nothing clouds men's minds and impairs their honesty like prejudice. M. Arnold.

senses.d: To blacken; to sully; to stain; to tarnish; to damage; — esp. used of reputation or character.
q: I would not be a stander-by to hear My sovereign mistress clouded so, without My present vengeance taken. Shak.

senses.d: To mark with, or darken in, veins or sports; to variegate with colors; as, to cloud yarn.
q: And the nice conduct of a clouded cane. Pope.

senses.d: To grow cloudy; to become obscure with clouds; — often used with up.
q: Worthies, away! The scene begins to cloud. Shak.

senses.d: Overcast or obscured with clouds; clouded; as, a cloudy sky.
Consisting of a cloud or clouds.
q: As Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended. Ex. xxxiii. 9

senses.d: Indicating gloom, anxiety, sullenness, or ill-nature; not open or cheerful.
Confused; indistinct; obscure; dark.
q: Cloudy and confused notions of things. Watts.

senses.d: Lacking clearness, brightness, or luster.
Marked with veins or sports of dark or various hues, as marble.
A cloth; a piece of cloth or leather; a patch; a rag.
q: His garments, nought but many ragged clouts, With thorns together pinned and patched was. Spenser.
A clout upon that head where late the diadem stood. Shak.

senses.d: A swadding cloth.
A piece; a fragment.
The center of the butt at which archers shoot; — probably once a piece of white cloth or a nail head.
q: A'must shoot nearer or he'll ne'er hit the clout. Shak.

senses.d: An iron plate on an axletree or other wood to keep it from wearing; a washer.
A blow with the hand.

Clout.etym: [AS. clūt a little cloth, piece of metal; cf. Sw. klut, Icel. klūtr a kerchief, or W. clwt a clout, Gael. clud.]

senses.d: To cover with cloth, leather, or other material; to bandage; patch, or mend, with a clout.
q: And old shoes and clouted upon their feet. Josh. ix. 5.
Paul, yea, and Peter, too, had more skill in . . . clouting an old tent than to teach lawyers. Latimer.

senses.d: To join or patch clumsily.
q: If fond Bavius vent his clouted song. P. Fletcher

senses.d: To quard with an iron plate, as an axletree.
To give a blow to; to strike.
q: The . . . queen of Spain took off one of her chopines and clouted Olivarez about the noddle with it. Howell.

senses.d: To stud with nails, as a timber, or a boot sole.

Clout.etym: [OE. clutien. clouten, to patch. See Clout, n.]

senses.d: from Cleave, v. t.
A number of things of the same kind growing together; a bunch.
q: Her deeds were like great clusters of ripe grapes, Which load the bunches of the fruitful vine. Spenser.

senses.d: A number of similar things collected together or lying contiguous; a group; as, a cluster of islands.
A number of individuals grouped together or collected in one place; a crowd; a mob.
q: As bees . . . Pour forth their populous youth about the hive In clusters. Milton.
We loved him; but, like beasts And cowardly nobles, gave way unto your clusters, Who did hoot him out o' the city. Shak.

Cluster.etym: [AS. cluster, clyster; cf. LG. kluster (also Sw. & Dan. klase a cluster of grapes, D. klissen to be entangled?.)]

senses.d: To grow in clusters or assemble in groups; to gather or unite in a cluster or clusters.
q: His sunny hair Cluster'd about his temples, like a god's. Tennyson.
The princes of the country clustering together. Foxe.

senses.d: To collect into a cluster or clusters; to gather into a bunch or close body.
q: Not less the bee would range her cells, . . . The foxglove cluster dappled bells. Tennyson.
Or from the forest falls the clustered snow. Thomson.

senses.d: A thoroughly charred, and extinguished or still ignited, fragment from wood or other combustible substance; charcoal.

A black, or brownish black, solid, combustible substance, dug from beds or veins in the earth to be used for fuel, and consisting, like charcoal, mainly of carbon, but more compact, and often affording, when heated, a large amount of volatile matter.

Coal.etym: [AS. col; akin to D. kool, OHG. chol, cholo, G. kohle, Icel. kol, pl., Sw. kol, Dan. kul; cf. Skr. jval to burn. Cf. Kiln, Collier.]

senses.d: To burn to charcoal; to char.
q: Charcoal of roots, coaled into great pieces. Bacon.

senses.d: To mark or delineate with charcoal.
To supply with coal; as, to coal a steamer.
To take in coal; as, the steamer coaled at Southampton.
The side of a thing.
The exterior line, limit, or border of a country; frontier border.
q: From the river, the river Euphrates, even to the uttermost sea, shall your coast be. Deut. xi. 24.

senses.d: The seashore, or land near it.
q: He sees in English ships the Holland coast. Dryden.
We the Arabian coast do know At distance, when the species blow. Waller.

Coast.etym: [OF. coste, F. côte, rib, hill, shore, coast, L. costa rib, side. Cf. Accost, v. t., Cutlet.]

senses.d: To draw or keep near; to approach.
q: Anon she hears them chant it lustily, And all in haste she coasteth to the cry. Shak.

senses.d: To sail by or near the shore.
q: The ancients coasted only in their navigation. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: To sail from port to port in the same country.
To slide down hill; to slide on a sled, upon snow or ice.

Coast.etym: [OE. costien, costeien, costen, OF. costier, costoier, F. côtoyer, fr. Of. coste coast, F. côte. See Coast, n.]

senses.d: To draw near to; to approach; to keep near, or by the side of.
To sail by or near; to follow the coast line of.
q: Nearchus, . . . not knowing the compass, was fain to coast that shore. Sir T. Browne.

senses.d: To conduct along a coast or river bank.
q: The Indians . . . coasted me along the river. Hakluyt.

senses.d: An outer garment fitting the upper part of the body; especially, such a garment worn by men.
q: Let each His adamantine coat gird well. Milton.

senses.d: A petticoat.
The habit or vesture of an order of men, indicating the order or office; cloth.
q: Men of his coat should be minding their prayers. Swift.
She was sought by spirits of richest coat. Shak.

senses.d: An external covering like a garment, as fur, skin, wool, husk, or bark; as, the horses coats were sleek.
q: Fruit of all kinds, in coat Rough or smooth rined, or bearded husk, or shell. Milton.

senses.d: A layer of any substance covering another; a cover; a tegument; as, the coats of the eye; the coats of an onion; a coat of tar or varnish.
Same as Coat of arms. See below.
q: Hark, countrymen! either renew the fight, Or tear the lions out of England's coat. Shak.

senses.d: A coat card. See below.
q: Here's a trick of discarded cards of us! We were ranked with coats as long as old master lived. Massinger.

Coat.etym: [OF. cote, F. cotte, petticoat, cotte d'armes coat of arms, cotte de mailles coat of mail, LL. cota, cotta, tunic, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. chozzo coarse mantle, G. klotze, D. kot, hut, E. cot. Cf. Cot a hut.]

senses.d: To cover with a coat or outer garment.
To cover with a layer of any substance; as, to coat a jar with tin foil; to coat a ceiling.
The male of birds, particularly of gallinaceous or domestic fowls.
A vane in the shape of a cock; a weathercock.
q: Drenched our steeples, drowned the cocks! Shak.

senses.d: A chief man; a leader or master.
q: Sir Andrew is the cock of the club, since he left us. Addison.

senses.d: The crow of a cock, esp. the first crow in the morning; cockcrow.
q: He begins at curfew, and walks till the first cock. Shak.

senses.d: A faucet or valve.
The style of gnomon of a dial.
The indicator of a balance.
The bridge piece which affords a bearing for the pivot of a balance in a clock or watch.

Cock.etym: [AS. coc; of unknown origin, perh. in imitation of the cry of the cock. Cf. Chicken.]

senses.d: To set erect; to turn up.
q: Our Lightfoot barks, and cocks his ears. Gay.
Dick would cock his nose in scorn. Swift.

senses.d: To shape, as a hat, by turning up the brim.
To set on one side in a pert or jaunty manner.
q: They cocked their hats in each other's faces. Macaulay.

senses.d: To turn (the eye) obliquely and partially close its lid, as an expression of derision or insinuation.
To strut; to swagger; to look big, pert, or menacing.
The act of cocking; also, the turn so given; as, a cock of the eyes; to give a hat a saucy cock.
The notch of an arrow or crossbow.
The hammer in the lock of a firearm.
To draw the hammer of (a firearm) fully back and set it for firing.
To draw back the hammer of a firearm, and set it for firing.
q: Cocked, fired, and missed his man. Byron.

senses.d: A small concial pile of hay.

Cock.etym: [Cf. Icel. kökkr lump, Dan. kok heap, or E. cock to set erect.]

senses.d: To put into cocks or heaps, as hay.
q: Under the cocked hay. Spenser.

senses.d: A small boat.
q: Yond tall anchoring bark Diminished to her cock; her cock, a buoy Almost too small for sight. Shak.

Cock.etym: [Of. coque, F. coche, a small vessel, L. concha muscle shell, a vessel. See Coach, and cf. Cog a small boat.]

senses.d: A corruption or disguise of the word God, used in oaths.
A fabulous serpent whose breath and look were said to be fatal. See Basilisk.
q: That bare vowel, I, shall poison more Than the death-darting eye of cockatrice. Shak.
