senses.d: A representation of this serpent. It has the head, wings, and legs of a bird, and tail of a serpent.
A venomous serpent which which cannot now be identified.
q: The weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice's [Rev. Ver. basilisk's] den. Is. xi. 8.

senses.d: Any venomous or deadly thing.
q: This little cockatrice of a king. Bacon.

Cockatrice.etym: [OF. cocatrice crocodile, F. cocatrix, cocatrice. The word is a corruption from the same source as E. crocodile, but was confused with cock the bird, F. coq, whence arose the fable that the animal was produced from a cock's egg. See Crocodile.]

senses.d: The time at which cocks first crow; the early morning.
A bivalve mollusk, with radiating ribs, of the genus Cardium, especially C. edule, used in Europe for food; — sometimes applied to similar shells of other genera.
A cockleshell.
The mineral black tourmaline or schorl; — so called by the Cornish miners.
The fire chamber of a furnace.
A hop-drying kiln; an oast.
The dome of a heating furnace.

Cockle.etym: [OE. cockes cockles, AS. sǣcoccas sea cockles, prob, from Celtic; cf. W. cocs cockles, Gael. cochull husk. Perh. influenced by F. coquille shell, a dim. from the root of E. conch. Cf. Coach.]

senses.d: To cause to contract into wrinkles or ridges, as some kinds of cloth after a wetting.
A plant or weed that grows among grain; the corn rose (Luchnis Githage).
The Lotium, or darnel.

Cockle.etym: [AS. coccel, cocel; cf. Gael. cogall tares, husks, cockle.]

senses.d: A casket, chest, or trunk; especially, one used for keeping money or other valuables.
q: In ivory coffers I have stuffed my crowns. Shak.

senses.d: Fig.: Treasure or funds; — usually in the plural.
q: He would discharge it without any burden to the queen's coffers, for honor sake. Bacon.
Hold, here is half my coffer. Shak.

senses.d: A panel deeply recessed in the ceiling of a vault, dome, or portico; a caisson.
A trench dug in the bottom of a dry moat, and extending across it, to enable the besieged to defend it by a raking fire.
The chamber of a canal lock; also, a caisson or a cofferdam.

Coffer.etym: [OF. cofre, F. coffre, L. cophinus basket, fr. Gr. �. Cf. Coffin, n.]

senses.d: To put into a coffer.
To secure from leaking, as a shaft, by ramming clay behind the masonry or timbering.
To form with or in a coffer or coffers; to furnish with a coffer or coffers.
The case in which a dead human body is inclosed for burial.
q: They embalmed him , and he was put in a coffin. Gen. 1. 26.

senses.d: A basket.
A casing or crust, or a mold, of pastry, as for a pie.
q: Of the paste a coffin I will rear. Shak.

senses.d: A conical paper bag, used by grocers.
The hollow crust or hoof of a horse's foot, below the coronet, in which is the coffin bone.

Coffin.etym: [OE., a basket, receptacle, OF. cofin, fr. L. cophinus. See Coffer, n.]

senses.d: To inclose in, or as in, a coffin.
q: Would'st thou have laughed, had I come coffined home? Shak.
Devotion is not coffined in a cell. John Hall (1646).

senses.d: The act of thinking; thought; meditation; contemplation.
A short ridge connecting two higher elevations or mountains; the pass over such a ridge.
Deprived of heat, or having a low temperature; not warm or hot; gelid; frigid.
Lacking the sensation of warmth; suffering from the absence of heat; chilly; shivering; as, to be cold.
Not pungent or acrid.
Wanting in ardor, intensity, warmth, zeal, or passion; spiritless; unconcerned; reserved.
q: A cold and unconcerned spectator. T. Burnet.
No cold relation is a zealous citizen. Burke.

senses.d: Unwelcome; disagreeable; unsatisfactory.
Wanting in power to excite; dull; uninteresting.
q: What a deal of cold business doth a man misspend the better part of life in! B. Jonson.
The jest grows cold . . . when in comes on in a second scene. Addison.

senses.d: Affecting the sense of smell (as of hunting dogs) but feebly; having lost its odor; as, a cold scent.
Not sensitive; not acute.
q: Smell this business with a sense as cold As is a dead man's nose. Shak.

senses.d: Distant; — said, in the game of hunting for some object, of a seeker remote from the thing concealed.
Having a bluish effect. Cf. Warm, 8.

Cold.syn: Gelid; bleak; frigid; chill; indifferent; unconcerned; passionless; reserved; unfeeling; stoical.
Cold.etym: [OE. cold, cald, AS. cald, ceald; akin to OS. kald, D. koud, G. kalt, Icel. kaldr, Dan. kold, Sw. kall, Goth. kalds, L. gelu frost, gelare to freeze. Orig. p. p. of AS. calan to be cold, Icel. kala to freeze. Cf. Cool, a., Chill, n.]

senses.d: The relative absence of heat or warmth.
The sensation produced by the escape of heat; chilliness or chillness.
q: When she saw her lord prepared to part, A deadly cold ran shivering to her heart. Dryden.

senses.d: A morbid state of the animal system produced by exposure to cold or dampness; a catarrh.
To become cold.
Something worn round the neck, whether for use, ornament, restraint, or identification; as, the collar of a coat; a lady's collar; the collar of a dog.
A ring or cincture.
The neck or line of junction between the root of a plant and its stem.
An ornament worn round the neck by knights, having on it devices to designate their rank or order.
A ringlike part of a mollusk in connection with esophagus.

A ring or round flange upon, surrounding, or against an object, and used for restraining motion within given limits, or for holding something to its place, or for hiding an opening around an object; as, a collar on a shaft, used to prevent endwise motion of the shaft; a collar surrounding a stovepipe at the place where it enters a wall. The flanges of a piston and the gland of a stuffing box are sometimes called collars.
An eye formed in the bight or bend of a shroud or stay to go over the masthead; also, a rope to which certain parts of rigging, as dead-eyes, are secured.
A curb, or a horizontal timbering, around the mouth of a shaft.

Collar.etym: [OE. coler, coller, OF. colier, F. collier, necklace, collar, fr. OF. col neck, F. cou, fr. L. collum; akin to AS. heals, G. & Goth. hals. Cf. Hals, n.]

senses.d: To seize by the collar.
To put a collar on.
The act or process of collecting or of gathering; as, the collection of specimens.
That which is collected
The act of inferring or concluding from premises or observed facts; also, that which is inferred.
q: We may safely say thus, that wrong collections have been hitherto made out of those words by modern divines. Milton.

senses.d: The jurisdiction of a collector of excise.

Collection.syn: Gathering; assembly; assemblage; group; crowd; congregation; mass; heap; compilation.

senses.d: A collection, body, or society of persons engaged in common pursuits, or having common duties and interests, and sometimes, by charter, peculiar rights and privileges; as, a college of heralds; a college of electors; a college of bishops.
q: The college of the cardinals. Shak.
Then they made colleges of sufferers; persons who, to secure their inheritance in the world to come, did cut off all their portion in this. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: A society of scholars or friends of learning, incorporated for study or instruction, esp. in the higher branches of knowledge; as, the colleges of Oxford and Cambridge Universities, and many American colleges.
A building, or number of buildings, used by a college.
Fig.: A community.
q: Thick as the college of the bees in May. Dryden.

College.etym: [F. collège, L. collegium, fr. collega colleague. See Colleague.]

senses.d: A small slice of meat; a piece of flesh.
q: God knows thou art a collop of my flesh. Shak.
Sweetbread and collops were with skewers pricked. Dryden.

senses.d: A part or piece of anything; a portion.
q: Cut two good collops out of the crown land. Fuller.

Collop.etym: [Of uncertain origin; cf. OF. colp blow, stroke, piece, F. coup, fr. L. colophus buffet, cuff, Gr. �]

senses.d: A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state; as, the British colonies in America.
q: The first settlers of New England were the best of Englishmen, well educated, devout Christians, and zealous lovers of liberty. There was never a colony formed of better materials. Ames.

senses.d: The district or country colonized; a settlement.
A company of persons from the same country sojourning in a foreign city or land; as, the American colony in Paris.
A number of animals or plants living or growing together, beyond their usual range.

Colony.etym: [L. colonia, fr. colonus farmer, fr. colere to cultivate, dwell: cf. F. colonie. Cf. Culture.]

senses.d: A cell family or group of common origin, mostly of unicellular organisms, esp. among the lower algæ. They may adhere in chains or groups, or be held together by a gelatinous envelope.
A cluster or aggregation of zooids of any compound animal, as in the corals, hydroids, certain tunicates, etc.
A community of social insects, as ants, bees, etc.
The young of the equine genus or horse kind of animals; — sometimes distinctively applied to the male, filly being the female. Cf. Foal.
A young, foolish fellow.
A short knotted rope formerly used as an instrument of punishment in the navy.

Colt.etym: [OE. colt a young horse, ass, or camel, AS. colt; cf. dial. Sw. kullt a boy, lad.]

senses.d: To frisk or frolic like a colt; to act licentiously or wantonly.
q: They shook off their bridles and began to colt. Spenser.

senses.d: To horse; to get with young.
To befool.
To move hitherward; to draw near; to approach the speaker, or some place or person indicated; — opposed to go.
q: Look, who comes yonder? Shak.
I did not come to curse thee. Tennyson.

senses.d: To complete a movement toward a place; to arrive.
q: When we came to Rome. Acts xxviii. 16.
Lately come from Italy. Acts xviii. 2.

senses.d: To approach or arrive, as if by a journey or from a distance.
q: The hour is coming, and now is. John. v. 25.
So quick bright things come to confusion. Shak.

senses.d: To approach or arrive, as the result of a cause, or of the act of another.
q: From whence come wars? James iv. 1.
Both riches and honor come of thee ! 1 Chron. xxix. 12.

senses.d: To arrive in sight; to be manifest; to appear.
q: Then butter does refuse to come. Hudibras.

senses.d: To get to be, as the result of change or progress; — with a predicate; as, to come untied.
q: How come you thus estranged? Shak.
How come her eyes so bright? Shak.
Think not that I am come to destroy. Matt. v. 17.
We are come off like Romans. Shak.
The melancholy days are come, the saddest of the year. Bryant.

Come.etym: [OE. cumen, comen, AS. cuman; akin to OS. kuman, D. komen, OHG. queman, G. kommen, Icel. koma, Sw. komma, Dan. komme, Goth. giman, L. venire (gvenire), Gr. � to go, Skr. gam. √23. Cf. Base, n., Convene, Adventure.]

senses.d: To carry through; to succeed in; as, you can't come any tricks here.
Coming.
The quality or state of being comely.
q: Comeliness is a disposing fair Of things and actions in fit time and place. Sir J. Davies.
Strength, comeliness of shape, or amplest merit. Milton.
Comeliness signifies something less forcible than beauty, less elegant than grace, and less light than prettiness. Johnson.

senses.d: Pleasing or agreeable to the sight; well-proportioned; good-looking; handsome.
q: He that is comely when old and decrepit, surely was very beautiful when he was young. South.
Not once perceive their foul disfigurement But boast themselves more comely than before. Milton.

senses.d: Suitable or becoming; proper; agreeable.
q: This is a happier and more comely time Than when these fellows ran about the streets, Crying confusion. Shak.
It is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely. Ps. cxlvii. 1.

Comely.etym: [OE. comeliche, AS. cymlīc; cyme suitable (fr. cuman to come, become) + līc like.]

senses.d: In a becoming manner.
One who comes, or who has come; one who has arrived, and is present.
To make strong; to invigorate; to fortify; to corroborate.
q: God's own testimony . . . doth not a little comfort and confirm the same. Hooker.

senses.d: To assist or help; to aid.
q: I . . . can not help the noble chevalier: God comfort him in this necessity! Shak.

senses.d: To impart strength and hope to; to encourage; to relieve; to console; to cheer.
q: Light excelleth in comforting the spirits of men. Bacon.
That we may be able to comfort them that are in any affliction. 2 Cor. i. 4 (Rev. Ver.).
A perfect woman, nobly planned, To warn, to comfort, and command. Wordsworth.

Comfort.syn: To cheer; solace; console; revive; encourage; enliven; invigorate; inspirit; gladden; recreate; exhilarate; refresh; animate; confirm; strengthen.
Comfort.etym: [F. conforter, fr. L. confortare to strengthen much; con- + fortis strong. See Fort.]

senses.d: Assistance; relief; support.
Encouragement; solace; consolation in trouble; also, that which affords consolation.
q: In comfort of her mother's fears. Shak.
Cheer thy spirit with this comfort. Shak.
Speaking words of endearment where words of comfort availed not. Longfellow.

senses.d: A state of quiet enjoyment; freedom from pain, want, or anxiety; also, whatever contributes to such a condition.
q: I had much joy and comfort in thy love. Phil. 7 (Rev. Ver.).
He had the means of living in comfort. Macaulay.

senses.d: A wadded bedquilt; a comfortable.
Unlawful support, countenance, or encouragement; as, to give aid and comfort to the enemy.
Strong; vigorous; valiant.
q: Thy conceit is nearer death than thy powers. For my sake be comfortable; hold death a while at the arm's end. Shak.

senses.d: Serviceable; helpful.
q: Be comfortable to my mother, your mistress, and make much of her. Shak.

senses.d: Affording or imparting comfort or consolation; able to comfort; cheering; as, a comfortable hope.
q: A comfortable provision made for their subsistence. Dryden.

senses.d: In a condition of comfort; having comforts; not suffering or anxious; hence, contented; cheerful; as, to lead a comfortable life.
q: My lord leans wondrously to discontent; His comfortable temper has forsook him: He is much out of health. Shak.

senses.d: Free, or comparatively free, from pain or distress; — used of a sick person.
A stuffed or quilted coverlet for a bed; a comforter; a comfort.
In a comfortable or comforting manner.
q: Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem. Is. xl. 2.

senses.d: One who administers comfort or consolation.
q: Let no comforter delight mine ear But such a one whose wrongs do suit with mine. Shak.

senses.d: The Holy Spirit, — referring to his office of comforting believers.
q: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things. John xiv. 26.

senses.d: A knit woolen tippet, long and narrow.
q: The American schoolboy takes off his comforter and unbuttons his jacket before going in for a snowball fight. Pop. Sci. Monthly.

senses.d: A wadded bedquilt; a comfortable.
Without comfort or comforts; in want or distress; cheerless.
q: Comfortless through tyranny or might. Spenser.
When all is coldly, comfortlessly costly. Milton.

Comfortless.syn: Forlorn; desolate; cheerless; inconsolable; disconsolate; wretched; miserable.

senses.d: Approaching; of the future, especially the near future; the next; as, the coming week or year; the coming exhibition.
q: Welcome the coming, speed the parting, guest. Pope.
Your coming days and years. Byron.

senses.d: Ready to come; complaisant; fond.
Approach; advent; manifestation; as, the coming of the train.
Specifically: The Second Advent of Christ.
To order with authority; to lay injunction upon; to direct; to bid; to charge.
q: We are commanded to forgive our enemies, but you never read that we are commanded to forgive our friends. Bacon.
Go to your mistress: Say, I command her come to me. Shak.

senses.d: To exercise direct authority over; to have control of; to have at one's disposal; to lead.
q: Monmouth commanded the English auxiliaries. Macaulay.
Such aid as I can spare you shall command. Shak.

senses.d: To have within a sphere of control, influence, access, or vision; to dominate by position; to guard; to overlook.
q: Bridges commanded by a fortified house. Motley.
Up to the eastern tower, Whose height commands as subject all the vale. Shak.
One side commands a view of the finest garden. Addison.

senses.d: To have power or influence of the nature of authority over; to obtain as if by ordering; to receive as a due; to challenge; to claim; as, justice commands the respect and affections of the people; the best goods command the best price.
q: 'Tis not in mortals to command success. Addison.

senses.d: To direct to come; to bestow.
q: I will command my blessing upon you. Lev. xxv. 21.

Command.syn: To bid; order; direct; dictate; charge; govern; rule; overlook.
Command.etym: [OE. comaunden, commanden, OF. comander, F. commander, fr. L. com- + mandare to commit to, to command. Cf. Commend, Mandate.]

senses.d: To have or to exercise direct authority; to govern; to sway; to influence; to give an order or orders.
q: And reigned, commanding in his monarchy. Shak.
For the king had so commanded concerning . Esth. iii. 2.

senses.d: To have a view, as from a superior position.
q: Far and wide his eye commands. Milton.

senses.d: An authoritative order requiring obedience; a mandate; an injunction.
q: Awaiting what command their mighty chief Had to impose. Milton.

senses.d: The possession or exercise of authority.
q: Command and force may often create, but can never cure, an aversion. Locke.

senses.d: Authority; power or right of control; leadership; as, the forces under his command.
Power to dominate, command, or overlook by means of position; scope of vision; survey.
q: The steepy stand Which overlooks the vale with wide command. Dryden.

senses.d: Control; power over something; sway; influence; as, to have command over one's temper or voice; the fort has command of the bridge.
q: He assumed an absolute command over his readers. Dryden.

senses.d: A body of troops, or any naval or military force or post, or the whole territory under the authority or control of a particular officer.

Command.syn: Control; sway; power; authority; rule; dominion; sovereignty; mandate; order; injunction; charge; behest. See Direction.

senses.d: A chief; one who has supreme authority; a leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.
q: A leader and commander to the people. Is. lv. 4.

senses.d: An officer who ranks next below a captain, — ranking with a lieutenant colonel in the army.
The chief officer of a commandery.
A heavy beetle or wooden mallet, used in paving, in sail lofts, etc.
Exercising authority; actually in command; as, a commanding officer.
Fitted to impress or control; as, a commanding look or presence.
Exalted; overlooking; having superior strategic advantages; as, a commanding position.
An order or injunction given by authority; a command; a charge; a precept; a mandate.
q: A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another. John xiii. 34.

senses.d: One of the ten laws or precepts given by God to the Israelites at Mount Sinai.
The act of commanding; exercise of authority.
q: And therefore put I on the countenance Of stern commandment. Shak.

senses.d: The offense of commanding or inducing another to violate the law.
To commit, intrust, or give in charge for care or preservation.
q: His eye commends the leading to his hand. Shak.
Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. Luke xxiii. 46.

senses.d: To recommend as worthy of confidence or regard; to present as worthy of notice or favorable attention.
q: Among the objects of knowledge, two especially commend themselves to our contemplation. Sir M. Hale.
I commend unto you Phebe our sister. Rom. xvi. 1.

senses.d: To mention with approbation; to praise; as, to commend a person or an act.
q: Historians commend Alexander for weeping when he read the actions of Achilles. Dryden.

senses.d: To mention by way of courtesy, implying remembrance and good will.
q: Commend me to my brother. Shak.

Commend.etym: [L. commendare; com- + mandare to intrust to one's charge, enjoin, command. Cf. Command, Mandate.]

senses.d: Commendation; praise.
q: Speak in his just commend. Shak.

senses.d: Compliments; greetings.
q: Hearty commends and much endeared love to you. Howell.

senses.d: The act of commending; praise; favorable representation in words; recommendation.
q: Need we . . . epistles of commendation? 2 Cor. iii. 1.
By the commendation of the great officers. Bacon.

senses.d: That which is the ground of approbation or praise.
q: Good nature is the most godlike commendation of a man. Dryden.

senses.d: A message of affection or respect; compliments; greeting.
q: Hark you, Margaret; No princely commendations to my king? Shak.

senses.d: The act of committing, doing, or performing; the act of perpetrating.
q: Every commission of sin introduces into the soul a certain degree of hardness. South.

senses.d: The act of intrusting; a charge; instructions as to how a trust shall be executed.
The duty or employment intrusted to any person or persons; a trust; a charge.
A formal written warrant or authority, granting certain powers or privileges and authorizing or commanding the performance of certain duties.
q: Let him see our commission. Shak.

senses.d: A certificate conferring military or naval rank and authority; as, a colonel's commission.
A company of persons joined in the performance of some duty or the execution of some trust; as, the interstate commerce commission.
q: A commission was at once appointed to examine into the matter. Prescott.

senses.d: The acting under authority of, or on account of, another.

Commission.syn: Charge; warrant; authority; mandate; office; trust; employment.

senses.d: To give a commission to; to furnish with a commission; to empower or authorize; as, to commission persons to perform certain acts; to commission an officer.
To send out with a charge or commission.
q: A chosen band He first commissions to the Latian land. Dryden.

Commission.syn: To appoint; depute; authorize; empower; delegate; constitute; ordain.

senses.d: To give in trust; to put into charge or keeping; to intrust; to consign; — used with to, unto.
q: Commit thy way unto the Lord. Ps. xxxvii. 5.
Bid him farewell, commit him to the grave. Shak.

senses.d: To put in charge of a jailor; to imprison.
q: These two were committed. Clarendon.

senses.d: To do; to perpetrate, as a crime, sin, or fault.
q: Thou shalt not commit adultery. Ex. xx. 14.

senses.d: To join for a contest; to match; — followed by with.
To pledge or bind; to compromise, expose, or endanger by some decisive act or preliminary step; — often used reflexively; as, to commit one's self to a certain course.
q: You might have satisfied every duty of political friendship, without commiting the honor of your sovereign. Junius.
Any sudden assent to the proposal . . . might possibly be considered as committing the faith of the United States. Marshall.

senses.d: To confound.
q: Committing short and long . Milton.

Commit.etym: [L. committere, commissum, to connect, commit; com- + mittere to send. See Mission.]

senses.d: To sin; esp., to be incontinent.
q: Commit not with man's sworn spouse. Shak.

senses.d: Adapted to its use or purpose, or to wants and necessities; serviceable; spacious and convenient; roomy and comfortable; as, a commodious house.
q: The haven was not commodious to winter in. Acts xxvii. 12.

Commodious.syn: Convenient; suitable; fit; proper; advantageous; serviceable; useful; spacious; comfortable.
Commodious.etym: [LL. commodiosus, fr. L. commodum convenience, fr. commodus. See Commode.]

senses.d: Belonging or relating equally, or similarly, to more than one; as, you and I have a common interest in the property.
q: Though life and sense be common to men and brutes. Sir M. Hale.

senses.d: Belonging to or shared by, affecting or serving, all the members of a class, considered together; general; public; as, properties common to all plants; the common schools; the Book of Common Prayer.
q: Such actions as the common good requireth. Hooker.
The common enemy of man. Shak.

senses.d: Often met with; usual; frequent; customary.
q: Grief more than common grief. Shak.

senses.d: Not distinguished or exceptional; inconspicuous; ordinary; plebeian; — often in a depreciatory sense.
q: The honest, heart-felt enjoyment of common life. W. Irving.
This fact was infamous And ill beseeming any common man, Much more a knight, a captain and a leader. Shak.
Above the vulgar flight of common souls. A. Murphy.

senses.d: Profane; polluted.
q: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Acts x. 15.

senses.d: Given to habits of lewdness; prostitute.
q: A dame who herself was common. L'Estrange.

Common.syn: General; public; popular; national; universal; frequent; ordinary; customary; usual; familiar; habitual; vulgar; mean; trite; stale; threadbare; commonplace. See Mutual, Ordinary, General.
Common.etym: [OE. commun, comon, OF. comun, F. commun, fr. L. communis; com- + munis ready to be of service; cf. Skr. mi to make fast, set up, build, Goth. gamains common, G. gemein, and E. mean low, common. Cf. Immunity, Commune, n. & v.]

senses.d: The people; the community.
An inclosed or uninclosed tract of ground for pleasure, for pasturage, etc., the use of which belongs to the public; or to a number of persons.

The right of taking a profit in the land of another, in common either with the owner or with other persons; — so called from the community of interest which arises between the claimant of the right and the owner of the soil, or between the claimants and other commoners entitled to the same right.
To converse together; to discourse; to confer.
q: Embassadors were sent upon both parts, and divers means of entreaty were commoned of. Grafton.

senses.d: To participate.
To have a joint right with others in common ground.
To board together; to eat at a table in common.
Usually; generally; ordinarily; frequently; for the most part; as, confirmed habits commonly continue through life.
In common; familiarly.
Commonwealth.
q: Such a prince, So kind a father of the commonweal. Shak.

senses.d: A state; a body politic consisting of a certain number of men, united, by compact or tacit agreement, under one form of government and system of laws.
q: The trappings of a monarchy would set up an ordinary commonwealth. Milton.

senses.d: The whole body of people in a state; the public.
Specifically, the form of government established on the death of Charles I., in 1649, which existed under Oliver Cromwell and his son Richard, ending with the abdication of the latter in 1659.
Disturbed or violent motion; agitation.
q: commotion in the winds ! Shak.

senses.d: A popular tumult; public disturbance; riot.
q: When ye shall hear of wars and commotions. Luke xxi. 9.

senses.d: Agitation, perturbation, or disorder, of mind; heat; excitement.

Commotion.syn: Excitement; agitation; perturbation; disturbance; tumult; disorder; violence.
Commotion.etym: [L. commotio: cf. F. commotion. See Motion.]

senses.d: To converse together with sympathy and confidence; to interchange sentiments or feelings; to take counsel.
q: I would commune with you of such things That want no ear but yours. Shak.

senses.d: To receive the communion; to partake of the eucharist or Lord's supper.
q: To commune under both kinds. Bp. Burnet.

Commune.etym: [OF. communier, fr. L. communicare to communicate, fr. communis common. See Common, and cf. Communicate.]

senses.d: Communion; sympathetic intercourse or conversation between friends.
q: For days of happy commune dead. Tennyson.

senses.d: The commonalty; the common people.
q: In this struggle — to use the technical words of the time — of the “commune”, the general mass of the inhabitants, against the “prudhommes” or “wiser” few. J. R. Green.

senses.d: A small territorial district in France under the government of a mayor and municipal council; also, the inhabitants, or the government, of such a district. See Arrondissement.
Absolute municipal self-government.
To share in common; to participate in.
q: To thousands that communicate our loss. B. Jonson

senses.d: To impart; to bestow; to convey; as, to communicate a disease or a sensation; to communicate motion by means of a crank.
q: Where God is worshiped, there he communicates his blessings and holy influences. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: To make known; to recount; to give; to impart; as, to communicate information to any one.
To administer the communion to.
q: She . . . may communicate him. Jer. Taylor.
He communicated those thoughts only with the Lord Digby. Clarendon.

Communicate.syn: To impart; bestow; confer; reveal; disclose; tell; announce; recount; make known.
Communicate.etym: [L. communicatus, p. p. of communicare to communicate, fr. communis common. See Commune, v. i.]

senses.d: To share or participate; to possess or enjoy in common; to have sympathy.
q: Ye did communicate with my affliction. Philip. iv. 4.

senses.d: To give alms, sympathy, or aid.
q: To do good and to communicate forget not. Heb. xiii. 16.

senses.d: To have intercourse or to be the means of intercourse; as, to communicate with another on business; to be connected; as, a communicating artery.
q: Subjects suffered to communicate and to have intercourse of traffic. Hakluyt.
The whole body is nothing but a system of such canals, which all communicate with one another. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: To partake of the Lord's supper; to commune.
q: The primitive Christians communicated every day. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: The act or fact of communicating; as, communication of smallpox; communication of a secret.
Intercourse by words, letters, or messages; interchange of thoughts or opinions, by conference or other means; conference; correspondence.
q: Argument . . . and friendly communication. Shak.

senses.d: Association; company.
q: Evil communications corrupt good manners. 1 Cor. xv. 33.

senses.d: Means of communicating; means of passing from place to place; a connecting passage; connection.
q: The Euxine Sea is conveniently situated for trade, by the communication it has both with Asia and Europe. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: That which is communicated or imparted; intelligence; news; a verbal or written message.
Participation in the Lord's supper.
A trope, by which a speaker assumes that his hearer is a partner in his sentiments, and says we, instead of I or you.
The act of sharing; community; participation.

Intercourse between two or more persons; esp., intimate association and intercourse implying sympathy and confidence; interchange of thoughts, purposes, etc.; agreement; fellowship; as, the communion of saints.
q: We are naturally induced to seek communion and fellowship with others. Hooker.
What communion hath light with darkness? 2 Cor. vi. 14.
Bare communion with a good church can never alone make a good man. South.

senses.d: A body of Christians having one common faith and discipline; as, the Presbyterian communion.
The sacrament of the eucharist; the celebration of the Lord's supper; the act of partaking of the sacrament; as, to go to communion; to partake of the communion.

Communion.syn: Share; participation; fellowship; converse; intercourse; unity; concord; agreement.
Communion.etym: [L. communio: cf. F. communion. See Common.]

senses.d: Joined or held together; leagued; confederated.
q: A pipe of seven reeds, compact with wax together. Peacham.

senses.d: Composed or made; — with of.
q: A wandering fire, Compact of unctuous vapor. Milton.

senses.d: Closely or firmly united, as the particles of solid bodies; firm; close; solid; dense.
q: Glass, crystal, gems, and other compact bodies. Sir I. Newton.

senses.d: Brief; close; pithy; not diffuse; not verbose; as, a compact discourse.

Compact.syn: Firm; close; solid; dense; pithy; sententious.
Compact.etym: [L. compactus, p. p. of compingere to join or unite; com- + pangere to fasten, fix: cf. F. compacte. See Pact.]

senses.d: To thrust, drive, or press closely together; to join firmly; to consolidate; to make close; — as the parts which compose a body.
q: Now the bright sun compacts the precious stone. Blackstone.

senses.d: To unite or connect firmly, as in a system.
q: The whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth. Eph. iv. 16.

senses.d: An agreement between parties; a covenant or contract.
q: The law of nations depends on mutual compacts, treaties, leagues, etc. Blackstone.
Wedlock is described as the indissoluble compact. Macaulay.
The federal constitution has been styled a compact between the States by which it was ratified. Wharton.

Compact.etym: [L. compactum, fr. compacisci, p. p. compactus, to make an agreement with; com- + pacisci to make an agreement. See Pact.]

senses.d: Compact; pressed close; concentrated; firmly united.

One who accompanies or is in company with another for a longer or shorter period, either from choice or casually; one who is much in the company of, or is associated with, another or others; an associate; a comrade; a consort; a partner.
q: The companions of his fall. Milton.
The companion of fools shall smart for it. Prov. xiii. 20 (Rev. Ver.).
Here are your sons again; and I must lose Two of the sweetest companions in the world. Shak.
A companion is one with whom we share our bread; a messmate. Trench.

senses.d: A knight of the lowest rank in certain orders; as, a companion of the Bath.
A fellow; — in contempt.
A skylight on an upper deck with frames and sashes of various shapes, to admit light to a cabin or lower deck.

Companion.syn: Associate; comrade; mate; compeer; partner; ally; confederate; coadjutor; accomplice.
Companion.etym: [F. compagnon, OF. compaing, fr. an assumed LL. companio (cf. companium fellowship, a mess), fr. L. com- + panis bread. See Pantry.]

senses.d: To be a companion to; to attend on; to accompany.
To qualify as a companion; to make equal.
q: Companion me with my mistress. Shak.

senses.d: The state of being a companion or companions; the act of accompanying; fellowship; companionship; society; friendly intercourse.
q: Evil company doth corrupt good manners. 1 Cor. xv. 33. (Rev. Ver.).
Brethren, farewell: your company along I will not wish. Milton.

senses.d: A companion or companions.
q: To thee and thy company I bid A hearty welcome. Shak.

senses.d: An assemblage or association of persons, either permanent or transient.
q: Thou shalt meet a company of prophets. 1 Sam. x. 5.

senses.d: Guests or visitors, in distinction from the members of a family; as, to invite company to dine.
Society, in general; people assembled for social intercourse.
q: Nature has left every man a capacity of being agreeable, though not of shining in company. Swift.

senses.d: An association of persons for the purpose of carrying on some enterprise or business; a corporation; a firm; as, the East India Company; an insurance company; a joint-stock company.
Partners in a firm whose names are not mentioned in its style or title; — often abbreviated in writing; as, Hottinguer & Co.
A subdivision of a regiment of troops under the command of a captain, numbering in the United States (full strength) 100 men.
The crew of a ship, including the officers; as, a whole ship's company.
The body of actors employed in a theater or in the production of a play.

Company.syn: Assemblage; assembly; society; group; circle; crowd; troop; crew; gang; corporation; association; fraternity; guild; partnership; copartnery; union; club; party; gathering.
Company.etym: [F. compagnie, fr. OF. compaing. See Companion.]

senses.d: To accompany or go with; to be companion to.
To associate.
q: Men which have companied with us all the time. Acts i. 21.

senses.d: To be a gay companion.
To have sexual commerce.
Capable of being compared; worthy of comparison.
q: There is no blessing of life comparable to the enjoyment of a discreet and virtuous friend. Addison.

senses.d: To examine the character or qualities of, as of two or more persons or things, for the purpose of discovering their resemblances or differences; to bring into comparison; to regard with discriminating attention.
q: Compare dead happiness with living woe. Shak.
The place he found beyond expression bright, Compared with aught on earth. Milton.
Compare our faces and be judge yourself. Shak.
To compare great things with small. Milton.

senses.d: To represent as similar, for the purpose of illustration; to liken.
q: Solon compared the people unto the sea, and orators and counselors to the winds; for that the sea would be calm and quiet if the winds did not trouble it. Bacon.

senses.d: To inflect according to the degrees of comparison; to state positive, comparative, and superlative forms of; as, most adjectives of one syllable are compared by affixing “- er” and “-est” to the positive form; as, black, blacker, blackest; those of more than one syllable are usually compared by prefixing “more” and “most”, or “less” and “least”, to the positive; as, beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful.

Compare.syn: To Compare, Compare with, Compare to.
Compare.etym: [L. comparare, fr. compar like or equal to another; com- + par equal: cf. F. comparer. See Pair, Peer an equal, and cf. Compeer.]

senses.d: To be like or equal; to admit, or be worthy of, comparison; as, his later work does not compare with his earlier.
q: I should compare with him in excellence. Shak.

senses.d: To vie; to assume a likeness or equality.
q: Shall pack horses . . . compare with Cæsars? Shak.

senses.d: Comparison.
q: His mighty champion, strong beyond compare. Milton.
Their small galleys may not hold compare With our tall ships. Waller.

senses.d: Illustration by comparison; simile.
q: Rhymes full of protest, of oath, and big compare. Shak.

senses.d: To get; to procure; to obtain; to acquire
q: To fill his bags, and richesse to compare. Spenser.

Compare.etym: [L. comparare to prepare, procure; com- + parare. See Prepare, Parade.]

senses.d: The act of comparing; an examination of two or more objects with the view of discovering the resemblances or differences; relative estimate.
q: As sharp legal practitioners, no class of human beings can bear comparison with them. Macaulay.
The miracles of our Lord and those of the Old Testament afford many interesting points of comparison. Trench.

senses.d: The state of being compared; a relative estimate; also, a state, quality, or relation, admitting of being compared; as, to bring a thing into comparison with another; there is no comparison between them.
That to which, or with which, a thing is compared, as being equal or like; illustration; similitude.
q: Whereto shall we liken the kingdom of God? Or with what comparison shall we compare it? Mark iv. 30.

senses.d: The modification, by inflection or otherwise, which the adjective and adverb undergo to denote degrees of quality or quantity; as, little, less, least, are examples of comparison.
A figure by which one person or thing is compared to another, or the two are considered with regard to some property or quality, which is common to them both; e.g., the lake sparkled like a jewel.
The faculty of the reflective group which is supposed to perceive resemblances and contrasts.

a mode of proving or disproving the genuineness of a signature or writing by comparing it with another proved or admitted to be genuine, in order to ascertain whether both were written by the same person.
To compare.
A passing round; circuit; circuitous course.
q: They fetched a compass of seven day's journey. 2 Kings iii. 9.
This day I breathed first; time is come round, And where I did begin, there shall I end; My life is run his compass. Shak.

senses.d: An inclosing limit; boundary; circumference; as, within the compass of an encircling wall.
An inclosed space; an area; extent.
q: Their wisdom . . . lies in a very narrow compass. Addison.

senses.d: Extent; reach; sweep; capacity; sphere; as, the compass of his eye; the compass of imagination.
q: The compass of his argument. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Moderate bounds, limits of truth; moderation; due limits; — used with within.
q: In two hundred years before (I speak within compass), no such commission had been executed. Sir J. Davies.

senses.d: The range of notes, or tones, within the capacity of a voice or instrument.
q: You would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my compass. Shak.

senses.d: An instrument for determining directions upon the earth's surface by means of a magnetized bar or needle turning freely upon a pivot and pointing in a northerly and southerly direction.
q: He that first discovered the use of the compass did more for the supplying and increase of useful commodities than those who built workhouses. Locke.

senses.d: A pair of compasses.
q: To fix one foot of their compass wherever they please. Swift.

senses.d: A circle; a continent.
q: The tryne compas [the threefold world containing earth, sea, and heaven. Skeat.] Chaucer.
Its leaves are turned to the north as true as the magnet: This is the compass flower. Longefellow.

senses.d: a saw with a narrow blade, which will cut in a curve; — called also fret saw and keyhole saw.
curved or crooked timber.
a circular bay window or oriel window.

Compass.etym: [F. compas, fr. LL. compassus circle, prop., a stepping together; com- + passus pace, step. See Pace, Pass.]

senses.d: To go about or entirely round; to make the circuit of.
q: Ye shall compass the city seven times. Josh. vi. 4.
We the globe can compass soon. Shak.

senses.d: To inclose on all sides; to surround; to encircle; to environ; to invest; to besiege; — used with about, round, around, and round about.
q: With terrors and with clamors compassed round. Milton.
Now all the blessings Of a glad father compass thee about. Shak.
Thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round. Luke xix. 43.

senses.d: To reach round; to circumvent; to get within one's power; to obtain; to accomplish.
q: If I can check my erring love, I will: If not, to compass her I'll use my skill. Shak.
How can you hope to compass your designs? Denham.

senses.d: To curve; to bend into a circular form.
To purpose; to intend; to imagine; to plot.
q: Compassing and imagining the death of the king are synonymous terms; compassing signifying the purpose or design of the mind or will, and not, as in common speech, the carrying such design to effect. Blackstone.

senses.d: Rounded; arched.
q: She came . . . into the compassed window. Shak.

senses.d: Curved; bent; as, compassing timbers.
Literally, suffering with another; a sensation of sorrow excited by the distress or misfortunes of another; pity; commiseration.
q: Womanly ingenuity set to work by womanly compassion. Macaulay.

Compassion.syn: Pity; sympathy; commiseration; fellow-feeling; mercy; condolence. See Pity.
Compassion.etym: [F., fr. L. compassio, fr. compati to have compassion; com- + pati to bear, suffer. See Patient.]

senses.d: To pity.
To drive or urge with force, or irresistibly; to force; to constrain; to oblige; to necessitate, either by physical or moral force.
q: Wolsey . . . compelled the people to pay up the whole subsidy at once. Hallam.
And they compel one Simon . . . to bear his cross. Mark xv. 21.

senses.d: To take by force or violence; to seize; to exact; to extort.
q: Commissions, which compel from each The sixth part of his substance. Shak.

senses.d: To force to yield; to overpower; to subjugate.
q: Easy sleep their weary limbs compelled. Dryden.
I compel all creatures to my will. Tennyson.

senses.d: To gather or unite in a crowd or company.
To call forth; to summon.
q: She had this knight from far compelled. Spenser.

Compel.syn: To force; constrain; oblige; necessitate; coerce. See Coerce.
Compel.etym: [L. compellere, compulsum, to drive together, to compel, urge; com- + pellere to drive: cf. OF. compellir. See Pulse.]

senses.d: To make one yield or submit.
To give utterance to expression of grief, pain, censure, regret. etc.; to lament; to murmur; to find fault; — commonly used with of. Also, to creak or squeak, as a timber or wheel.
q: O loss of sight, of thee I most complain! Milton.

senses.d: To make a formal accusation; to make a charge.
q: Now, Master Shallow, you'll complain of me to the king? Shak.

Complain.syn: To repine; grumble; deplore; bewail; grieve; mourn; regret; murmur.
Complain.etym: [F. complaindre, LL. complangere; com- + L. plangere to strike, beat, to beat the breast or head as a sign of grief, to lament. See Plaint.]

senses.d: To lament; to bewail.
q: They might the grievance inwardly complain. Daniel.
By chaste Lucrece's soul that late complain'd Her wrongs to us. Shak.

senses.d: One who complains or laments; one who finds fault; a murmurer.
q: Speechless complainer, I will learn thy thought. Shak.

senses.d: Expression of grief, regret, pain, censure, or resentment; lamentation; murmuring; accusation; fault-finding.
q: I poured out my complaint before him. Ps. cxlii. 2.
Grievous complaints of you. Shak.

senses.d: Cause or subject of complaint or murmuring.
q: The poverty of the clergy in England hath been the complaint of all who wish well to the church. Swift.

senses.d: An ailment or disease of the body.
q: One in a complaint of his bowels. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: A formal allegation or charge against a party made or presented to the appropriate court or officer, as for a wrong done or a crime committed (in the latter case, generally under oath); an information; accusation; the initial bill in proceedings in equity.

Complaint.syn: Lamentation; murmuring; sorrow; grief; disease; illness; disorder; malady; ailment.

senses.d: Filled up; with no part or element lacking; free from deficiency; entire; perfect; consummate.
q: Ye are complete in him. Col. ii. 10.
That thou, dead corse, again in complete steel Revisit'st thus the glimpses of the moon. Shak.

senses.d: Finished; ended; concluded; completed; as, the edifice is complete.
q: This course of vanity almost complete. Prior.

senses.d: Having all the parts or organs which belong to it or to the typical form; having calyx, corolla, stamens, and pistil.

Complete.etym: [L. completus, p. p. of complere to fill up; com- + plere to fill. See Full, a., and cf. Comply, Compline.]

senses.d: To bring to a state in which there is no deficiency; to perfect; to consummate; to accomplish; to fulfill; to finish; as, to complete a task, or a poem; to complete a course of education.
q: Bred only and completed to the taste Of lustful appetence. Milton.
And, to complete her bliss, a fool for mate. Pope.

Complete.syn: To perform; execute; terminate; conclude; finish; end; fill up; achieve; realize; effect; consummate; accomplish; effectuate; fulfill; bring to pass.

senses.d: The act or art of composing, or forming a whole or integral, by placing together and uniting different things, parts, or ingredients.
The state of being put together or composed; conjunction; combination; adjustment.
q: View them in composition with other things. I. Watts.
The elementary composition of bodies. Whewell.

senses.d: A mass or body formed by combining two or more substances; as, a chemical composition.
q: A composition that looks . . . like marble. Addison.

senses.d: A literary, musical, or artistic production, especially one showing study and care in arrangement; — often used of an elementary essay or translation done as an educational exercise.
Consistency; accord; congruity.
q: There is no composition in these news That gives them credit. Shak.

senses.d: Mutual agreement to terms or conditions for the settlement of a difference or controversy; also, the terms or conditions of settlement; agreement.
q: Thus we are agreed: I crave our composition may be written. Shak.

senses.d: The adjustment of a debt, or avoidance of an obligation, by some form of compensation agreed on between the parties; also, the sum or amount of compensation agreed upon in the adjustment.
q: Compositions for not taking the order of knighthood. Hallam.
Cleared by composition with their creditors. Blackstone.

senses.d: Synthesis as opposed to analysis.
q: The investigation of difficult things by the method of analysis ought ever to precede the method of composition. Sir I. Newton.

Composition.etym: [F. composition, fr. L. compositio. See Composite.]

senses.d: In the East Indies, an inclosure containing a house, outbuildings, etc.
To form or make by combining different elements, ingredients, or parts; as, to compound a medicine.
q: Incapacitating him from successfully compounding a tale of this sort. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To put together, as elements, ingredients, or parts, in order to form a whole; to combine, mix, or unite.
q: We have the power of altering and compounding those images into all the varieties of picture. Addison.

senses.d: To modify or change by combination with some other thing or part; to mingle with something else.
q: Only compound me with forgotten dust. Shak.

senses.d: To compose; to constitute.
q: His pomp and all what state compounds. Shak.

senses.d: To settle amicably; to adjust by agreement; to compromise; to discharge from obligation upon terms different from those which were stipulated; as, to compound a debt.
q: I pray, my lords, let me compound this strife. Shak.

Compound.etym: [OE. componen, compounen, L. componere, compositum; com-+ ponere to put set. The d is excrescent. See Position, and cf. Componé.]

senses.d: To effect a composition; to come to terms of agreement; to agree; to settle by a compromise; — usually followed by with before the person participating, and for before the thing compounded or the consideration.
q: Here's a fellow will help you to-morrow; . . . compound with him by the year. Shak.
They were at last glad to compound for his bare commitment to the Tower. Clarendon.
Cornwall compounded to furnish ten oxen after Michaelmas for thirty pounds. R. Carew.
Compound for sins they are inclined to By damning those they have no mind to. Hudibras.

senses.d: Composed of two or more elements, ingredients, parts; produced by the union of several ingredients, parts, or things; composite; as, a compound word.
q: Compound substances are made up of two or more simple substances. I. Watts.

Compound.etym: [OE. compouned, p. p. of compounen. See Compound, v. t.]

senses.d: That which is compounded or formed by the union or mixture of elements ingredients, or parts; a combination of simples; a compound word; the result of composition.
q: Rare compound of oddity, frolic, and fun. Goldsmith.
When the word “bishopric” was first made, it was made as a compound. Earle.

senses.d: A union of two or more ingredients in definite proportions by weight, so combined as to form a distinct substance; as, water is a compound of oxygen and hydrogen.
To contain; to embrace; to include; as, the states comprehended in the Austrian Empire.
q: Who hath . . . comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure. Is. xl. 12.

senses.d: To take in or include by construction or implication; to comprise; to imply.
q: Comprehended all in this one word, Discretion. Hobbes.
And if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying. Rom. xiii. 9.

senses.d: To take into the mind; to grasp with the understanding; to apprehend the meaning of; to understand.
q: At a loss to comprehend the question. W. Irwing.
Great things doeth he, which we can not comprehend. Job. xxxvii. 5.

Comprehend.syn: To contain; include; embrace; comprise; inclose; grasp; embody; involve; imply; apprehend; imagine; conceive; understand. See Apprehend.
Comprehend.etym: [L. comprehendere, comprehensum; com- + prehendere to grasp, seize; prae before + hendere (used only in comp.). See Get, and cf. Comprise.]

senses.d: To hide or withdraw from observation; to cover; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discovery of; to withhold knowledge of.
q: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing. Prov. xxv. 2.
Declare ye among the nations, . . . publish and conceal not. Jer. l. 2.
He which finds him shall deserve our thanks, . . . He that conceals him, death. Shak.
Bur double griefs afflict concealing hearts. Spenser.
Both dissemble deeply their affections. Shak.
We have in these words a primary sense, which reveals a future state, and a secondary sense, which hides and secretes it. Warburton.

Conceal.syn: To hide; secrete; screen; cover; disguise; dissemble; mask; veil; cloak; screen.
Conceal.etym: [OF. conceler, L. concelare; con- + celareto hide; akin to AS. helan, G. hehlen, E. hele (to cover), helmet. See Hell, Helmet.]

senses.d: Hidden; kept from sight; secreted.
That which is conceived, imagined, or formed in the mind; idea; thought; image; conception.
q: In laughing, there ever procedeth a conceit of somewhat ridiculous. Bacon.
A man wise in his own conceit. Prov. xxvi. 12.

senses.d: Faculty of conceiving ideas; mental faculty; apprehension; as, a man of quick conceit.
q: How often, alas! did her eyes say unto me that they loved! and yet I, not looking for such a matter, had not my conceit open to understand them. Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: Quickness of apprehension; active imagination; lively fancy.
q: His wit's as thick as Tewksbury mustard; there's more conceit in him than is in a mallet. Shak.

senses.d: A fanciful, odd, or extravagant notion; a quant fancy; an unnatural or affected conception; a witty thought or turn of expression; a fanciful device; a whim; a quip.
q: On his way to the gibbet, a freak took him in the head to go off with a conceit. L'Estrange.
Some to conceit alone their works confine, And glittering thoughts struck out at every line. Pope.
Tasso is full of conceits . . . which are not only below the dignity of heroic verse but contrary to its nature. Dryden.

senses.d: An overweening idea of one's self; vanity.
q: Plumed with conceit he calls aloud. Cotton.

senses.d: Design; pattern.

Conceit.etym: [Through French, fr. L. conceptus a conceiving, conception, fr. concipere to conceive: cf. OF. p. p. nom. conciez conceived. See Conceive, and cf. Concept, Deceit.]

senses.d: To conceive; to imagine.
q: The strong, by conceiting themselves weak, are therebly rendered as inactive . . . as if they really were so. South.
One of two bad ways you must conceit me, Either a coward or a flatterer. Shak.

senses.d: To form an idea; to think.
q: Those whose . . . vulgar apprehensions conceit but low of matrimonial purposes. Milton.

senses.d: To receive into the womb and begin to breed; to begin the formation of the embryo of.
q: She hath also conceived a son in her old age. Luke i. 36.

senses.d: To form in the mind; to plan; to devise; to generate; to originate; as, to conceive a purpose, plan, hope.
q: It was among the ruins of the Capitol that I first conceived the idea of a work which has amused and exercised near twenty years of my life. Gibbon.
Conceiving and uttering from the heart words of falsehood. Is. lix. 13.

senses.d: To apprehend by reason or imagination; to take into the mind; to know; to imagine; to comprehend; to understand.
q: O horror, horror, horror! Tongue nor heart Cannot conceive nor name thee! Shak.
You will hardly conceive him to have been bred in the same climate. Swift.

Conceive.syn: To apprehend; imagine; suppose; understand; comprehend; believe; think.
Conceive.etym: [OF. conzoivre, concever, conceveir, F. concevoir, fr. L. oncipere to take, to conceive; con- + capere to seize or take. See Capable, and cf. Conception.]

senses.d: To have an embryo or fetus formed in the womb; to breed; to become pregnant.
q: A virgin shall conceive, and bear a son. Isa. vii. 14.

senses.d: To have a conception, idea, or opinion; think; — with of.
q: Conceive of things clearly and distinctly in their own natures. I. Watts.

senses.d: The act of conceiving in the womb; the initiation of an embryonic animal life.
q: I will greaty multiply thy sorrow and thy conception. Gen. iii. 16.

senses.d: The state of being conceived; beginning.
q: Joy had the like conception in our eyes. Shak.

senses.d: The power or faculty of apprehending of forming an idea in the mind; the power of recalling a past sensation or perception.
q: Under the article of conception, I shall confine myself to that faculty whose province it is to enable us to form a notion of our past sensations, or of the objects of sense that we have formerly perceived. Stewart.

senses.d: The formation in the mind of an image, idea, or notion, apprehension.
q: Conception consists in a conscious act of the understanding, bringing any given object or impression into the same class with any number of other objects or impression, by means of some character or characters common to them all. Coleridge.

senses.d: The image, idea, or notion of any action or thing which is formed in the mind; a concept; a notion; a universal; the product of a rational belief or judgment. See Concept.
q: He says that the sun draws or attracts the water; a metaphorical term obviously intended to denote some more general and abstract conception than that of the visible operation which the word primarily signifies. Whewell.

senses.d: Idea; purpose; design.
q: Note this dangerous conception. Shak.

senses.d: Conceit; affected sentiment or thought.
q: He . . . is full of conceptions, points of epigram, and witticism. Dryden.

Conception.etym: [F. conception, L. conceptio, fr. concipere to conceive. See Conceive.]

senses.d: To relate or belong to; to have reference to or connection with; to affect the interest of; to be of importance to.
q: Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ. Acts xxviii. 31.
Our wars with France have affected us in our most tender interests, and concerned us more than those with any other nation. Addison.
It much concerns a preacher first to learn The genius of his audience and their turn. Dodsley.
Ignorant, so far as the usual instruction is concerned. J. F. Cooper.

senses.d: To engage by feeling or sentiment; to interest; as, a good prince concerns himself in the happiness of his subjects.
q: They think themselves out the reach of Providence, and no longer concerned to solicit his favor. Rogers.

Concern.etym: [F. concerner, LL. concernere to regard, concern, fr. L. concernere to mix or mingle together, as in a sieve for separating; con- + cernere to separate, sift, distinguish by the senses, and especially by the eyes, to perceive, see. See Certain.]

senses.d: To be of importance.
q: Which to deny concerns more than avails. Shak.

senses.d: That which relates or belongs to one; business; affair.
q: The private concerns of fanilies. Addison.

senses.d: That which affects the welfare or happiness; interest; moment.
q: Mysterious secrets of a high concern. Roscommon.

senses.d: Interest in, or care for, any person or thing; regard; solicitude; anxiety.
q: O Marcia, let me hope thy kind concerns And gentle wishes follow me to battle. Addison.

senses.d: Persons connected in business; a firm and its business; as, a banking concern.

Concern.syn: Care; anxiety; solicitude; interest; regard; business; affair; matter; moment. See Care.

senses.d: Pertaining to; regarding; having relation to; respecting; as regards.
q: I have accepted thee concerning this thing. Gen. xix. 21.
The Lord hath spoken good concerning Israel. Num. x. 29.

senses.d: Important.
q: So great and so concerning truth. South.

senses.d: That in which one is concerned or interested; concern; affair; interest.
q: To mix with thy concernments I desist. Milton.

senses.d: Importance; moment; consequence.
q: Let every action of concernment to begun with prayer. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Concern; participation; interposition.
q: He married a daughter to the earl without any other approbation of her father or concernment in it, than suffering him and her come into his presence. Clarendon.

senses.d: Emotion of mind; solicitude; anxiety.
q: While they are so eager to destroy the fame of others, their ambition is manifest in their concernment. Dryden.

senses.d: A cutting off; a division; a schism; a faction.

Concision.etym: [L. concisio: cf. F. concision. See Concise.]

senses.d: To shut up; to inclose.
q: The very person of Christ concluded within the grave. Hooker.

senses.d: To include; to comprehend; to shut up together; to embrace.
q: For God hath concluded all in unbelief. Rom. xi. 32.
The Scripture hath concluded all under sin. Gal. iii. 22.

senses.d: To reach as an end of reasoning; to infer, as from premises; to close, as an argument, by inferring; — sometimes followed by a dependent clause.
q: No man can conclude God's love or hatred to any person by anything that befalls him. Tillotson.
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith. Rom. iii. 28.

senses.d: To make a final determination or judgment concerning; to judge; to decide.
q: But no frail man, however great or high, Can be concluded blest before he die. Addison.
Is it concluded he shall be protector? Shak.

senses.d: To bring to an end; to close; to finish.
q: I will conclude this part with the speech of a counselor of state. Bacon.

senses.d: To bring about as a result; to effect; to make; as, to conclude a bargain.
To shut off; to restrain; to limit; to estop; to bar; — generally in the passive; as, the defendant is concluded by his own plea; a judgment concludes the introduction of further evidence argument.
q: If therefore they will appeal to revelation for their creation they must be concluded by it. Sir M. Hale.

Conclude.syn: To infer; decide; determine; settle; close; finish; terminate; end.
Conclude.etym: [L. concludere, conclusum; con- + claudere to shut. See Close, v. t.]

senses.d: To come to a termination; to make an end; to close; to end; to terminate.
q: A train of lies, That, made in lust, conclude in perjuries. Dryden.
And, to conclude, The victory fell on us. Shak.

senses.d: To form a final judgment; to reach a decision.
q: Can we conclude upon Luther's instability? Bp. Atterbury.
Conclude and be agreed. Shak.

senses.d: The last part of anything; close; termination; end.
q: A fluorish of trumpets announced the conclusion of the contest. Prescott.

senses.d: Final decision; determination; result.
q: And the conclusion is, she shall be thine. Shak.

senses.d: Any inference or result of reasoning.
The inferred proposition of a syllogism; the necessary consequence of the conditions asserted in two related propositions called premises. See Syllogism.
q: He granted him both the major and minor, but denied him the conclusion. Addison.

senses.d: Drawing of inferences.
q: Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes And still conclusion. Shak.

senses.d: An experiment, or something from which a conclusion may be drawn.
q: We practice likewise all conclusions of grafting and inoculating. Bacon.

senses.d: The end or close of a pleading, e.g., the formal ending of an indictment, “against the peace,” etc.
q: Like the famous ape, To try conclusions, in the basket creep. Shak.

Conclusion.syn: Inference; deduction; result; consequence; end; decision. See Inference.

senses.d: A state of agreement; harmony; union.
q: Love quarrels oft in pleasing concord end. Milton.

senses.d: Agreement by stipulation; compact; covenant; treaty or league.
q: The concord made between Henry and Roderick. Davies.

senses.d: Agreement of words with one another, in gender, number, person, or case.
An agreement between the parties to a fine of land in reference to the manner in which it should pass, being an acknowledgment that the land in question belonged to the complainant. See Fine.
An agreeable combination of tones simultaneously heard; a consonant chord; consonance; harmony.

Concord.etym: [F. concorde, L. concordia, fr. concors of the same mind, agreeing; con- + cor, cordis, heart. See Heart, and cf. Accord.]

senses.d: A variety of American grape, with large dark blue (almost black) grapes in compact clusters.
To agree; to act together.
A moving, flowing, or running together; confluence.
q: The good frame of the universe was not the product of chance or fortuitous concourse of particles of matter. Sir M. Hale.

senses.d: An assembly; a gathering formed by a voluntary or spontaneous moving and meeting in one place.
q: Amidst the concourse were to be seen the noble ladies of Milan, in gay, fantastic cars, shining in silk brocade. Prescott.

senses.d: The place or point of meeting or junction of two bodies.
q: The drop will begin to move toward the concourse of the glasses. Sir I. Newton.

senses.d: An open space where several roads or paths meet; esp. an open space in a park where several roads meet.
Concurrence; coöperation.
q: The divine providence is wont to afford its concourse to such proceeding. Barrow.

Concourse.etym: [F. concours, L. concursus, fr. concurrere to run together. See Concur.]

senses.d: A woman who cohabits with a man without being his wife; a paramour.

A wife of inferior condition; a lawful wife, but not united to the man by the usual ceremonies, and of inferior condition. Such were Hagar and Keturah, the concubines of Abraham; and such concubines were allowed by the Roman laws. Their children were not heirs of their father.

Concubine.etym: [F., fr. L. concubina; con- + cubare to lie down, concumbere to lie together, akin to E. cubit.]

senses.d: Sexual lust; morbid carnal passion.
q: Concupiscence like a pestilence walketh in darkness. Horne.

senses.d: To pronounce to be wrong; to disapprove of; to censure.
q: Condemn the fault, and not the actor of it! Why, every fault's condemned ere it be done. Shak.
Wilt thou condemn him that is most just? Job xxxiv. 17.

senses.d: To declare the guilt of; to make manifest the faults or unworthiness of; to convict of guilt.
q: The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it. Matt. xii. 42.

senses.d: To pronounce a judicial sentence against; to sentence to punishment, suffering, or loss; to doom; — with to before the penalty.
q: Driven out from bliss, condemned In this abhorred deep to utter woe. Milton.
To each his sufferings; all are men, Condemned alike to groan. Gray.
And they shall condemn him to death. Matt. xx. 18.
The thief condemned, in law already dead. Pope.
No flocks that range the valley free, To slaughter I condemn. Goldsmith.

senses.d: To amerce or fine; — with in before the penalty.
q: The king of Egypt . . . condemned the land in a hundred talents of silver. 2 Cron. xxxvi. 3.

senses.d: To adjudge or pronounce to be unfit for use or service; to adjudge or pronounce to be forfeited; as, the ship and her cargo were condemned.
To doom to be taken for public use, under the right of eminent domain.

Condemn.syn: To blame; censure; reprove; reproach; upbraid; reprobate; convict; doom; sentence; adjudge.
Condemn.etym: [L. condemnare; con- + damnare to condemn: cf. F. condamner. See Damn.]

senses.d: The act of condemning or pronouncing to be wrong; censure; blame; disapprobation.
q: In every other sense of condemnation, as blame, censure, reproof, private judgment, and the like. Paley.

senses.d: The act of judicially condemning, or adjudging guilty, unfit for use, or forfeited; the act of dooming to punishment or forfeiture.
q: A legal and judicial condemnation. Paley.
Whose condemnation is pronounced. Shak.

senses.d: The state of being condemned.
q: His pathetic appeal to posterity in the hopeless hour of condemnation. W. Irving.

senses.d: The ground or reason of condemning.
q: This is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather light, because their deeds were evil. John iii. 19.

senses.d: Pronounced to be wrong, guilty, worthless, or forfeited; adjudged or sentenced to punishment, destruction, or confiscation.
Used for condemned persons.
q: Richard Savage . . . had lain with fifty pounds weight of irons on his legs in the condemned ward of Newgate. Macaulay.

senses.d: To stoop or descend; to let one's self down; to submit; to waive the privilege of rank or dignity; to accommodate one's self to an inferior.
q: Can they think me so broken, so debased With corporal servitude, that my mind ever Will condescend to such absurd commands? Milton.
Spain's mighty monarch, In gracious clemency, does condescend, On these conditions, to become your friend. Dryden.
Those who thought they were honoring me by condescending to address a few words to me. F. W. Robinson.

senses.d: To consent.
q: All parties willingly condescended heruento. R. Carew.

Condescend.syn: To yield; stoop; descend; deign; vouchsafe.
Condescend.etym: [F. condescendre, LL. condescendere, fr. L. con- + descendere. See Descend.]

senses.d: Mode or state of being; state or situation with regard to external circumstances or influences, or to physical or mental integrity, health, strength, etc.; predicament; rank; position, estate.
q: I am in my condition A prince, Miranda; I do think, a king. Shak.
And O, what man's condition can be worse Than his whom plenty starves and blessings curse? Cowley.
The new conditions of life. Darwin.

senses.d: Essential quality; property; attribute.
q: It seemed to us a condition and property of divine powers and beings to be hidden and unseen to others. Bacon.

senses.d: Temperament; disposition; character.
q: The condition of a saint and the complexion of a devil. Shak.

senses.d: That which must exist as the occasion or concomitant of something else; that which is requisite in order that something else should take effect; an essential qualification; stipulation; terms specified.
q: I had as lief take her dowry with this condition, to be whipped at the high cross every morning. Shak.
Many are apt to believe remission of sins, but they believe it without the condition of repentance. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: A clause in a contract, or agreement, which has for its object to suspend, to defeat, or in some way to modify, the principal obligation; or, in case of a will, to suspend, revoke, or modify a devise or bequest. It is also the case of a future uncertain event, which may or may not happen, and on the occurrence or non-occurrence of which, the accomplishment, recission, or modification of an obligation or testamentary disposition is made to depend.

Condition.syn: State; situation; circumstances; station; case; mode; plight; predicament; stipulation; qualification; requisite; article; provision; arrangement. See State.
Condition.etym: [F., fr. L. conditio (better condicio) agreement, compact, condition; con- + a root signifying to show, point out, akin to dicere to say, dicare to proclaim, dedicate. See Teach, Token.]

senses.d: To make terms; to stipulate.
q: Pay me back my credit, And I'll condition with ye. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To impose upon an object those relations or conditions without which knowledge and thought are alleged to be impossible.
q: To think of a thing is to condition. Sir W. Hamilton.

senses.d: To invest with, or limit by, conditions; to burden or qualify by a condition; to impose or be imposed as the condition of.
q: Seas, that daily gain upon the shore, Have ebb and flow conditioning their march. Tennyson.

senses.d: To contract; to stipulate; to agree.
q: It was conditioned between Saturn and Titan, that Saturn should put to death all his male children. Sir W. Raleigh.

senses.d: To put under conditions; to require to pass a new examination or to make up a specified study, as a condition of remaining in one's class or in college; as, to condition a student who has failed in some branch of study.
To test or assay, as silk (to ascertain the proportion of moisture it contains).
The act or method of conducting; guidance; management.
q: Christianity has humanized the conduct of war. Paley.
The conduct of the state, the administration of its affairs. Ld. Brougham.

senses.d: Skillful guidance or management; generalship.
q: Conduct of armies is a prince's art. Waller.
Attacked the Spaniards . . . with great impetuosity, but with so little conduct, that his forces were totally routed. Robertson.

senses.d: Convoy; escort; guard; guide.
q: I will be your conduct. B. Jonson.
In my conduct shall your ladies come. Shak.

senses.d: That which carries or conveys anything; a channel; a conduit; an instrument.
q: Although thou hast been conduct of my shame. Shak.

senses.d: The manner of guiding or carrying one's self; personal deportment; mode of action; behavior.
q: All these difficulties were increased by the conduct of Shrewsbury. Macaulay.
What in the conduct of our life appears So well designed, so luckily begun, But when we have our wish, we wish undone? Dryden.

senses.d: Plot; action; construction; manner of development.
q: The book of Job, in conduct and diction. Macaulay.

Conduct.syn: Behavior; carriage; deportment; demeanor; bearing; management; guidance. See Behavior.
Conduct.etym: [LL. conductus defense, escort, fr. L. conductus, p. p. of conducere. See Conduce, and cf. Conduit.]

senses.d: To lead, or guide; to escort; to attend.
q: I can conduct you, lady, to a low But loyal cottage, where you may be safe. Milton.

senses.d: To lead, as a commander; to direct; to manage; to carry on; as, to conduct the affairs of a kingdom.
q: Little skilled in the art of conducting a siege. Prescott.

senses.d: To behave; — with the reflexive; as, he conducted himself well.
To serve as a medium for conveying; to transmit, as heat, light, electricity, etc.
To direct, as the leader in the performance of a musical composition.
To act as a conductor (as of heat, electricity, etc.); to carry.
To conduct one's self; to behave.
A pipe, canal, channel, or passage for conveying water or fluid.
q: All the conduits of my blood froze up. Shak.
This is the fountain of all those bitter waters, of which, through a hundred different conduits, we have drunk. Burke.

senses.d: A structure forming a reservoir for water.
A narrow passage for private communication.

Conduit.etym: [F., fr. LL. conductus escort, conduit. See Conduct.]

senses.d: A rabbit. See Cony.
A fish. See Cony.
A composition of different materials.
q: A new confection of mold. Bacon.

senses.d: A preparation of fruits or roots, etc., with sugar; a sweetmeat.
q: Certain confections . . . are like to candied conserves, and are made of sugar and lemons. Bacon.

senses.d: A composition of drugs.
A soft solid made by incorporating a medicinal substance or substances with sugar, sirup, or honey.
A confectioner.
q: He will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks. 1 Sam. viii. 13.

senses.d: Prepared as a confection.
q: The biscuit or confectionary plum. Cowper.

senses.d: A league or compact between two or more persons, bodies of men, or states, for mutual support or common action; alliance.
q: The friendships of the world are oft Confederacies in vice or leagues of pleasure. Addison.
He hath heard of our confederacy. Shak.
Virginia promoted a confederacy. Bancroft.

senses.d: The persons, bodies, states, or nations united by a league; a confederation.
q: The Grecian common wealth, . . . the most heroic confederacy that ever existed. Harris.
Virgil has a whole confederacy against him. Dryden.

senses.d: A combination of two or more persons to commit an unlawful act, or to do a lawful act by unlawful means. See Conspiracy.

Confederacy.syn: League; compact; alliance; association; union; combination; confederation.

senses.d: With the, the Confederate States of America.
United in a league; allied by treaty; engaged in a confederacy; banded together; allied.
q: All the swords In Italy, and her confederate arms, Could not have made this peace. Shak.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the government of the eleven Southern States of the United States which (1860-1865) attempted to establish an independent nation styled the Confederate States of America; as, the Confederate congress; Confederate money.

Confederate.etym: [L. confoederatus, p. p. of confoederare to join by a league; con- + foederare to establish by treaty or league, fr. foedus league, compact. See Federal.]

senses.d: One who is united with others in a league; a person or a nation engaged in a confederacy; an ally; also, an accomplice in a bad sense.
q: He found some of his confederates in gaol. Macaulay.

senses.d: A name designating an adherent to the cause of the States which attempted to withdraw from the Union (1860-1865).
To unite in a league or confederacy; to ally.
q: With these the Piercies them confederate. Daniel.

senses.d: To unite in a league; to join in a mutual contract or covenant; to band together.
q: By words men . . . covenant and confederate. South.

senses.d: To bring together for comparison; to compare.
q: If we confer these observations with others of the like nature, we may find cause to rectify the general opinion. Boyle.

senses.d: To grant as a possession; to bestow.
q: The public marks of honor and reward Conferred upon me. Milton.

senses.d: To contribute; to conduce.
q: The closeness and compactness of the parts resting together doth much confer to the strength of the union. Glanvill.

Confer.etym: [L. conferre to bring together, contribute, consult; con- + ferre to bear: cf. F. conférer. See 1st Bear.]

senses.d: To have discourse; to consult; to compare views; to deliberate.
q: Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered. Acts xxv. 12.
You shall hear us confer of this. Shak.

senses.d: The act of comparing two or more things together; comparison.
q: Helps and furtherances which . . . the mutual conference of all men's collections and observations may afford. Hocker.

senses.d: The act of consulting together formally; serious conversation or discussion; interchange of views.
q: Nor with such free and friendly conference As he hath used of old. Shak.

senses.d: A meeting for consultation, discussion, or an interchange of opinions.
A meeting of the two branches of a legislature, by their committees, to adjust between them.
A stated meeting of preachers and others, invested with authority to take cognizance of ecclesiastical matters.
A voluntary association of Congregational churches of a district; the district in which such churches are.
To make acknowledgment or avowal in a matter pertaining to one's self; to acknowledge, own, or admit, as a crime, a fault, a debt.
q: And there confess Humbly our faults, and pardon beg. Milton.
I must confess I was most pleased with a beautiful prospect that none of them have mentioned. Addison.

senses.d: To acknowledge faith in; to profess belief in.
q: Whosoever, therefore, shall confess me before men, him will I confess, also, before my Father which is in heaven. Matt. x. 32.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess both. Acts xxiii. 8.

senses.d: To admit as true; to assent to; to acknowledge, as after a previous doubt, denial, or concealment.
q: I never gave it him. Send for him hither, And let him confess a truth. Shak.
As I confess it needs must be. Tennyson.
As an actor confessed without rival to shine. Goldsmith.

senses.d: To make known or acknowledge, as one's sins to a priest, in order to receive absolution; — sometimes followed by the reflexive pronoun.
q: Our beautiful votary took an opportunity of confessing herself to this celebrated father. Addison.

senses.d: To hear or receive such confession; — said of a priest.
q: He . . . heard mass, and the prince, his son, with him, and the most part of his company were confessed. Ld. Berners.

senses.d: To disclose or reveal, as an effect discloses its cause; to prove; to attest.
q: Tall thriving trees confessed the fruitful mold. Pope.

Confess.syn: Admit; grant; concede; avow; own; assent; recognize; prove; exhibit; attest.
