Confess.etym: [F. confesser, fr. L. confessus, p. p. of confiteri to confess; con- + fateri to confess; akin to fari to speak. See 2d Ban, Fame.]

senses.d: To make confession; to disclose sins or faults, or the state of the conscience.
q: Every tongue shall confess to God. Rom. xiv. 11.

senses.d: To acknowledge; to admit; to concede.
q: But since (And I confess with right) you think me bound. Tennyson.

senses.d: Acknowledgment; avowal, especially in a matter pertaining to one's self; the admission of a debt, obligation, or crime.
q: With a crafty madness keeps aloof, When we would bring him on to some confession Of his true state. Shak.

senses.d: Acknowledgment of belief; profession of one's faith.
q: With the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Rom. x. 10.

senses.d: The act of disclosing sins or faults to a priest in order to obtain sacramental absolution.
q: Auricular confession . . . or the private and special confession of sins to a priest for the purpose of obtaining his absolution. Hallam.

senses.d: A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to or signed, as a preliminary to admission to membership of a church; a confession of faith.
An admission by a party to whom an act is imputed, in relation to such act. A judicial confession settles the issue to which it applies; an extrajudical confession may be explained or rebutted.
The act of confiding, trusting, or putting faith in; trust; reliance; belief; — formerly followed by of, now commonly by in.
q: Society is built upon trust, and trust upon confidence of one another's integrity. South.
A cheerful confidence in the mercy of God. Macaulay.

senses.d: That in which faith is put or reliance had.
q: The Lord shall be thy confidence. Prov. iii. 26.

senses.d: The state of mind characterized by one's reliance on himself, or his circumstances; a feeling of self-sufficiency; such assurance as leads to a feeling of security; self-reliance; — often with self prefixed.
q: Your wisdom is consumed in confidence; Do not go forth to-day. Shak.
But confidence then bore thee on secure Either to meet no danger, or to find Matter of glorious trial. Milton.

senses.d: Private conversation; (pl.) secrets shared; as, there were confidences between them.
q: Sir, I desire some confidence with you. Shak.
I am confident that very much be done. Boyle.

senses.d: Trustful; without fear or suspicion; frank; unreserved.
q: Be confident to speak, Northumberland; We three are but thyself. Shak.

senses.d: Having self-reliance; bold; undaunted.
q: As confident as is the falcon's flight Against a bird, do I with Mowbray fight. Shak.

senses.d: Having an excess of assurance; bold to a fault; dogmatical; impudent; presumptuous.
q: The fool rageth and is confident. Prov. xiv. 16.

senses.d: Giving occasion for confidence.
q: The cause was more confident than the event was prosperous. Jer. Taylor.

Confidence.etym: [L. confidentia firm trust in, self-confidence: cf. F. confidence.]

senses.d: With confidence; with strong assurance; positively.
To make firm or firmer; to add strength to; to establish; as, health is confirmed by exercise.
q: Confirm the crown to me and to mine heirs. Shak.
And confirmed the same unto Jacob for a law. Ps. cv. 10.

senses.d: To strengthen in judgment or purpose.
q: Confirmed, then, I resolve Adam shall share with me in bliss or woe. Milton.

senses.d: To give new assurance of the truth of; to render certain; to verify; to corroborate; as, to confirm a rumor.
q: Your eyes shall witness and confirm my tale. Pope.
These likelihoods confirm her flight. Shak.

senses.d: To render valid by formal assent; to complete by a necessary sanction; to ratify; as, to confirm the appoinment of an official; the Senate confirms a treaty.
q: That treaty so prejudicial ought to have been remitted rather than confimed. Swift.

senses.d: To administer the rite of confirmation to. See Confirmation, 3.
q: Those which are thus confirmed are thereby supposed to be fit for admission to the sacrament. Hammond.

Confirm.syn: To strengthen; corroborate; substantiate; establish; fix; ratify; settle; verify; assure.
Confirm.etym: [OE. confermen, confirmen, OF. confermer, F. confirmer, fr. L. confirmare; con- + firmare to make firm, fr. firmus firm. See Firm.]

senses.d: The act of confirming or strengthening; the act of establishing, ratifying, or sanctioning; as, the confirmation of an appointment.
q: Their blood is shed In confirmation of the noblest claim. Cowper.

senses.d: That which confirms; that which gives new strength or assurance; as to a statement or belief; additional evidence; proof; convincing testimony.
q: Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ. Shak.

senses.d: A rite supplemental to baptism, by which a person is admitted, through the laying on of the hands of a bishop, to the full privileges of the church, as in the Roman Catholic, the Episcopal Church, etc.
q: This ordinance is called confirmation, because they who duly receive it are confirmed or strengthened for the fulfillment of their Christian duties, by the grace therein bestowed upon them. Hook.

senses.d: A conveyance by which a voidable estate is made sure and not voidable, or by which a particular estate is increased; a contract, express or implied, by which a person makes that firm and binding which was before voidable.
The act or process of taking property or condemning it to be taken, as forfeited to the public use.
q: The confiscations following a subdued rebellion. Hallam.

senses.d: A striking or dashing together; violent collision; as, a conflict of elements or waves.
A strife for the mastery; hostile contest; battle; struggle; fighting.
q: As soon as he was himself again, he became eager for action and conflict. Macaulay.
An irrepressible conflict between opposing and enduring forces. W. H. Seward.

Conflict.syn: Contest; collision; struggle; combat; strife; contention; battle; fight; encounter. See Contest.
Conflict.etym: [L. conflictus a striking together, fr. confligere, -flictum, to strike together, to fight: cf. F. conflit, formerly also conflict. See Conflict, v.]

senses.d: To strike or dash together; to meet in violent collision; to collide.
q: Fire and water conflicting together. Bacon.

senses.d: To maintain a conflict; to contend; to engage in strife or opposition; to struggle.
q: A man would be content to . . . conflict with great difficulties, in hopes of a mighty reward. Abp. Tillotson.

senses.d: To be in opposition; to be contradictory.
q: The laws of the United States and of the individual States may, in some cases, conflict with each other. Wheaton.

Conflict.syn: To fight; contend; contest; resist; struggle; combat; strive; battle.
Conflict.etym: [L. conflictus, p. p. of confligere to conflict (cf. conflictare); con- + fligere to strike; cf. Gr. φλίβειν, θλίβειν, to press, L. flagrum whip.]

senses.d: Of the same form; similar in import; conformable.
q: Care must be taken that the interpretation be every way conform to the analogy of faith. Bp.Hall.

Conform.etym: [L. conformis; con- + forma form: cf. F. conforme.]

senses.d: To shape in accordance with; to make like; to bring into harmony or agreement with; — usually with to or unto.
q: Demand of them wherefore they conform not themselves unto the order of the church. Hooker.

Conform.etym: [F. conformer, L. conformare, -formatum; con- + formare to form, forma form. See Form.]

senses.d: To be in accord or harmony; to comply; to be obedient; to submit; — with to or with.
q: A rule to which experience must conform. Whewell.

senses.d: To comply with the usages of the Established Church; to be a conformist.
q: About two thousand ministers whose consciences did not suffer them to conform were driven from their benefices in a day. Macaulay.

senses.d: Corresponding in form, character, opinions, etc.; similar; like; consistent; proper or suitable; — usually followed by to.
q: The fragments of Sappho give us a taste of her way of writing perfectly conformable with that character. Addison.
Conformable to Scripture as well as to philosophy. Whewell.
To make matters somewhat conformable for the old knight. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Disposed to compliance or obedience; ready to follow directions; submissive; compliant.
q: I have been to you a true and humble wife, At all times to your will conformable. Shak.

senses.d: Parallel, or nearly so; — said of strata in contact.
To mingle and blend, so that different elements can not be distinguished; to confuse.
q: They who strip not ideas from the marks men use for them, but confound them with words, must have endless dispute. Locke.
Let us go down, and there confound their language. Gen. xi. 7.

senses.d: To mistake for another; to identify falsely.
q: They were generally vagrants and pilferers, and were often confounded with the gypsies. Macaulay.

senses.d: To throw into confusion or disorder; to perplex; to strike with amazement; to dismay.
q: The gods confound... The Athenians both within and out that wall. Shak.
They trusted in thee and were not confounded. Ps. xxii. 5.
So spake the Son of God, and Satan stood A while as mute, confounded what to say. Milton.

senses.d: To destroy; to ruin; to waste.
q: One man's lust these many lives confounds. Shak.
How couldst thou in a mile confound an hour? Shak.

Confound.syn: To abash; confuse; baffle; dismay; astonish; defeat; terrify; mix; blend; intermingle. See Abash.
Confound.etym: [F. confondre, fr. L. confundere, -fusum, to pour together; con- + fundere to pour. See Fuse to melt, and cf. Confuse.]

senses.d: Confused; perplexed.
q: A cloudy and confounded philosopher. Cudworth.

senses.d: Excessive; extreme; abominable.
q: He was a most confounded tory. Swift.
The tongue of that confounded woman. Sir. W. Scott.

senses.d: Confused, disturbed.
Mixed; confounded.

Confuse.etym: [F. confus, L. confusus, p. p. of confundere. See Confound.]

senses.d: To mix or blend so that things can not be distinguished; to jumble together; to confound; to render indistinct or obscure; as, to confuse accounts; to confuse one's vision.
q: A universal hubbub wild Of stunning sounds and voices all confused. Milton.

senses.d: To perplex; to disconcert; to abash; to cause to lose self-possession.
q: Nor thou with shadowed hint confuse A life that leads melodious days. Tennyson.
Confused and sadly she at length replied. Pope.

Confuse.syn: To abash; disorder; disarrange; disconcert; confound; obscure; distract. See Abash.

senses.d: The state of being mixed or blended so as to produce indistinctness or error; indistinct combination; disorder; tumult.
q: The confusion of thought to which the Aristotelians were liable. Whewell.
Moody beggars starving for a time Of pellmell havoc and confusion. Shak.

senses.d: The state of being abashed or disconcerted; loss self-possession; perturbation; shame.
q: Confusion dwelt in every face And fear in every heart. Spectator.

senses.d: Overthrow; defeat; ruin.
q: Ruin seize thee, ruthless king, Confusion on thy banners wait. Gray.

senses.d: One who confuses; a confounder.
To change from a fluid to a solid state by cold; to freeze.
q: A vapory deluge lies to snow congealed. Thomson.

senses.d: To affect as if by freezing; to check the flow of, or cause to run cold; to chill.
q: As if with horror to congeal his blood. Stirling.

Congeal.etym: [F. congeler, L. congelare, -gelatumn; con- + gelare to freeze, gelu frost. See Gelid.]

senses.d: To grow hard, stiff, or thick, from cold or other causes; to become solid; to freeze; to cease to flow; to run cold; to be chilled.
q: Lest zeal, now melted . . . Cool and congeal again to what it was. Shak.

senses.d: To address with expressions of sympathetic pleasure on account of some happy event affecting the person addressed; to wish joy to.
q: It is the king's most sweet pleasure and affection to congratulate the princess at her pavilion. Shak.
Felicitations are little better than compliments; congratulations are the expression of a genuine sympathy and joy. Trench.

Congratulate.etym: [L. congratulatus, p. p. of congratulari to wish joy abundantly; con- + gratulari to wish joy, from gratus pleasing. See Grateful.]

senses.d: To express of feel sympathetic joy; as, to congratulate with one's country.
q: The subjects of England may congratulate to themselves. Dryden.

senses.d: The act of congregating, or bringing together, or of collecting into one aggregate or mass.
q: The means of reduction in the fire is but by the congregation of homogeneal parts. Bacon.

senses.d: A collection or mass of separate things.
q: A foul and pestilent congregation of vapors. Shak.

senses.d: An assembly of persons; a gathering; esp. an assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction; a body of people who habitually so meet.
q: He rode every year to London, and preached there to large and attentive congregations. Macaulay.

senses.d: The whole body of the Jewish people; — called also Congregation of the Lord.
q: It is a sin offering for the congregation. Lev. iv. 21.

senses.d: A body of cardinals or other ecclesiastics to whom as intrusted some department of the church business; as, the Congregation of the Propaganda, which has charge of the missions of the Roman Catholic Church.
The assemblage of Masters and Doctors at Oxford or Cambrige University, mainly for the granting of degrees.
the name assumed by the Protestant party under John Knox. The leaders called themselves (1557) Lords of the Congregation.
To gain or acquire by force; to take possession of by violent means; to gain dominion over; to subdue by physical means; to reduce; to overcome by force of arms; to cause to yield; to vanquish.
q: If we be conquer'd, let men conquer us. Shak.
We conquered France, but felt our captive's charms. Pope.

senses.d: To subdue or overcome by mental or moral power; to surmount; as, to conquer difficulties, temptation, etc.
q: By winning words to conquer hearts, And make persuasion do the work of fear. Milton.

senses.d: To gain or obtain, overcoming obstacles in the way; to win; as, to conquer freedom; to conquer a peace.

Conquer.syn: To subdue; vanquish; overcome; overpower; overthrow; defeat; rout; discomfit; subjugate; reduce; humble; crush; surmount; subject; master.
Conquer.etym: [OF. conquerre, F. conquérir, fr. L. conquirere, -quisitum, to seek or search for, to bring together, LL., to conquer; con- + quaerere to seek. See Quest.]

senses.d: To gain the victory; to overcome; to prevail.
q: He went forth conquering and to conquer. Rev. vi. 2.
The champions resolved to conquer or to die. Waller.

senses.d: One who conquers.
Knowledge of one's own thoughts or actions; consciousness.
q: The sweetest cordial we receive, at last, Is conscience of our virtuous actions past. Denham.

senses.d: The faculty, power, or inward principle which decides as to the character of one's own actions, purposes, and affections, warning against and condemning that which is wrong, and approving and prompting to that which is right; the moral faculty passing judgment on one's self; the moral sense.
q: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, And every tongue brings in a several tale, And every tale condemns me for a villain. Shak.

As science means knowledge, conscience etymologically means self-knowledge . . . But the English word implies a moral standard of action in the mind as well as a consciousness of our own actions. . . . Conscience is the reason, employed about questions of right and wrong, and accompanied with the sentiments of approbation and condemnation. Whewell.

senses.d: The estimate or determination of conscience; conviction or right or duty.
q: Conscience supposes the existence of some such [i.e., moral] faculty, and properly signifies our consciousness of having acted agreeably or contrary to its directions. Adam Smith.

senses.d: Tenderness of feeling; pity.

Conscience.etym: [F. conscience, fr. L. conscientia, fr. consciens, p. pr. of conscire to know, to be conscious; con- + scire to know. See Science.]

senses.d: Consecrated; devoted; dedicated; sacred.
q: They were assembled in that consecrate place. Bacon.

Consecrate.etym: [L. consceratus, p. p. of conscerare to conscerate; con- + sacrare to consecrate, sacer sacred. See Sacred.]

senses.d: To make, or declare to be, sacred; to appropriate to sacred uses; to set apart, dedicate, or devote, to the service or worship of God; as, to consecrate a church; to give (one's self) unreservedly, as to the service of God.
q: One day in the week is . . . consecrated to a holy rest. Sharp.

senses.d: To set apart to a sacred office; as, to consecrate a bishop.
q: Thou shalt consecrate Aaron and his sons. Ex. xxix. 9.

senses.d: To canonize; to exalt to the rank of a saint; to enroll among the gods, as a Roman emperor.
To render venerable or revered; to hallow; to dignify; as, rules or principles consecrated by time.
The act or ceremony of consecrating; the state of being consecrated; dedication.
q: Until the days of your consecration be at an end. Lev. viii. 33.
Consecration makes not a place sacred, but only solemnly declares it so. South.

senses.d: To agree in opinion or sentiment; to be of the same mind; to accord; to concur.
q: And Saul was consenting unto his death. Acts. viii. 1.
Flourishing many years before Wyclif, and much consenting with him in jugdment. Fuller.

senses.d: To indicate or express a willingness; to yield to guidance, persuasion, or necessity; to give assent or approval; to comply.
q: My poverty, but not my will, consents. Shak.
And whispering “I will ne'er consent,” — consented. Byron.

Consent.syn: To accede; yield; assent; comply; agree; allow; concede; permit; admit; concur; acquiesce.
Consent.etym: [F. consentir, fr. L. consentire, -sensum, to feel together, agree; con- + sentire to feel. See Sense.]

senses.d: To grant; to allow; to assent to; to admit.
q: Interpreters . . . will not consent it to be a true story. Milton.

senses.d: Agreement in opinion or sentiment; the being of one mind; accord.
q: All with one consent began to make excuse. Luke xiv. 18.
They fell together all, as by consent. Shak.

senses.d: Correspondence in parts, qualities, or operations; agreement; harmony; coherence.
q: The melodious consent of the birds. Holland.
Such is the world's great harmony that springs From union, order, full consent of things. Pope.

senses.d: Voluntary accordance with, or concurrence in, what is done or proposed by another; acquiescence; compliance; approval; permission.
q: Thou wert possessed of David's throne By free consent of all. Milton.

senses.d: Capable, deliberate, and voluntary assent or agreement to, or concurrence in, some act or purpose, implying physical and mental power and free action.
Sympathy. See Sympathy, 4.

Consent.syn: Assent; acquiescence; concurrence; agreement; approval; permission. See Assent.

senses.d: To fix the mind on, with a view to a careful examination; to think on with care; to ponder; to study; to meditate on.
q: I will consider thy testimonies. Ps. cxix. 95.
Thenceforth to speculations high or deep I turned my thoughts, and with capacious mind Considered all things visible. Milton.

senses.d: To look at attentively; to observe; to examine.
q: She considereth a field, and buyeth it. Prov. xxxi. 16.

senses.d: To have regard to; to take into view or account; to pay due attention to; to respect.
q: Consider, sir, the chance of war: the day Was yours by accident. Shak.
England could grow into a posture of being more united at home, and more considered abroad. Sir W. Temple.

senses.d: To estimate; to think; to regard; to view.
q: Considered as plays, his works are absurd. Macaulay.

Consider.syn: To ponder; weigh; revolve; study; reflect or meditate on; contemplate; examine. See Ponder.
Consider.etym: [F. considérer, L. considerare, -sideratum, to consider, view attentively, prob. fr. con- + sidus, sideris, star, constellation; orig., therefore, to look at the stars. See Sidereal, and cf. Desire.]

senses.d: To think seriously; to make examination; to reflect; to deliberate.
q: We will consider of your suit. Shak.
'T were to consider too curiously, to consider so. Shak.
She wished she had taken a moment to consider, before rushing down stairs. W. Black

senses.d: To hesitate.
To stand firm; to be in a fixed or permanent state, as a body composed of parts in union or connection; to hold together; to be; to exist; to subsist; to be supported and maintained.
q: He is before all things, and by him all things consist. Col. i. 17.

senses.d: To be composed or made up; — followed by of.
q: The land would consist of plains and valleys. T. Burnet.

senses.d: To have as its substance or character, or as its foundation; to be; — followed by in.
q: If their purgation did consist in words. Shak.
A man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. Luke xii. 15.

senses.d: To be consistent or harmonious; to be in accordance; — formerly used absolutely, now followed by with.
q: This was a consisting story. Bp. Burnet.
Health consists with temperance alone. Pope.
For orders and degrees Jar not with liberty, but well consist. Milton.

senses.d: To insist; — followed by on.

Consist.syn: To Consist, Consist of, Consist in.
Consist.etym: [L. consistere to stand still or firm; con- + sistere to stand, cause to stand, stare to stand: cf. F. consister. See Stand.]

senses.d: The act of consoling; the state of being consoled; allevation of misery or distress of mind; refreshment of spirit; comfort; that which consoles or comforts the spirit.
q: Against such cruelties With inward consolations recompensed. Milton.
Are the consolations of God small with thee? Job xv. 11.

senses.d: One who shares the lot of another; a companion; a partner; especially, a wife or husband.
q: He single chose to live, and shunned to wed, Well pleased to want a consort of his bed. Dryden.
The consort of the queen has passed from this troubled sphere. Thakeray.
The snow-white gander, invariably accompanied by his darker consort. Darwin.

senses.d: A ship keeping company with another.
Concurrence; conjunction; combination; association; union.
q: Take it singly, and it carries an air of levity; but, in consort with the rest, has a meaning quite different. Atterbury.

senses.d: An assembly or association of persons; a company; a group; a combination.
q: In one consort' there sat Cruel revenge and rancorous despite, Disloyal treason, and heart-burning hate. Spenser.
Lord, place me in thy consort. Herbert.

senses.d: Harmony of sounds; concert, as of musical instruments.
q: To make a sad consort'; Come, let us join our mournful song with theirs. Spenser.

Consort.etym: [L. consore, -sortis; con- + sors lot, fate, share. See Sort.]

senses.d: To unite or to keep company; to associate; — used with with.
q: Which of the Grecian chiefs consorts with thee? Dryden.

senses.d: To unite or join, as in affection, harmony, company, marriage, etc.; to associate.
q: He with his consorted Eve. Milton.
For all that pleasing is to living ears Was there consorted in one harmony. Spenser.
He begins to consort himself with men. Locke.

senses.d: To attend; to accompany.
q: Thou, wretched boy, that didst consort him here, Shalt with him hence. Shak.

senses.d: A combination of men for an evil purpose; an agreement, between two or more persons, to commit a crime in concert, as treason; a plot.
q: When shapen was all his conspiracy From point to point. Chaucer.
They made a conspiracy against . 2 Kings xiv. 19.
I had forgot that foul conspiracy
Of the beast Caliban and his confederates. Shak.

senses.d: A concurence or general tendency, as of circumstances, to one event, as if by agreement.
q: A conspiracy in all heavenly and earthly things. Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: An agreement, manifesting itself in words or deeds, by which two or more persons confederate to do an unlawful act, or to use unlawful to do an act which is lawful; confederacy.
One who engages in a conspiracy; a plotter.
To make an agreement, esp. a secret agreement, to do some act, as to commit treason or a crime, or to do some unlawful deed; to plot together.
q: They conspired against to slay him. Gen. xxxvii. 18.
You have conspired against our royal person, Joined with an enemy proclaimed. Shak.

senses.d: To concur to one end; to agree.
q: The press, the pulpit, and the stage Conspire to censure and expose our age. Roscommon.

Conspire.syn: To unite; concur; complot; confederate; league.
Conspire.etym: [F. conspirer, L. conspirare to blow together, harmonize, agree, plot; con- + spirare to breathe, blow. See Spirit.]

senses.d: To plot; to plan; to combine for.
q: Angry clouds conspire your overthrow. Bp. Hall.

senses.d: Firm; solid; fixed; immovable; — opposed to fluid.
q: If . . . you mix them, you may turn these two fluid liquors into a constant body. Boyle.

senses.d: Not liable, or given, to change; permanent; regular; continuous; continually recurring; steadfast; faithful; not fickle.
q: Both loving one fair maid, they yet remained constant friends. Sir P. Sidney.
I am constant to my purposes. Shak.
His gifts, his constant courtship, nothing gained. Dryden.
Onward the constant current sweeps. Longfellow.

senses.d: Remaining unchanged or invariable, as a quantity, force, law, etc. Contrasted with variable.
Consistent; logical.

Constant.syn: Fixed; steadfast; unchanging; permanent; unalterable; immutable; invariable; perpetual; continual; resolute; firm; unshaken; determined.
Constant.etym: [L. onstans, -antis, p. pr. of constare to stand firm, to be consistent; con- + stare to stand: cf. F. constant. See Stand and cf. Cost, v. t.]

senses.d: That which is not subject to change; that which is invariable.
A quantity that does not change its value; — used in countradistinction to variable.

A number whose value, when ascertained (as by observation) and substituted in a general mathematical formula expressing an astronomical law, completely determines that law and enables predictions to be made of its effect in particular cases.
A number expressing some property or condition of a substance or of an instrument of precision; as, the dielectric constant of quartz; the collimation constant of a transit instrument.
With constancy; steadily; continually; perseveringly; without cessation; uniformly.
q: But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Acts. xii. 15.

senses.d: A cluster or group of fixed stars, or division of the heavens, designated in most cases by the name of some animal, or of some mythologial personage, within whose imaginary outline, as traced upon the heavens, the group is included.
q: The constellations seem to have been almost purposely named and delineated to cause as much confusion and inconvenience as possible. Sir J. Herschel.

senses.d: An assemblage of splendors or excellences.
q: The constellations of genius had already begun to show itself . . . which was to shed a glory over the meridian and close of Philip's reign. Prescott.

senses.d: Fortune; fate; destiny.
q: It is constellation, which causeth all that a man doeth. Gower.

senses.d: To secure by bonds; to chain; to bond or confine; to hold tightly; to constringe.
q: He binds in chains The drowsy prophet, and his limbs constrains. Dryden.
When winter frosts constrain the fields with cold. Dryden.

senses.d: To bring into a narrow compass; to compress.
q: How the strait stays the slender waist constrain. Gay.

senses.d: To hold back by force; to restrain; to repress.
q: My sire in caves constrains the winds. Dryden.

senses.d: To compel; to force; to necessitate; to oblige.
q: The love of Christ constraineth us. 2. Cor. v. 14.
I was constrained to appeal unto Cæsar. Acts xxviii. 19.

senses.d: To violate; to ravish.
To produce in such a manner as to give an unnatural effect; as, a constrained voice.

Constrain.syn: To compel; force; drive; impel; urge; press.
Constrain.etym: [OF. constraindre, F. contrainde, L. constringere; con- + stringere to draw tight. See Strain, and. cf. Constrict, Constringe.]

senses.d: Marked by constraint; not free; not voluntary; embarrassed; as, a constrained manner; a constrained tone.
The act of constraining, or the state of being constrained; that which compels to, or restrains from, action; compulsion; restraint; necessity.
q: Long imprisonment and hard constraint. Spenser.
Not by constraint, but by my choice, I came. Dryden.

senses.d: To seek the opinion or advice of another; to take counsel; to deliberate together; to confer.
q: Let us consult upon to-morrow's business. Shak.
All the laws of England have been made by the kings England, consulting with the nobility and commons. Hobbes.

Consult.etym: [L. consultare, fr. consulere to consult: cf. f. consulter. Cf. Counsel.]

senses.d: To ask advice of; to seek the opinion of; to apply to for information or instruction; to refer to; as, to consult a physician; to consult a dictionary.
q: Men forgot, or feared, to consult nature . . . ; they were content to consult libraries. Whewell.

senses.d: To have reference to, in judging or acting; to have regard to; to consider; as, to consult one's wishes.
q: We are . . . to consult the necessities of life, rather than matters of ornament and delight. L'Estrange.

senses.d: To deliberate upon; to take for.
q: Manythings were there consulted for the future, yet nothing was positively resolved. Clarendon.

senses.d: To bring about by counsel or contrivance; to devise; to contrive.
q: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people. Hab. ii. 10.

senses.d: The act of consulting or deliberating; consultation; also, the result of consulation; determination; decision.
q: The council broke; And all grave consults dissolved in smoke. Dryden.

senses.d: A council; a meeting for consultation.
Agreement; concert
The act of consulting or conferring; deliberation of two or more persons on some matter, with a view to a decision.
q: Thus they doubtful consultations dark Ended. Milton.

senses.d: A council or conference, as of physicians, held to consider a special case, or of lawyers restained in a cause.
One who consults, or asks counsel or information.
To destroy, as by decomposition, dissipation, waste, or fire; to use up; to expend; to waste; to burn up; to eat up; to devour.
q: If he were putting to my house the brand That shall consume it. Shak.
Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth consume. Matt. vi. 20 (Rev. Ver.).
Let me alone . . . that I may consume them. Ex. xxxii. 10.

Consume.syn: To destroy; swallow up; ingulf; absorb; waste; exhaust; spend; expend; squander; lavish; dissipate.
Consume.etym: [L. consumere to take wholly or completely, to consume; con- + sumere to take; sub + emere to buy. See Redeem.]

senses.d: To waste away slowly.
q: Therefore, let Benedick, like covered fire, Consume away in sighs. Shak.

senses.d: The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated; completion; perfection; termination; end (as of the world or of life).
q: “'T is a consummation Devoutly to be wished. Shak.
From its original to its consummation. Addison.
Quiet consummation have, And renownéd be thy grave. Shak.

senses.d: The act or process of consuming by use, waste, etc.; decay; destruction.
q: Every new advance of the price to the consumer is a new incentive to him to retrench the quality of his consumption. Burke.

senses.d: The state or process of being consumed, wasted, or diminished; waste; diminution; loss; decay.

A progressive wasting away of the body; esp., that form of wasting, attendant upon pulmonary phthisis and associated with cough, spitting of blood, hectic fever, etc.; pulmonary phthisis; — called also pulmonary consumption.
To hold within fixed limits; to comprise; to include; to inclose; to hold.
q: Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can not contain thee; how much less this house! 2 Chron. vi. 18.
When that this body did contain a spirit. Shak.
What thy stores contain bring forth. Milton.

senses.d: To have capacity for; to be able to hold; to hold; to be equivalent to; as, a bushel contains four pecks.
To put constraint upon; to restrain; to confine; to keep within bounds.
q: The king's person contains the unruly people from evil occasions. Spenser.
Fear not, my lord: we can contain ourselves. Shak.

Contain.etym: [OE. contenen, conteinen, F. contenir, fr. L. continere, -tentum; con- + tenere to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Countenance.]

senses.d: To restrain desire; to live in continence or chastity.
q: But if they can not contain, let them marry. 1 Cor. vii. 9.

senses.d: To view or treat with contempt, as mean and despicable; to reject with disdain; to despise; to scorn.
q: Thy pompous delicacies I contemn. Milton.
One who contemned divine and human laws. Dryden.

Contemn.syn: To despise; scorn; disdain; spurn; slight; neglect; underrate; overlook.
Contemn.etym: [L. contemnere, -temptum; con- + temnere to slight, despise: cf. OF. contemner.]

senses.d: The act of contemning or despising; the feeling with which one regards that which is esteemed mean, vile, or worthless; disdain; scorn.
q: Criminal contempt of public feeling. Macaulay.
Nothing, says Longinus, can be great, the contempt of which is great. Addison.

senses.d: The state of being despised; disgrace; shame.
q: Contempt and begarry hangs upon thy back. Shak.

senses.d: An act or expression denoting contempt.
q: Little insults and contempts. Spectator.
The contempt and anger of his lip. Shak.

senses.d: Disobedience of the rules, orders, or process of a court of justice, or of rules or orders of a legislative body; disorderly, contemptuous, or insolent language or behavior in presence of a court, tending to disturb its proceedings, or impair the respect due to its authority.

Contempt.syn: Disdain; scorn; derision; mockery; contumely; neglect; disregard; slight.
Contempt.etym: [L. contemptus, fr. contemnere: cf. OF. contempt. See Contemn.]

senses.d: Worthy of contempt; deserving of scorn or disdain; mean; vile; despicable.
q: The arguments of tyranny are ascontemptible as its force is dreadful. Burke.

senses.d: Despised; scorned; neglected; abject.
Insolent; scornful; contemptuous.
q: If she should make tender of her love, 't is very possible he 'll scorn it; for the man . . . hath a contemptible spirit. Shak.

Contemptible.syn: Despicable; abject; vile; mean; base; paltry; worthless; sorry; pitiful; scurrile.

senses.d: Manifesting or expressing contempt or disdain; scornful; haughty; insolent; disdainful.
q: A proud, contemptuous behavior. Hammond.
Savage invective and contemptuous sarcasm. Macaulay.
Rome . . . entertained the most contemptuous opinion of the Jews. Atterbury.

Contemptuous.syn: Scornful; insolent; haughty; disdainful; supercilious; insulting; contumelious.

senses.d: In a contemptuous manner; with scorn or disdain; despitefully.
q: The apostles and most eminent Christians were poor, and used contemptuously. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: To strive in opposition; to contest; to dispute; to vie; to quarrel; to fight.
q: For never two such kingdoms did contend Without much fall of blood. Shak.
The Lord said unto me, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle. Deut. ii. 9.
In ambitious strength I did Contend against thy valor. Shak.

senses.d: To struggle or exert one's self to obtain or retain possession of, or to defend.
q: You sit above, and see vain men below Contend for what you only can bestow. Dryden.

senses.d: To strive in debate; to engage in discussion; to dispute; to argue.
q: The question which our author would contend for. Locke.
Many things he fiercely contended about were trivial. Dr. H. More.

Contend.syn: To struggle; fight; combat; vie; strive; oppose; emulate; contest; litigate; dispute; debate.
Contend.etym: [OF. contendre, L. contendere, -tentum; con- + tendere to strech. See Tend.]

senses.d: To struggle for; to contest.
q: Carthage shall contend the world with Rome.Dryden.

senses.d: Contained within limits; hence, having the desires limited by that which one has; not disposed to repine or grumble; satisfied; contented; at rest.
q: Having food and rai ment, let us be therewith content. 1 Tim. vi. 8.

Content.etym: [F. content, fr. L. contentus, p. p. of contenire to hold together, restrain. See Contain.]

senses.d: That which is contained; the thing or things held by a receptacle or included within specified limits; as, the contents of a cask or bale or of a room; the contents of a book.
q: I shall prove these writings . . . authentic, and the contents true, and worthy of a divine original. Grew.

senses.d: Power of containing; capacity; extent; size.
q: Strong ship's, of great content. Bacon.

senses.d: Area or quantity of space or matter contained within certain limits; as, solid contents; superficial contents.
q: The geometrical content, figure, and situation of all the lands of a kingdom. Graunt.

senses.d: To satisfy the desires of; to make easy in any situation; to appease or quiet; to gratify; to please.
q: Do not content yourselves with obscure and confused ideas, where clearer are to be attained. I. Watts.
Pilate, willing to content the people, released Barabbas unto them. Mark xv. 15.

senses.d: To satisfy the expectations of; to pay; to requite.
q: Come the next Sabbath, and I will content you. Shak.

Content.syn: To satisfy; appease; please. See Satiate.
Content.etym: [F. contenter, LL. contentare, fr. L. contentus, p. p. See Content, a.]

senses.d: Rest or quietness of the mind in one's present condition; freedom from discontent; satisfaction; contentment; moderate happiness.
q: Such is the fullness of my heart's content. Shak.

senses.d: Acquiescence without examination.
q: The sense they humbly take upon content. Pope.

senses.d: That which contents or satisfies; that which if attained would make one happy.
q: So will I in England work your grace's full content. Shak.

senses.d: An expression of assent to a bill or motion; an affirmative vote; also, a member who votes “Content.”.
q: Supposing the number of “Contents” and “Not contents” strictly equal in number and consequence. Burke.

senses.d: A violent effort or struggle to obtain, or to resist, something; contest; strife.
q: I would my arms could match thee in contention. Shak.

senses.d: Strife in words; controversy; altercation; quarrel; dispute; as, a bone of contention.
q: Contentions and strivings about the law. Titus iii. 9.

senses.d: Vehemence of endeavor; eagerness; ardor; zeal.
q: An end . . . worthy our utmost contention to obtain. Rogers.

senses.d: A point maintained in an argument, or a line of argument taken in its support; the subject matter of discussion or strife; a position taken or contended for.
q: All men seem agreed what is to be done; the contention is how the subject is to be divided and defined. Bagehot.
This was my original contention, and I still maintain that you should abide by your former decision. Jowett.

Contention.syn: Struggle; strife; contest; quarrel; combat; conflict; feud; litigation; controversy; dissension; variance; disagreement; debate; competition; emulation.

senses.d: Fond of contention; given to angry debate; provoking dispute or contention; quarrelsome.
q: Despotic and contentious temper. Macaulay.

senses.d: Relating to contention or strife; involving or characterized by contention.
q: More cheerful, though not less contentious, regions. Brougham.

senses.d: Contested; litigated; litigious; having power to decide controversy.

Contentious.syn: Quarrelsome; pugnacious; dissentious; wrangling; litigious; perverse; peevish.

senses.d: The state of being contented or satisfied; content.
q: Contentment without external honor is humility. Grew.
Godliness with contentment is great gain. 1 Tim. vi. 6.

senses.d: The act or process of contenting or satisfying; as, the contentment of avarice is impossible.
Gratification; pleasure; satisfaction.
q: At Paris the prince spent one whole day to give his mind some contentment in viewing of a famous city. Sir H. Wotton.

Contentment.etym: [Cf. F. contentement. See Content, v. t.]

senses.d: Proceeding without interruption or cesstaion; continuous; unceasing; lasting; abiding.
q: He that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast. Prov. xv. 15.

senses.d: Occuring in steady and rapid succession; very frequent; often repeated.
q: The eye is deligh by a continental succession of small landscapes. W. Irwing.

Continual.syn: Constant; prepetual; incessant; unceasing; uninterrupted; unintermitted; continuous. See Constant, and Continuous.

senses.d: Without cessation; unceasingly; continuously; as, the current flows continually.
q: Why do not all animals continually increase in bigness? Bentley.

senses.d: In regular or repeated succession; very often.
q: Thou shalt eat bread at my table continually. 2 Sam. ix. 7.

senses.d: A holding on, or remaining in a particular state; permanence, as of condition, habits, abode, etc.; perseverance; constancy; duration; stay.
q: Great plagues, and of long continuance. Deut. xxviii. 59.
Patient continuance in well-doing. Rom. ii. 7.

senses.d: Uninterrupted succession; continuation; constant renewal; perpetuation; propagation.
q: The brute immediately regards his own preservation or the continuance of his species. Addison.

senses.d: A holding together; continuity.
The adjournment of the proceedings in a cause from one day, or from one stated term of a court, to another.
To remain in a given place or condition; to remain in connection with; to abide; to stay.
q: Here to continue, and build up here A growing empire. Milton.
They continue with me now three days, and have nothing to eat. Matt. xv. 32.

senses.d: To be permanent or durable; to endure; to last.
q: But now thy kingdom shall not continue. 1 Sam. xiii. 14.

senses.d: To be steadfast or constant in any course; to persevere; to abide; to endure; to persist; to keep up or maintain a particular condition, course, or series of actions; as, the army continued to advance.
q: If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed. John viii. 31.

Continue.etym: [F. continuer, L. continuare, -tinuatum, to connect, continue, fr. continuus. See Continuous, and cf. Continuate.]

senses.d: To unite; to connect.
q: the use of the navel is to continue the infant unto the mother. Sir T. browne.

senses.d: To protract or extend in duration; to preserve or persist in; to cease not.
q: O continue thy loving kindness unto them that know thee. Ps. xxxvi. 10.
You know how to make yourself happy by only continuing such a life as you have been long accustomed to lead. Pope.

senses.d: To carry onward or extend; to prolong or produce; to add to or draw out in length.
q: A bridge of wond'rous length, From hell continued, reaching th' utmost orb of this frail world. Milton.

senses.d: To retain; to suffer or cause to remain; as, the trustees were continued; also, to suffer to live.
q: And how shall we continue Claudio. Shak.

senses.d: Having extension of time, space, order of events, exertion of energy, etc.; extended; protracted; uninterrupted; also, resumed after interruption; extending through a succession of issues, session, etc.; as, a continued story.
To assert the contrary of; to oppose in words; to take issue with; to gainsay; to deny the truth of, as of a statement or a speaker; to impugn.
q: Dear Duff, I prithee, contradict thyself, And say it is not so. Shak.
The future can not contradict the past. Wordsworth.

senses.d: To be contrary to; to oppose; to resist.
q: No truth can contradict another truth. Hooker.
A greater power than we can contradict Hath thwarted our intents. Shak.

Contradict.etym: [L. contradictus, p. p. of contradicere to speak against; contra + dicere to speak. See Diction.]

senses.d: To oppose in words; to gainsay; to deny, or assert the contrary of, something.
q: They . . . spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming. Acts xiii. 45.

senses.d: An assertion of the contrary to what has been said or affirmed; denial of the truth of a statement or assertion; contrary declaration; gainsaying.
q: His fair demands Shall be accomplished without contradiction. Shak.

senses.d: Direct opposition or repugnancy; inconsistency; incongruity or contrariety; one who, or that which, is inconsistent.
q: can he make deathless death? That were to make Strange contradiction. Milton.
We state our experience and then we come to a manly resolution of acting in contradiction to it. Burke.
Both parts of a contradiction can not possibly be true. Hobbes.
Of contradictions infinite the slave. Wordsworth.

Contradiction.etym: [L. contradictio answer, objection: cf. F. contradiction.]

senses.d: On the contrary; oppositely; on the other hand.
q: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing; but contrariwise, blessing. 1 Pet. iii. 9.

senses.d: In a contrary order; conversely.
q: Everything that acts upon the fluids must, at the same time, act upon the solids, and contrariwise. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse; as, contrary winds.
q: And if ye walk contrary unto me, and will not hearken unto me. Lev. xxvi. 21.
We have lost our labor; they are gone a contrary way. Shak.

senses.d: Opposed; contradictory; repugnant; inconsistent.
q: Fame, if not double-faced, is double mouthed, And with contrary blast proclaims most deeds. Milton.
The doctrine of the earth's motion appeared to be contrary to the sacred Scripture. Whewell.

senses.d: Given to opposition; perverse; forward; wayward; as, a contrary disposition; a contrary child.
Affirming the opposite; so opposed as to destroy each other; as, contrary propositions.

Contrary.syn: Adverse; repugnant; hostile; inimical; discordant; inconsistent.
Contrary.etym: [OE. contrarie, contraire, F. contraire, fr. L. contrarius, fr. contra. See Contra-.]

senses.d: A thing that is of contrary or opposite qualities.
q: No contraries hold more antipathy Than I and such a knave. Shak.

senses.d: An opponent; an enemy.
the opposite; a proposition, fact, or condition incompatible with another; as, slender proofs which rather show the contrary. See Converse, n., 1.
To contradict or oppose; to thwart.
q: I was advised not to contrary the king. Bp. Latimer.

senses.d: The act of contributing.
That which is contributed; — either the portion which an individual furnishes to the common stock, or the whole which is formed by the gifts of individuals.
q: A certain contribution for the poor saints which are at jerusalem. Rom. xv. 26.
Aristotle's actual contributions to the physical sciences. Whewell.

senses.d: An irregular and arbitrary imposition or tax leved on the people of a town or country.
q: These sums, . . . and the forced contributions paid by luckless peasants, enabled him to keep his straggling troops together. Motley.

senses.d: Payment, by each of several jointly liable, of a share in a loss suffered or an amount paid by one of their number for the common benefit.
Thoroughly bruised or broken.
Broken down with grief and penitence; deeply sorrowful for sin because it is displeasing to God; humbly and thoroughly penitent.
q: A contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. Ps. li. 17.
Be penitent, and for thy fault contrite. Milton.

Contrite.etym: [L. contritus bruised, p. p. of contrere to grind, bruise; con- + terere to rub, grind: cf. F. contrit See Trite.]

senses.d: A contrite person.
In a contrite manner.
Contention; dispute; debate; discussion; agitation of contrary opinions.
q: This left no room for controversy about the title. Locke.
A dispute is commonly oral, and a controversy in writing. Johnson.

senses.d: Quarrel; strife; cause of variance; difference.
q: The Lord hath a controversy with the nations. Jer. xxv. 31.

senses.d: A suit in law or equity; a question of right.
q: When any man that had a controversy came to the king for judgment. 2 Sam. xv. 2.

Controversy.syn: Dispute; debate; disputation; disagreement; altercation; contention; wrangle; strife; quarrel.
Controversy.etym: [L. controversia, fr. controversus turned against, disputed; contro- = contra + versus, p. p. of vertere to turn. See Verse.]

senses.d: Fit or adapted; suitable; proper; becoming; appropriate.
q: Feed me with food convenient for me. Prov. xxx. 8.
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient. Eph. v. 4.

senses.d: Affording accommodation or advantage; well adapted to use; handly; as, a convenient house; convenient implements or tools.
Seasonable; timely; opportune; as, a convenient occasion; a convenient season.
Near at hand; easy of access.
q: Hereties used to be brought thither, convenient for burning. Thackeray.

Convenient.syn: Fit; suitable; proper; adapted; fitted; suited; handly; commodious.
Convenient.etym: [L. conveniens, -entis, suitable, p. pr. of convenire to be suitable, to come. See Convene, v. i.]

senses.d: In a convenient manner, form, or situation; without difficulty.
Having frequent or customary intercourse; familiary associated; intimately acquainted.
q: I have been conversant with the first persons of the age. Dryden.

senses.d: Familiar or acquainted by use or study; well-informed; versed; — generally used with with, sometimes with in.
q: Deeply conversant in the Platonic philosophy. Dryden.
he uses the different dialects as one who had been conversant with them all. Pope.
Conversant only with the ways of men. Cowper.

senses.d: Concerned; occupied.
q: Education . . . is conversant about children. W. Wotton.

Conversant.etym: [L. conversans, p. pr. of conversari: cf. F. conversant.]

senses.d: One who converses with another; a convenser.
General course of conduct; behavior.
q: Let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel. Philip. i. 27.

senses.d: Familiar intercourse; intimate fellowship or association; close acquaintance.
q: I set down, out of long experience in business and much conversation in books, what I thought pertinent to this business. Bacon.

senses.d: Commerce; intercourse; traffic.
q: All traffic and mutual conversation. Hakluyt.

senses.d: Colloquial discourse; oral interchange of sentiments and observations; informal dialogue.
q: The influence exercised by his conversation was altogether without a parallel. Macaulay.

senses.d: Sexual intercourse; as, criminal conversation.

Conversation.syn: Intercourse; communion; commerce; familiarity; discourse; dialogue; colloquy; talk; chat.
Conversation.etym: [OE. conversacio (in senses 1 & 2), OF. conversacion, F. conversation, fr. L. conversatio frequent abode in a place, intercourse, LL. also, manner of life.]

senses.d: The act of turning or changing from one state or condition to another, or the state of being changed; transmutation; change.
q: Artificial conversion of water into ice. Bacon.
The conversion of the aliment into fat. Arbuthnot.

senses.d: The act of changing one's views or course, as in passing from one side, party, or from of religion to another; also, the state of being so changed.
An appropriation of, and dealing with the property of another as if it were one's own, without right; as, the conversion of a horse.
q: Or bring my action of conversion And trover for my goods. Hudibras.

senses.d: The act of interchanging the terms of a proposition, as by putting the subject in the place of the predicate, or the contrary.
A change or reduction of the form or value of a proposition; as, the conversion of equations; the conversion of proportions.
A change of front, as a body of troops attacked in the flank.

A spiritual and moral change attending a change of belief with conviction; a change of heart; a change from the service of the world to the service of God; a change of the ruling disposition of the soul, involving a transformation of the outward life.
q: He oft Frequented their assemblies, . . . and to them preached Conversion and repentance, as to souls In prison under judgments imminent. Milton.

Conversion.etym: [L. conversio: cf. F. conversion. See Convert.]

senses.d: To cause to turn; to turn.
q: O, which way shall I first convert myself? B. Jonson.

senses.d: To change or turn from one state or condition to another; to alter in form, substance, or quality; to transform; to transmute; as, to convert water into ice.
q: If the whole atmosphere were converted into water. T. Burnet.
That still lessens The sorrow, and converts it nigh to joy. Milton.

senses.d: To change or turn from one belief or course to another, as from one religion to another or from one party or sect to another.
q: No attempt was made to convert the Moslems. Prescott.

senses.d: To produce the spiritual change called conversion in (any one); to turn from a bad life to a good one; to change the heart and moral character of (any one) from the controlling power of sin to that of holiness.
q: He which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death. Lames v. 20.

senses.d: To apply to any use by a diversion from the proper or intended use; to appropriate dishonestly or illegally.
q: When a bystander took a coin to get it changed, and converted it, held no larceny. Cooley.

senses.d: To exchange for some specified equivalent; as, to convert goods into money.
To change (one proposition) into another, so that what was the subject of the first becomes the predicate of the second.
To turn into another language; to translate.
q: Which story . . . Catullus more elegantly converted. B. Jonson.

Convert.etym: [L. convertere, -versum; con- + vertere to turn: cf. F. convertir. See Verse.]

senses.d: To be turned or changed in character or direction; to undergo a change, physically or morally.
q: If Nebo had had the preaching that thou hast, they would have converted. Latimer.
A red dust which converth into worms. Sandys.
The public hope And eye to thee converting. Thomson.

senses.d: A person who is converted from one opinion or practice to another; a person who is won over to, or heartily embraces, a creed, religious system, or party, in which he has not previously believed; especially, one who turns from the controlling power of sin to that of holiness, or from unbelief to Christianity.
q: The Jesuits did not persuade the converts to lay aside the use of images. Bp. Stillingfleet.

senses.d: A lay friar or brother, permitted to enter a monastery for the service of the house, but without orders, and not allowed to sing in the choir.
To carry from one place to another; to bear or transport.
q: I will convey them by sea in floats. 1 Kings v. 9.
Convey me to my bed, then to my grave. Shak.

senses.d: To cause to pass from one place or person to another; to serve as a medium in carrying (anything) from one place or person to another; to transmit; as, air conveys sound; words convey ideas.
To transfer or deliver to another; to make over, as property;
q: The Earl of Desmond . . . secretly conveyed all his lands to feoffees in trust. Spenser.

senses.d: To impart or communicate; as, to convey an impression; to convey information.
q: Men fill one another's heads with noise and sound, but convey not thereby their thoughts. Locke.

senses.d: To manage with privacy; to carry out.
q: I . . . will convey the business as I shall find means. Shak.

senses.d: To carry or take away secretly; to steal; to thieve.
To accompany; to convoy.

Convey.syn: To carry; transport; bear; transmit; transfer.
Convey.etym: [OF. conveir, convoier, to escort, convoy, F. convoyer, LL. conviare, fr. L. con- + via way. See Viaduct, Voyage, and cf. Convoy.]

senses.d: To play the thief; to steal.
q: But as I am Crack, I will convey, crossbite, and cheat upon Simplicius. Marston.

senses.d: Proved or found guilty; convicted.
q: Convict by flight, and rebel to all law. Milton.

Convict.etym: [L. convictus, p. p. of convincere to convict, prove. See Convice.]

senses.d: A person proved guilty of a crime alleged against him; one legally convicted or sentenced to punishment for some crime.
A criminal sentenced to penal servitude.
To prove or find guilty of an offense or crime charged; to pronounce guilty, as by legal decision, or by one's conscience.
q: He . . . had been convicted by a jury. Macaulay.
They which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one. John viii. 9.

senses.d: To prove or show to be false; to confute; to refute.
To demonstrate by proof or evidence; to prove.
q: Imagining that these proofs will convict a testament, to have that in it which other men can nowhere by reading find. Hooker.

senses.d: To defeat; to doom to destruction.
q: A whole armado of convicted sail. Shak.

senses.d: To overpower; to overcome; to subdue or master.
q: His two chamberlains Will I with wine and wassail so convince That memory, the warder of the brain, Shall be a fume. Shak.

senses.d: To overcome by argument; to force to yield assent to truth; to satisfy by proof.
q: Such convincing proofs and assurances of it as might enable them to convince others. Atterbury.

senses.d: To confute; to prove the fallacy of.
q: God never wrought miracle to convince atheism, because his ordinary works convince it. Bacon.

senses.d: To prove guilty; to convict.
q: Which of you convinceth me of sin? John viii. 46.
Seek not to convince me of a crime Which I can ne'er repent, nor you can pardon. Dryden.

Convince.etym: [L. convincere, -victum, to refute, prove; con- + vincere to conquer. See Victor, and cf. Convict.]

senses.d: The act of calling or assembling by summons.
An assembly or meeting.
q: In the first day there shall be a holy convocation. Ex. xii. 16.

senses.d: An assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
An academical assembly, in which the business of the university is transacted.

Convocation.syn: meeting; assembly; congregation; congress; diet; convention; synod; council.
Convocation.etym: [L. convocatio: cf. F. convocation. See Convoke.]

senses.d: A rabbit, esp., the European rabbit (Lepus cuniculus)
A simpleton.
q: It is a most simple animal; whence are derived our usual phrases of cony and cony catcher. Diet's Dry Dinner (1599).

senses.d: An important edible West Indian fish (Epinephelus apua); the hind of Bermuda.

Cony.etym: [OE. coning, conig, coni, OF. connin, conin, connil, fr. L. cuniculus a rabbit, cony, prob. an Hispanic word.]

senses.d: To make a low repeated cry or sound, like the characteristic note of pigeons or doves.
q: The stockdove only through the forest cooes, Mournfully hoarse. Thomson.

senses.d: To show affection; to act in a loving way. See under Bill, v. i.
To make the noise of the cuckoo.
q: Constant cuckoos cook on every side. The Silkworms (1599).

senses.d: To throw.
One whose occupation is to prepare food for the table; one who dresses or cooks meat or vegetables for eating.
A fish, the European striped wrasse.

Cook.etym: [AS. cōc, fr. l. cocus, coquus, coquus, fr. coquere to cook; akin to Gr. �, Skr. pac, and to E. apricot, biscuit, concoct, dyspepsia, precocious. Cf. Pumpkin.]

senses.d: To prepare, as food, by boiling, roasting, baking, broiling, etc.; to make suitable for eating, by the agency of fire or heat.
To concoct or prepare; hence, to tamper with or alter; to garble; — often with up; as, to cook up a story; to cook an account.
q: They all of them receive the same advices from abroad, and very often in the same words; but their way of cooking it is so different. Addison.

senses.d: To prepare food for the table.
Moderately cold; between warm and cold; lacking in warmth; producing or promoting coolness.
q: Fanned with cool winds. Milton.

senses.d: Not ardent, warm, fond, or passionate; not hasty; deliberate; exercising self-control; self-possessed; dispassionate; indifferent; as, a cool lover; a cool debater.
q: For a patriot, too cool. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Not retaining heat; light; as, a cool dress.
Manifesting coldness or dislike; chilling; apathetic; as, a cool manner.
Quietly impudent; negligent of propriety in matters of minor importance, either ignorantly or willfully; presuming and selfish; audacious; as, cool behavior.
q: Its cool stare of familiarity was intolerable. Hawthorne.

senses.d: Applied facetiously, in a vague sense, to a sum of money, commonly as if to give emphasis to the largeness of the amount.
q: He had lost a cool hundred. Fielding.
Leaving a cool thousand to Mr. Matthew Pocket. Dickens.

Cool.syn: Calm; dispassionate; self-possessed; composed; repulsive; frigid; alienated; impudent.
Cool.etym: [AS. cōl; akin to D. koel, G. kühl, OHG. chouli, Dan. kölig, Sw. kylig, also to AS. calan to be cold, Icel. kala. See Cold, and cf. Chill.]

senses.d: A moderate state of cold; coolness; — said of the temperature of the air between hot and cold; as, the cool of the day; the cool of the morning or evening.
To make cool or cold; to reduce the temperature of; as, ice cools water.
q: Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue. Luke xvi. 24.

senses.d: To moderate the heat or excitement of; to allay, as passion of any kind; to calm; to moderate.
q: We have reason to cool our raging motions, our carnal stings, our unbitted lusts. Shak.

senses.d: To become less hot; to lose heat.
q: I saw a smith stand with his hammer, thus, the whilst his iron did on the anvil cool. Shak.

senses.d: To lose the heat of excitement or passion; to become more moderate.
q: I will not give myself liberty to think, lest I should cool. Congreve.

senses.d: The top of a thing; the head; a crest.
q: Cop they used to call The tops of many hills. Drayton.

senses.d: A conical or conical-ended mass of coiled thread, yarn, or roving, wound upon a spindle, etc.
A tube or quill upon which silk is wound.
Same as Merlon.
A policeman.

Cop.etym: [AS. cop; cf. G. kopf head. Cf. Cup, Cob.]

senses.d: A covering for the head.
Anything regarded as extended over the head, as the arch or concave of the sky, the roof of a house, the arch over a door.

An ecclesiastical vestment or cloak, semicircular in form, reaching from the shoulders nearly to the feet, and open in front except at the top, where it is united by a band or clasp. It is worn in processions and on some other occasions.
q: A hundred and sixty priests all in their copes. Bp. Burnet.

senses.d: An ancient tribute due to the lord of the soil, out of the lead mines in Derbyshire, England.
The top part of a flask or mold; the outer part of a loam mold.

Cope.etym: [A doublet of cape. See Cape, Cap.]

senses.d: To form a cope or arch; to bend or arch; to bow.
q: Some bending down and coping toward the earth. Holland.

senses.d: To pare the beak or talons of (a hawk).
To exchange or barter.
To encounter; to meet; to have to do with.
q: Horatio, thou art e'en as just a man As e'er my conversation coped withal. Shak.

senses.d: To enter into or maintain a hostile contest; to struggle; to combat; especially, to strive or contend on equal terms or with success; to match; to equal; — usually followed by with.
q: Host coped with host, dire was the din of war. Philips.
Their generals have not been able to cope with the troops of Athens. Addison.

Cope.etym: [OE. copen, coupen, to buy, bargain, prob. from D. koopen to buy, orig., to bargain. See Cheap.]

senses.d: To bargain for; to buy.
To make return for; to requite; to repay.
q: three thousand ducats due unto the Jew, We freely cope your courteous pains withal. Shak.

senses.d: To match one's self against; to meet; to encounter.
q: I love to cope him in these sullen fits. Shak.
They say he yesterday coped Hector in the battle, and struck him down. Shak.

senses.d: The highest or covering course of masonry in a wall, often with sloping edges to carry off water; — sometimes called capping.

A common metal of a reddish color, both ductile and malleable, and very tenacious. It is one of the best conductors of heat and electricity. Symbol Cu. Atomic weight 63.3. It is one of the most useful metals in itself, and also in its alloys, brass and bronze.
A coin made of copper; a penny, cent, or other minor coin of copper.
q: My friends filled my pockets with coppers. Franklin.

senses.d: A vessel, especially a large boiler, made of copper.
the boilers in the galley for cooking; as, a ship's coppers.
q: All in a hot and copper sky. Coleridge.

Copper.etym: [OE. coper (cf. D. koper, Sw. koppar, Dan. kobber, G. kupfer), LL. cuper, fr. L. cuprum for earlier Cyprium, Cyprium aes, i.e., Cyprian brass, fr. Gr. � of Cyprus (Gr. �), anciently renowned for its copper mines. Cf. Cypreous.]

senses.d: To cover or coat with copper; to sheathe with sheets of copper; as, to copper a ship.
One whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils; a worker in copper.
The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.
q: Wit, you know, is the unexpected copulation of ideas. Johnson.

senses.d: The coming together of male and female in the act of generation; sexual union; coition.
An abundance or plenty of anything.
q: She was blessed with no more copy of wit, but to serve his humor thus. B. Jonson.

senses.d: An imitation, transcript, or reproduction of an original work; as, a copy of a letter, an engraving, a painting, or a statue.
q: I have not the vanity to think my copy equal to the original. Denham.

senses.d: An individual book, or a single set of books containing the works of an author; as, a copy of the Bible; a copy of the works of Addison.
That which is to be imitated, transcribed, or reproduced; a pattern, model, or example; as, his virtues are an excellent copy for imitation.
q: Let him first learn to write, after a copy, all the letters. Holder.

senses.d: Manuscript or printed matter to be set up in type; as, the printers are calling for more copy.
A writing paper of a particular size. Same as Bastard. See under Paper.
Copyhold; tenure; lease.

Copy.etym: [F. copie, fr. L. copia abundance, number, LL. also, a transcript; co- + the root of opes riches. See Opulent, and cf. Copious.]

senses.d: To make a copy or copies of; to write; print, engrave, or paint after an original; to duplicate; to reproduce; to transcribe; as, to copy a manuscript, inscription, design, painting, etc.; — often with out, sometimes with off.
q: I like the work well; ere it be demanded (As like enough it will), I'd have it copied. Shak.
Let this be copied out, And keep it safe for our remembrance. Shak.

senses.d: To imitate; to attempt to resemble, as in manners or course of life.
q: We copy instinctively the voices of our companions, their accents, and their modes of pronunciation. Stewart.

Copy.etym: [Cf. F. copir, fr. LL. copiare. See Copy, n.]

senses.d: To make a copy or copies; to imitate.
To yield a duplicate or transcript; as, the letter did not copy well.
q: Some . . . never fail, when they copy, to follow the bad as well as the good things. Dryden.

senses.d: A Hebrew measure of capacity; a homer.
The hard parts or skeleton of various Anthozoa, and of a few Hydrozoa. Similar structures are also formed by some Bryozoa.
The ovaries of a cooked lobster; — so called from their color.
A piece of coral, usually fitted with small bells and other appurtenances, used by children as a plaything.

Coral.etym: [Of. coral, F, corail, L. corallum, coralium, fr. Gr. κοράλλιον.]

senses.d: An offering of any kind, devoted to God and therefore not to be appropriated to any other use; esp., an offering in fulfillment of a vow.
An alms basket; a vessel to receive gifts of charity; a treasury of the church, where offerings are deposited.
A string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together.
A solid measure, equivalent to 128 cubic feet; a pile of wood, or other coarse material, eight feet long, four feet high, and four feet broad; — originally measured with a cord or line.
Fig.: Any moral influence by which persons are caught, held, or drawn, as if by a cord; an enticement; as, the cords of the wicked; the cords of sin; the cords of vanity.
q: The knots that tangle human creeds, The wounding cords that bind and strain The heart until it bleeds. Tennyson.

senses.d: Any structure having the appearance of a cord, esp. a tendon or a nerve. See under Spermatic, Spinal, Umbilical, Vocal.

Cord.etym: [F. corde, L. chorda catgut, chord, cord, fr. Gr. χορδή; cf. χολάδεσ intestines, L. haruspex soothsayer (inspector of entrails), Icel. görn, pl. garnir gut, and E. yarn. Cf. Chord, Yarn.]

senses.d: To bind with a cord; to fasten with cords; to connect with cords; to ornament or finish with a cord or cords, as a garment.
To arrange (wood, etc.) in a pile for measurement by the cord.
A body of individuals; an assemblage.
q: He was in a core of people. Bacon.

senses.d: A miner's underground working time or shift.
A Hebrew dry measure; a cor or homer.
The heart or inner part of a thing, as of a column, wall, rope, of a boil, etc.; especially, the central part of fruit, containing the kernels or seeds; as, the core of an apple or quince.
q: A fever at the core, Fatal to him who bears, to all who ever bore. Byron.

senses.d: The center or inner part, as of an open space; as, the core of a square.
The most important part of a thing; the essence; as, the core of a subject.

The portion of a mold which shapes the interior of a cylinder, tube, or other hollow casting, or which makes a hole in or through a casting; a part of the mold, made separate from and inserted in it, for shaping some part of the casting, the form of which is not determined by that of the pattern.
A disorder of sheep occasioned by worms in the liver.
The bony process which forms the central axis of the horns in many animals.

Core.etym: [OF. cor, coer, cuer, F. cœur, fr. L. cor heart. See Heart.]

senses.d: To take out the core or inward parts of; as, to core an apple.
q: He's like a corn upon my great toe . . . he must be cored out. Marston.

senses.d: To form by means of a core, as a hole in a casting.
A mass of iron, usually made of thin plates, upon which the conductor of an armature or of a transformer is wound.
An umbelliferous plant, the Coriandrum sativum, the fruit or seeds of which have a strong smell and a spicy taste, and in medicine are considered as stomachic and carminative.

Coriander.etym: [L. coriandrum, fr. Gr. ����, ����, perh. fr. ��� bug, on account of the buglike or fetid smell of its leaves: cf. F. coriandre.]

senses.d: A city of Greece, famed for its luxury and extravagance.
A small fruit; a currant.
Of or relating to Corinth.
Of or pertaining to the Corinthian order of architecture, invented by the Greeks, but more commonly used by the Romans.
q: This is the lightest and most ornamental of the three orders used by the Greeks. Parker.

senses.d: Debauched in character or practice; impure.
Of or pertaining to an amateur sailor or yachtsman; as, a corinthian race (one in which the contesting yachts must be manned by amateurs.)
A native or inhabitant of Corinth.
A gay, licentious person.
A man of fashion given to pleasuring or sport; a fashionable man about town; esp., a man of means who drives his own horse, sails his own yacht, or the like.

Any species of Phalacrocorax, a genus of sea birds having a sac under the beak; the shag. Cormorants devour fish voraciously, and have become the emblem of gluttony. They are generally black, and hence are called sea ravens, and coalgeese.
A voracious eater; a glutton, or gluttonous servant.

Cormorant.etym: [F. cormoran, fr. Armor. mōr-vran a sea raven; mōr sea + bran raven, with cor, equiv. to L. corvus raven, pleonastically prefixed; or perh. fr. L. corvus marinus sea raven.]

senses.d: A thickening of the epidermis at some point, esp. on the toes, by friction or pressure. It is usually painful and troublesome.
q: Welcome, gentlemen! Ladies that have their toes Unplagued with corns, will have a bout with you. Shak.

Corn.etym: [L. cornu horn: cf. F. corne horn, hornlike excrescence. See Horn.]

senses.d: A single seed of certain plants, as wheat, rye, barley, and maize; a grain.
The various farinaceous grains of the cereal grasses used for food, as wheat, rye, barley, maize, oats.
The plants which produce corn, when growing in the field; the stalks and ears, or the stalks, ears, and seeds, after reaping and before thrashing.
q: In one night, ere glimpse of morn, His shadowy flail had thrashed the corn. Milton.

senses.d: A small, hard particle; a grain.

Corn.etym: [AS. corn; akin to OS. korn, D. koren, G., Dan., Sw., & Icel. korn, Goth. kaúrn, L. granum, Russ. zerno. Cf. Grain, Kernel.]

senses.d: To preserve and season with salt in grains; to sprinkle with salt; to cure by salting; now, specifically, to salt slightly in brine or otherwise; as, to corn beef; to corn a tongue.
To form into small grains; to granulate; as, to corn gunpowder.
To feed with corn or (in Sctland) oats; as, to corn horses.
To render intoxicated; as, ale strong enough to corn one.
The point where two converging lines meet; an angle, either external or internal.
The space in the angle between converging lines or walls which meet in a point; as, the chimney corner.
An edge or extremity; the part farthest from the center; hence, any quarter or part.
q: From the four corners of the earth they come. Shak.

senses.d: A secret or secluded place; a remote or out of the way place; a nook.
q: This thing was not done in a corner. Acts xxvi. 26.

senses.d: Direction; quarter.
q: Sits the wind in that corner! Shak.

senses.d: The state of things produced by a combination of persons, who buy up the whole or the available part of any stock or species of property, which compels those who need such stock or property to buy of them at their own price; as, a corner in a railway stock.

Corner.etym: [OF. corniere, cornier, LL. cornerium, corneria, fr. L. cornu horn, end, point. See Horn.]

senses.d: To drive into a corner.
To drive into a position of great difficulty or hopeless embarrassment; as, to corner a person in argument.
To get command of (a stock, commodity, etc.), so as to be able to put one's own price on it; as, to corner the shares of a railroad stock; to corner petroleum.
A free kick from close to the nearest corner flag post, allowed to the opposite side when a player has sent the ball behind his own goal line.
An obsolete rude reed instrument (Ger. Zinken), of the oboe family.
A cap of paper twisted at the end, used by retailers to inclose small wares.
A troop of cavalry; — so called from its being accompanied by a cornet player.
A headdress

Cornet.etym: [F. cornet, m. (for senses 1 & 2), cornette, f. & m. (for senses 3 & 4), dim. of corne horn, L. cornu. See Horn.]

senses.d: A thrashing floor.
The human body, whether living or dead.
q: By what craft in my corps, it cometh and where. Piers Plowman.

senses.d: A body of men; esp., an organized division of the military establishment; as, the marine corps; the corps of topographical engineers; specifically, an army corps.
q: A corps operating with an army should consist of three divisions of the line, a brigade of artillery, and a regiment of cavalry. Gen. Upton (U. S. Tactics. )

senses.d: A body or code of laws.
q: The whole corps of the law. Bacon.

senses.d: The land with which a prebend or other ecclesiastical office is endowed.
q: The prebendaries over and above their reserved rents have a corps. Bacon.

Corps.etym: [F., fr. L. corpus body. See Corpse.]

senses.d: In some countries of Europe, a form of students' social society binding the members to strict adherence to certain student customs and its code of honor; — Ger. spelling usually korps.
A human body in general, whether living or dead; — sometimes contemptuously.
The dead body of a human being; — used also Fig.
q: He touched the dead corpse of Public Credit, and it sprung upon its feet. D. Webster.

Corpse.etym: [OF. cors (sometimes written corps), F. corps, L. corpus; akin to AS. hrif womb. See Midriff, and cf. Corse, Corselet, Corps, Cuerpo.]

senses.d: Set right, or made straight; hence, conformable to truth, rectitude, or propriety, or to a just standard; not faulty or imperfect; free from error; as, correct behavior; correct views.
q: Always use the most correct editions. Felton.

Correct.syn: Accurate; right, exact; precise; regular; faultless. See Accurate.
Correct.etym: [L. correctus, p. p. of corrigere to make straight, to correct; cor- + regere to lead straight: cf. F. correct. See Regular, Right, and cf. Escort.]

senses.d: To make right; to bring to the standard of truth, justice, or propriety; to rectify; as, to correct manners or principles.
q: This is a defect in the first make of some men's minds which can scarce ever be corrected afterwards. T. Burnet.

senses.d: To remove or retrench the faults or errors of; to amend; to set right; as, to correct the proof (that is, to mark upon the margin the changes to be made, or to make in the type the changes so marked).

To bring back, or attempt to bring back, to propriety in morals; to reprove or punish for faults or deviations from moral rectitude; to chastise; to discipline; as, a child should be corrected for lying.
q: My accuser is my 'prentice; and when I did correct him for his fault the other day, he did vow upon his knees he would be even with me. Shak.

senses.d: To counteract the qualities of one thing by those of another; — said of whatever is wrong or injurious; as, to correct the acidity of the stomach by alkaline preparations.

Correct.syn: To amend; rectify; emend; reform; improve; chastise; punish; discipline; chasten. See Amend.

senses.d: The act of correcting, or making that right which was wrong; change for the better; amendment; rectification, as of an erroneous statement.
q: The due correction of swearing, rioting, neglect of God's word, and other scandalouss vices. Strype.

senses.d: The act of reproving or punishing, or that which is intended to rectify or to cure faults; punishment; discipline; chastisement.
q: Correction and instruction must both work Ere this rude beast will profit. Shak.

senses.d: That which is substituted in the place of what is wrong; an emendation; as, the corrections on a proof sheet should be set in the margin.
Abatement of noxious qualities; the counteraction of what is inconvenient or hurtful in its effects; as, the correction of acidity in the stomach.
An allowance made for inaccuracy in an instrument; as, chronometer correction; compass correction.
Changed from a sound to a putrid state; spoiled; tainted; vitiated; unsound.
q: Who with such corrupt and pestilent bread would feed them. Knolles.

senses.d: Changed from a state of uprightness, correctness, truth, etc., to a worse state; vitiated; depraved; debased; perverted; as, corrupt language; corrupt judges.
q: At what ease Might corrupt minds procure knaves as corrupt To swear against you. Shak.

senses.d: Abounding in errors; not genuine or correct; as, the text of the manuscript is corrupt.

Corrupt.etym: [L. corruptus, p. p. of corrumpere to corrupt; cor- + rumpere to break. See Rupture.]

senses.d: To change from a sound to a putrid or putrescent state; to make putrid; to putrefy.
To change from good to bad; to vitiate; to deprave; to pervert; to debase; to defile.
q: Evil communications corrupt good manners. 1. Cor. xv. 33.

senses.d: To draw aside from the path of rectitude and duty; as, to corrupt a judge by a bribe.
q: Heaven is above all yet; there sits a Judge That no king can corrupt. Shak.

senses.d: To debase or render impure by alterations or innovations; to falsify; as, to corrupt language; to corrupt the sacred text.
q: He that makes an ill use of it , though he does not corrupt the fountains of knowledge, . . . yet he stops the pines. Locke.

senses.d: To waste, spoil, or consume; to make worthless.
q: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt. Matt. vi. 19.
