senses.d: To become putrid or tainted; to putrefy; to rot.
To become vitiated; to lose purity or goodness.
One who corrupts; one who vitiates or taints; as, a corrupter of morals.
Capable of being made corrupt; subject to decay.
q: Ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold. 1 Pet. i. 18.

senses.d: Capable of being corrupted, or morally vitiated; susceptible of depravation.
q: They systematically corrupt very corruptible race. Burke.

senses.d: That which may decay and perish; the human body.
The act of corrupting or making putrid, or state of being corrupt or putrid; decomposition or disorganization, in the process of putrefaction; putrefaction; deterioration.
q: The inducing and accelerating of putrefaction is a subject of very universal inquiry; for corruption is a reciprocal to “generation”. Bacon.

senses.d: The product of corruption; putrid matter.
The act of corrupting or of impairing integrity, virtue, or moral principle; the state of being corrupted or debased; loss of purity or integrity; depravity; wickedness; impurity; bribery.
q: It was necessary, by exposing the gross corruptions of monasteries, . . . to exite popular indignation against them. Hallam.
They abstained from some of the worst methods of corruption usual to their party in its earlier days. Bancroft.

senses.d: The act of changing, or of being changed, for the worse; departure from what is pure, simple, or correct; as, a corruption of style; corruption in language.
q: Corruption of blood can be removed only by act of Parliament. Blackstone.

Corruption.syn: Putrescence; putrefaction; defilement; contamination; deprivation; debasement; adulteration; depravity; taint. See Depravity.

senses.d: In a corrupt manner; by means of corruption or corrupting influences; wrongfully.
A rib; a side; a region or coast.
q: Betwixt the costs of a ship. B. Jonson.

senses.d: To require to be given, expended, or laid out therefor, as in barter, purchase, acquisition, etc.; to cause the cost, expenditure, relinquishment, or loss of; as, the ticket cost a dollar; the effort cost his life.
q: A diamond gone, cost me two thousand ducats. Shak.
Though it cost me ten nights' watchings. Shak.

senses.d: To require to be borne or suffered; to cause.
q: To do him wanton rites, which cost them woe. Milton.

Cost.etym: [OF. coster, couster, F. coûter, fr. L. constare to stand at, to cost; con- + stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Constant.]

senses.d: The amount paid, charged, or engaged to be paid, for anything bought or taken in barter; charge; expense; hence, whatever, as labor, self-denial, suffering, etc., is requisite to secure benefit.
q: One day shall crown the alliance on 't so please you, Here at my house, and at my proper cost. Shak.
At less cost of life than is often expended in a skirmish, saved Europe from invasion. Prescott.

senses.d: Loss of any kind; detriment; pain; suffering.
q: I know thy trains, Though dearly to my cost, thy gins and toils. Milton.

senses.d: Expenses incurred in litigation.

Cost.etym: [OF. cost, F. coût. See Cost, v. t. ]

senses.d: The quality of being costy; expensiveness; sumptuousness.
Of great cost; expensive; dear.
q: He had fitted up his palace in the most costly and sumptuous style, for the accomodation of the princess. Prescott.

senses.d: Gorgeous; sumptuous.
q: To show how costly summer was at hand. Shak.

senses.d: A small house; a cottage or hut.
q: The sheltered cot, the cultivated farm. Goldsmith.

senses.d: A pen, coop, or like shelter for small domestic animals, as for sheep or pigeons; a cote.
A cover or sheath; as, a roller cot (the clothing of a drawing roller in a spinning frame); a cot for a sore finger.
A small, rudely-formed boat.

Cot.etym: [OE. cot, cote, AS. cot, cote, cottage; akin to D. & Icel. kot, G. koth, kot, kothe. Cf. Coat.]

senses.d: A sleeping place of limited size; a little bed; a cradle; a piece of canvas extended by a frame, used as a bed.

Cot.etym: [AS. cot cottage, bedchamber; or cf. OF. coite, F. couette (E. quilt), LL. cottum, cottus, mattress. See Cot a cottage.]

senses.d: A cottage or hut.
A shed, shelter, or inclosure for small domestic animals, as for sheep or doves.
q: Watching where shepherds pen their flocks, at eve, In hurdled cotes. Milton.

senses.d: To go side by side with; hence, to pass by; to outrun and get before; as, a dog cotes a hare.
q: We coted them on the way, and hither are they coming. Shak.

Cote.etym: [Prob. from F. côté side, OF. costet, LL. costatus, costatum, fr. L. costu rib, side: cf. F. côtoyer to go or keep at the side of. See Coast.]

senses.d: To quote.
A small house; a cot; a hut.
To lay upon a bed or other resting place.
q: Where unbruised youth, with unstuffed brain, Does couch his limbs, there golden sleep doth reign. Shak.

senses.d: To arrange or dispose as in a bed; — sometimes followed by the reflexive pronoun.
q: The waters couch themselves as may be to the center of this globe, in a spherical convexity. T. Burnet.

senses.d: To lay or deposit in a bed or layer; to bed.
q: It is at this day in use at Gaza, to couch potsherds, or vessels of earth, in their walls. Bacon.

senses.d: To transfer (as sheets of partly dried pulp) from the wire cloth mold to a felt blanket, for further drying.
To conceal; to include or involve darkly.
q: There is all this, and more, that lies naturally couched under this allegory. L'Estrange.

senses.d: To arrange; to place; to inlay.
To put into some form of language; to express; to phrase; — used with in and under.
q: A well-couched invective. Milton.
I had received a letter from Flora couched in rather cool terms. Blackw. Mag.

senses.d: To treat by pushing down or displacing the opaque lens with a needle; as, to couch a cataract.
q: He stooped his head, and couched his spear, And spurred his steed to full career. Sir W. Scott.

Couch.etym: [F. coucher to lay down, lie down, OF. colchier, fr. L. collocare to lay, put, place; col- + locare to place, fr. locus place. See Locus.]

senses.d: To lie down or recline, as on a bed or other place of rest; to repose; to lie.
q: Where souls do couch on flowers, we 'll hand in hand. Shak.
If I court moe women, you 'll couch with moe men. Shak.

senses.d: To lie down for concealment; to hide; to be concealed; to be included or involved darkly.
q: We 'll couch in the castle ditch, till we see the light of our fairies. Shak.
The half-hidden, hallf-revealed wonders, that yet couch beneath the words of the Scripture. I. Taylor.

senses.d: To bend the body, as in reverence, pain, labor, etc.; to stoop; to crouch.
q: An aged squire That seemed to couch under his shield three-square. Spenser.

senses.d: A bed or place for repose or sleep; particularly, in the United States, a lounge.
q: Gentle sleep . . . why liest thou with the vile In loathsome beds, and leavest the kingly couch? Shak.
Like one that wraps the drapery of his couch About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams. Bryant.

senses.d: Any place for repose, as the lair of a beast, etc.
A mass of steeped barley spread upon a floor to germinate, in malting; or the floor occupied by the barley; as, couch of malt.
A preliminary layer, as of color, size, etc.

Couch.etym: [F. couche, OF. colche, culche, fr. colchier. See Couch, v. t. ]

senses.d: Same as Couch�.
The operation of putting down or displacing the opaque lens in cataract.
Embroidering by laying the materials upon the surface of the foundation, instead of drawing them through.
Was, should be, or would be, able, capable, or susceptible. Used as an auxiliary, in the past tense or in the conditional present.

Could.etym: [OF. coude. The l was inserted by mistake, under the influence of should and would.]

senses.d: Same as Colter.
An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation, or advice; as, a council of physicians for consultation in a critical case.
A body of man elected or appointed to constitute an advisory or a legislative assembly; as, a governor's council; a city council.
q: An old lord of the council rated me the other day. Shak.

senses.d: Act of deliberating; deliberation; consultation.
q: Satan . . . void of rest, His potentates to council called by night. Milton.
O great in action and in council wise. Pope.

Council.syn: Assembly; meeting; congress; diet; parliament; convention; convocation; synod.
Council.etym: [F. concile, fr. L. concilium; con- + calare to call, akin to Gr. ��� to call, and E. hale, v., haul. Cf. Conciliate. This word is often confounded with counsel, with which it has no connection.]

senses.d: Interchange of opinions; mutual advising; consultation.
q: All the chief priest and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, to put him to death. Matt. xxvii. 1.

senses.d: Examination of consequences; exercise of deliberate judgment; prudence.
q: They all confess, therefore, in the working of that first cause, that counsel is used. Hooker.

senses.d: Result of consultation; advice; instruction.
q: I like thy counsel; well hast thou advised. Shak.
It was ill counsel had misled the girl. Tennyson.

senses.d: Deliberate purpose; design; intent; scheme; plan.
q: The counsel of the Lord standeth forever. Ps. xxxiii. 11.
The counsels of the wicked are deceit. Prov. xii. 5.

senses.d: A secret opinion or purpose; a private matter.
q: Thilke lord . . . to whom no counsel may be hid. Gower.

senses.d: One who gives advice, especially in legal matters; one professionally engaged in the trial or management of a cause in court; also, collectively, the legal advocates united in the management of a case; as, the defendant has able counsel.
q: The King found his counsel as refractory as his judges. Macaulay.
The players can not keep counsel: they 'll tell all. Shak.

Counsel.syn: Advice; consideration; consultation; purpose; scheme; opinion.
Counsel.etym: [OE. conseil, F. conseil, fr. L. consilium, fr. the root of consulere to consult, of uncertain origin. Cf. Consult, Consul.]

senses.d: To give advice to; to advice, admonish, or instruct, as a person.
q: Good sir, I do in friendship counsel you To leave this place. Shak.

senses.d: To advise or recommend, as an act or course.
q: They who counsel war. Milton.
Thus Belial, with words clothed in reason's garb, Counseled ignoble ease and peaceful sloth. Milton.

Counsel.etym: [OE. conseilen, counseilen, F. conseiller, fr. L. consiliari, fr. consilium counsel.]

senses.d: To tell or name one by one, or by groups, for the purpose of ascertaining the whole number of units in a collection; to number; to enumerate; to compute; to reckon.
q: Who can count the dust of Jacob? Num. xxiii. 10.
In a journey of forty miles, Avaux counted only three miserable cabins. Macaulay.

senses.d: To place to an account; to ascribe or impute; to consider or esteem as belonging.
q: Abracham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Rom. iv. 3.

senses.d: To esteem; to account; to reckon; to think, judge, or consider.
q: I count myself in nothing else so happy As in a soul remembering my good friends. Shak.

Count.syn: To calculate; number; reckon; compute; enumerate. See Calculate.
Count.etym: [OF. conter, and later (etymological spelling) compter, in modern French thus distinguished; conter to relate (cf. Recount, Account), compter to count; fr. L. computuare to reckon, compute; com- + putare to reckon, settle, order, prune, orig., to clean. See Pure, and cf. Compute.]

senses.d: To number or be counted; to possess value or carry weight; hence, to increase or add to the strength or influence of some party or interest; as, every vote counts; accidents count for nothing.
q: This excellent man . . . counted among the best and wisest of English statesmen. J. A. Symonds.

senses.d: To reckon; to rely; to depend; — with on or upon.
q: He was brewer to the palace; and it was apprehended that the government counted on his voice. Macaulay.
I think it a great error to count upon the genius of a nation as a standing argument in all ages. Swift.

senses.d: To take account or note; — with
To plead orally; to argue a matter in court; to recite a count.
The act of numbering; reckoning; also, the number ascertained by counting.
q: Of blessed saints for to increase the count. Spenser.
By this count, I shall be much in years. Shak.

senses.d: An object of interest or account; value; estimation.

A formal statement of the plaintiff's case in court; in a more technical and correct sense, a particular allegation or charge in a declaration or indictment, separately setting forth the cause of action or prosecution.

Count.etym: [F. conte and compte, with different meanings, fr. L. computus a computation, fr. computare. See Count, v. t.]

senses.d: A nobleman on the continent of Europe, equal in rank to an English earl.

Count.etym: [F. conte, fr. L. comes, comitis, associate, companion, one of the imperial court or train, properly, one who goes with another; com- + ire to go, akin to Skr. i to go.]

senses.d: Appearance or expression of the face; look; aspect; mien.
q: So spake the Son, and into terror changed His countenance. Milton.

senses.d: The face; the features.
q: In countenance somewhat doth resemble you. Shak.

senses.d: Approving or encouraging aspect of face; hence, favor, good will, support; aid; encouragement.
q: Thou hast made him . . . glad with thy countenance. Ps. xxi. 6.
This is the magistrate's peculiar province, to give countenance to piety and virtue, and to rebuke vice. Atterbury.

senses.d: Superficial appearance; show; pretense.
q: The election being done, he made countenance of great discontent thereat. Ascham.

Countenance.etym: [OE. contenance, countenaunce, demeanor, composure, F. contenance demeanor, fr. L. continentia continence, LL. also, demeanor, fr. L. continere to hold together, repress, contain. See Contain, and cf. Continence.]

senses.d: To encourage; to favor; to approve; to aid; to abet.
q: This conceit, though countenanced by learned men, is not made out either by experience or reason. Sir T. Browne.
Error supports custom, custom countenances error. Milton.

senses.d: To make a show of; to pretend.
q: Which to these ladies love did countenance. Spenser.

senses.d: To act against with equal force, power, or effect; to thwart or overcome by such action; to furnish an equivalent to or for; to counterbalance; to compensate.
q: Upon balancing the account, the profit at last will hardly countervail the inconveniences that go allong with it. L'Estrange.

Countervail.etym: [OF. contrevaloir; contre (L. contra) + valoir to avail, fr. L. valere to be strong, avail. See Vallant.]

senses.d: Power or value sufficient to obviate any effect; equal weight, strength, or value; equivalent; compensation; requital.
q: Surely, the present pleasure of a sinful act is a poor countervail for the bitterness of the review. South.

senses.d: A tract of land; a region; the territory of an independent nation; (as distinguished from any other region, and with a personal pronoun) the region of one's birth, permanent residence, or citizenship.
q: Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred. Gen. xxxxii. 9.
I might have learned this by my last exile, that change of countries cannot change my state. Stirling.
Many a famous realm And country, whereof here needs no account Milton.

senses.d: Rural regions, as opposed to a city or town.
q: As they walked, on their way into the country. Mark xvi. 12 (Rev. Ver. ).
God made the covatry, and man made the town. Cowper.
Only very great men were in the habit of dividing the year between town and country. Macaulay.

senses.d: The inhabitants or people of a state or a region; the populace; the public. Hence: (a) One's constituents. (b) The whole body of the electors of state; as, to dissolve Parliament and appeal to the country.
q: All the country in a general voice Cried hate upon him. Shak.

senses.d: A jury, as representing the citizens of a country.
The rock through which a vein runs.

Country.etym: [F. contrée, LL. contrata, fr. L. contra over against, on the opposite side. Cf. Counter, adv., Contra.]

senses.d: Pertaining to the regions remote from a city; rural; rustic; as, a country life; a country town; the country party, as opposed to city.
Destitute of refinement; rude; unpolished; rustic; not urbane; as, country manners.
Pertaining, or peculiar, to one's own country.
q: She, bowing herself towards him, laughing the cruel tyrant to scorn, spake in her country language. 2 Macc. vii. 27.

senses.d: That which joins or links two things together; a bond or tie; a coupler.
q: It is in some sort with friends as it is with dogs in couples; they should be of the same size and humor. L'Estrange.
I'll go in couples with her. Shak.

senses.d: Two of the same kind connected or considered together; a pair; a brace.
q: Adding one to one we have the complex idea of a couple. Locke.
met him with a couple of asses saddled. 2 Sam. xvi. 1.

senses.d: A male and female associated together; esp., a man and woman who are married or betrothed.
q: Such were our couple, man and wife. Lloyd.
Fair couple linked in happy, nuptial league. Milton.

senses.d: One of the pairs of plates of two metals which compose a voltaic battery; — called a voltaic couple or galvanic couple.
Two rotations, movements, etc., which are equal in amount but opposite in direction, and acting along parallel lines or around parallel axes.

Couple.etym: [F. couple, fr. L. copula a bond, band; co- + apere, aptum, to join. See Art, a., and cf. Copula.]

senses.d: To link or tie, as one thing to another; to connect or fasten together; to join.
q: Huntsman, I charge thee, tender well my hounds, . . . And couple Clowder with the deep-mouthed brach. Shak.

senses.d: To join in wedlock; to marry.
q: A parson who couples all our beggars. Swift.

Couple.etym: [F. coupler, fr. L. copulare. See Couple, n., and cf. Copulate, Cobble, v.]

senses.d: To come together as male and female; to copulate.
The act of bringing or coming together; connection; sexual union.

A device or contrivance which serves to couple or connect adjacent parts or objects; as, a belt coupling, which connects the ends of a belt; a car coupling, which connects the cars in a train; a shaft coupling, which connects the ends of shafts.
The heart; spirit; temper; disposition.
q: So priketh hem nature in here corages. Chaucer.
My lord, cheer up your spirits; our foes are nigh, and this soft courage makes your followers faint. Shak.

senses.d: Heart; inclination; desire; will.
q: I'd such a courage to do him good. Shak.

senses.d: That quality of mind which enables one to encounter danger and difficulties with firmness, or without fear, or fainting of heart; valor; boldness; resolution.
q: The king-becoming graces . . . Devotion, patience, courage, fortitude, I have no relish of them. Shak.
Courage that grows from constitution often forsakes a man when he has occasion for it. Addison.

Courage.syn: Heroism; bravery; intrepidity; valor; gallantry; daring; firmness; hardihood; boldness; dauntlessness; resolution.
Courage.etym: [OE. corage heart, mind, will, courage, OF. corage, F. courage, fr. a LL. derivative of L. cor heart. See Heart.]

senses.d: To inspire with courage.
q: Paul writeth unto Timothy . . . to courage him. Tyndale.

senses.d: Possessing, or characterized by, courage; brave; bold.
q: With this victory, the women became most courageous and proud, and the men waxed . . . fearful and desperate. Stow.

Courageous.syn: Gallant; brave; bold; daring; valiant; valorous; heroic; intrepid; fearless; hardy; stout; adventurous; enterprising. See Gallant.

senses.d: In a courageous manner.
The act of moving from one point to another; progress; passage.
q: And when we had finished our course from Tyre, we came to Ptolemais. Acts xxi. 7.

senses.d: The ground or path traversed; track; way.
q: The same horse also run the round course at Newmarket. Pennant.

senses.d: Motion, considered as to its general or resultant direction or to its goal; line progress or advance.
q: A light by which the Argive squadron steers Their silent course to Ilium's well known shore. Dennham.
Westward the course of empire takes its way. Berkeley.

senses.d: Progress from point to point without change of direction; any part of a progress from one place to another, which is in a straight line, or on one direction; as, a ship in a long voyage makes many courses; a course measured by a surveyor between two stations; also, a progress without interruption or rest; a heat; as, one course of a race.
Motion considered with reference to manner; or derly progress; procedure in a certain line of thought or action; as, the course of an argument.
q: The course of true love never did run smooth. Shak.

senses.d: Customary or established sequence of events; recurrence of events according to natural laws.
q: By course of nature and of law. Davies.
Day and night, Seedtime and harvest, heat and hoary frost, Shall hold their course. Milton.

senses.d: Method of procedure; manner or way of conducting; conduct; behavior.
q: My lord of York commends the plot and the general course of the action. Shak.
By perseverance in the course prescribed. Wodsworth.
You hold your course without remorse. Tennyson.

senses.d: A series of motions or acts arranged in order; a succession of acts or practices connectedly followed; as, a course of medicine; a course of lectures on chemistry.
The succession of one to another in office or duty; order; turn.
q: He appointed . . . the courses of the priests 2 Chron. viii. 14.

senses.d: That part of a meal served at one time, with its accompaniments.
q: He wore fine clothes, gave dinners of several courses, paid court to venal beauties. Macaulay.

senses.d: A continuous level range of brick or stones of the same height throughout the face or faces of a building.
The lowest sail on any mast of a square-rigged vessel; as, the fore course, main course, etc.

Course.syn: Way; road; route; passage; race; series; succession; manner; method; mode; career; progress.
Course.etym: [F. cours, course, L. cursus, fr. currere to run. See Current.]

senses.d: To run, hunt, or chase after; to follow hard upon; to pursue.
q: We coursed him at the heels. Shak.

senses.d: To cause to chase after or pursue game; as, to course greyhounds after deer.
To run through or over.
q: The bounding steed courses the dusty plain. Pope.

senses.d: To run as in a race, or in hunting; to pursue the sport of coursing; as, the sportsmen coursed over the flats of Lancashire.
To move with speed; to race; as, the blood courses through the veins.
An inclosed space; a courtyard; an uncovered area shut in by the walls of a building, or by different building; also, a space opening from a street and nearly surrounded by houses; a blind alley.
q: The courts of the house of our God. Ps. cxxxv. 2.
And round the cool green courts there ran a row Of cloisters. Tennyson.
Goldsmith took a garret in a miserable court. Macaulay.

senses.d: The residence of a sovereign, prince, nobleman, or other dignitary; a palace.
q: Attends the emperor in his royal court. Shak.
This our court, infected with their manners, Shows like a riotous inn. Shak.

senses.d: The collective body of persons composing the retinue of a sovereign or person high in authority; all the surroundings of a sovereign in his regal state.
q: My lord, there is a nobleman of the court at door would speak with you. Shak.
Love rules the court, the camp, the grove. Sir. W. Scott.

senses.d: Any formal assembling of the retinue of a sovereign; as, to hold a court.
q: The princesses held their court within the fortress. Macaulay.

senses.d: Attention directed to a person in power; conduct or address designed to gain favor; courtliness of manners; civility; compliment; flattery.
q: No solace could her paramour intreat Her once to show, ne court, nor dalliance. Spenser.
I went to make my court to the Duke and Duchess of Newcastle. Evelyn.

senses.d: The hall, chamber, or place, where justice is administered.
q: Most heartily I do beseech the court To give the judgment. Shak.

senses.d: The session of a judicial assembly.
Any jurisdiction, civil, military, or ecclesiastical.
A place arranged for playing the game of tennis; also, one of the divisions of a tennis court.

Court.etym: [OF. court, curt, cort, F. cour, LL. cortis, fr. L. cohors, cors, chors, gen. cohortis, cortis, chortis, an inclosure, court, thing inclosed, crowd, throng; co- + a root akin to Gr. χορτόσ inclosure, feeding place, and to E. garden, yard, orchard. See Yard, and cf. Cohort, Curtain.]

senses.d: To endeavor to gain the favor of by attention or flattery; to try to ingratiate one's self with.
q: By one person, hovever, Portland was still assiduously courted. Macaulay.

senses.d: To endeavor to gain the affections of; to seek in marriage; to woo.
q: If either of you both love Katharina . . . Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure. Shak.

senses.d: To attempt to gain; to solicit; to seek.
q: They might almost seem to have courted the crown of martyrdom. Prescott.
Guilt and misery . . . court privacy and solitude. De Quincey.

senses.d: To invite by attractions; to allure; to attract.
q: A well-worn pathway courted us To one green wicket in a privet hedge. Tennyson.

senses.d: To play the lover; to woo; as, to go courting.

a court for settling claims against a state or government; specif., a court of the United States, created by act of Congress, and holding its sessions at Washington. It is given jurisdiction over claims on contracts against the government, and sometimes may advise the government as to its liabilities.
Of courtlike manners; pertaining to, or expressive of, courtesy; characterized by courtesy; civil; obliging; well bred; polite; affable; complaisant.
q: A patient and courteous bearing. Prescott.
His behavior toward his people is grave and courteous. Fuller.

Courteous.etym: [OE. cortais, corteis, cortois, rarely corteous, OF. corties, corteis, F. courtois. See Court.]

senses.d: In a courteous manner.
One collaterally related more remotely than a brother or sister; especially, the son or daughter of an uncle or aunt.
q: Thou art, great lord, my father's sister's son, A cousin-german to great Priam's seed. Shak.

senses.d: A title formerly given by a king to a nobleman, particularly to those of the council. In English writs, etc., issued by the crown, it signifies any earl.
q: My noble lords and cousins, all, good morrow. Shak.

Cousin.etym: [F. cousin, LL. cosinus, cusinus, contr. from L. consobrinus the child of a mother's sister, cousin; con- + sobrinus a cousin by the mother's side, a form derived fr. soror (forsosor) sister. See Sister, and cf. Cozen, Coz.]

senses.d: Allied; akin.
A retired nook; especially, a small, sheltered inlet, creek, or bay; a recess in the shore.
q: Vessels which were in readiness for him within secret coves and nooks. Holland.

senses.d: A strip of prairie extending into woodland; also, a recess in the side of a mountain.
A concave molding.

Cove.etym: [AS. cofa room; akin to G. koben pigsty, orig., hut, Icel. kofi hut, and perh. to E. cobalt.]

senses.d: To arch over; to build in a hollow concave form; to make in the form of a cove.
q: The mosques and other buildings of the Arabians are rounded into domes and coved roofs. H. Swinburne.

senses.d: To brood, cover, over, or sit over, as birds their eggs.
q: Not being able to cove or sit upon them , she bestoweth them in the gravel. Holland.

Cove.etym: [CF. F. couver, It. covare. See Covey.]

senses.d: A boy or man of any age or station.
q: There's a gentry cove here. Wit's Recreations (1654).
Now, look to it, coves, that all the beef and drink Be not filched from us. Mrs. Browning.

Cove.etym: [A gypsy word, covo that man, covi that woman.]

senses.d: A mutual agreement of two or more persons or parties, or one of the stipulations in such an agreement.
q: Then Jonathan and David made a covenant. 1 Sam. xviiii. 3.
Let there be covenants drawn between us. Shak.
If we conclude a peace, It shall be with such strict and severe covenants As little shall the Frenchmen gain thereby. Shak.

senses.d: An agreement made by the Scottish Parliament in 1638, and by the English Parliament in 1643, to preserve the reformed religion in Scotland, and to extirpate popery and prelacy; — usually called the “Solemn League and Covenant.”
q: He was born in the days of the Covenant, and was the heir of a covenanted house. Macaulay.

senses.d: The promises of God as revealed in the Scriptures, conditioned on certain terms on the part of man, as obedience, repentance, faith, etc.
q: I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee. Gen. xvii. 7.

senses.d: A solemn compact between members of a church to maintain its faith, discipline, etc.

An undertaking, on sufficient consideration, in writing and under seal, to do or to refrain from some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation; also, the document or writing containing the terms of agreement.

Covenant.syn: Agreement; contract; compact; bargain; arrangement; stipulation.
Covenant.etym: [OF. covenant, fr. F. & OF. convenir to agree, L. convenire. See Convene.]

senses.d: To agree (with); to enter into a formal agreement; to bind one's self by contract; to make a stipulation.
q: Jupiter covenanted with him, that it should be hot or cold, wet or dry, . . . as the tenant should direct. L'Estrange.
And they covenanted with him for thyrty pieces of silver. Matt. xxvi. 15.

senses.d: To grant or promise by covenant.
q: My covenant of peace that I covenanted with you. Wyclif.

senses.d: To overspread the surface of (one thing) with another; as, to cover wood with paint or lacquer; to cover a table with a cloth.
To envelop; to clothe, as with a mantle or cloak.
q: And with the majesty of darkness round Covers his throne. Milton.
All that beauty than doth cover thee. Shak.

senses.d: To invest (one's self with something); to bring upon (one's self); as, he covered himself with glory.
q: The powers that covered themselves with everlasting infamy by the partition of Poland. Brougham.

senses.d: To hide sight; to conceal; to cloak; as, the enemy were covered from our sight by the woods.
q: A cloud covered the mount. Exod. xxiv. 15.
In vain shou striv'st to cover shame with shame. Milton.

senses.d: To brood or sit on; to incubate.
q: While the hen is covering her eggs, the male . . . diverts her with his songs. Addison.
The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen. Ex. xiv. 28.

senses.d: To shelter, as from evil or danger; to protect; to defend; as, the cavalry covered the retreat.
q: His calm and blameless life Does with substantial blessedness abound, And the soft wings of peace cover him round. Cowley.

senses.d: To remove from remembrance; to put away; to remit.

To extend over; to be sufficient for; to comprehend, include, or embrace; to account for or solve; to counterbalance; as, a mortgage which fully covers a sum loaned on it; a law which covers all possible cases of a crime; receipts than do not cover expenses.
To put the usual covering or headdress on.
q: Cover thy head . . . ; nay, prithee, be covered. Shak.

senses.d: To copulate with (a female); to serve; as, a horse covers a mare; — said of the male.

Cover.syn: To shelter; screen; shield; hide; overspread.
Cover.etym: [OF. covrir, F. couvrir, fr. L. cooperire; co- + operire to cover; probably fr. ob towards, over + the root appearing in aperire to open. Cf. Aperient, Overt, Curfew.]

senses.d: Anything which is laid, set, or spread, upon, about, or over, another thing; an envelope; a lid; as, the cover of a book.
Anything which veils or conceals; a screen; disguise; a cloak.
q: A handsome cover for imperfections. Collier.

senses.d: Shelter; protection; as, the troops fought under cover of the batteries; the woods afforded a good cover.
q: Being compelled to lodge in the field . . . whilst his army was under cover, they might be forced to retire. Clarendon.

senses.d: The woods, underbrush, etc., which shelter and conceal game; covert; as, to beat a cover; to ride to cover.
The lap of a slide valve.
A tablecloth, and the other table furniture; esp., the table furniture for the use of one person at a meal; as, covers were laid for fifty guests.
q: Letters . . . dispatched under cover to her ladyship. Thackeray.

senses.d: To spread a table for a meal; to prepare a banquet.
Under cover; screened; sheltered; not exposed; hidden.
Anything which covers or conceals, as a roof, a screen, a wrapper, clothing, etc.
q: Noah removed the covering of the ark. Gen. viii. 13.
They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold. Job. xxiv. 7.
A covering over the well's mouth. 2 Sam. xvii. 19.

senses.d: Covered over; private; hid; secret; disguised.
q: How covert matters may be best disclosed. Shak.
Whether of open war or covert guile. Milton

senses.d: Sheltered; not open or exposed; retired; protected; as, a covert nook.
q: Of either side the green, to plant a covert alley. Bacon.

senses.d: Under cover, authority or protection; as, a feme covert, a married woman who is considered as being under the protection and control of her husband.

Covert.syn: Hidden; secret; private; covered; disguised; insidious; concealed. See Hidden.
Covert.etym: [OF. covert, F. couvert, p. p. of couvrir. See Cover, v. t.]

senses.d: A place that covers and protects; a shelter; a defense.
q: A tabernacle . . . for a covert from storm. Is. iv. 6.
The highwayman has darted from his covered by the wayside. Prescott.

senses.d: One of the special feathers covering the bases of the quills of the wings and tail of a bird. See Illust. of Bird.
To wish for with eagerness; to desire possession of; — used in a good sense.
q: Covet earnestly the best gifts. 1. Cor. xxii. 31.
If it be a sin to covet honor, I am the most offending soul alive. Shak.

senses.d: To long for inordinately or unlawfully; to hanker after (something forbidden).
q: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's house. Ex. xx. 17.

Covet.syn: To long for; desire; hanker after; crave.
Covet.etym: [OF. coveitier, covoitier, F. convoiter, from a derivative fr. L. cupere to desire; cf. Skr. kup to become excited. Cf. Cupidity.]

senses.d: To have or indulge inordinate desire.
q: Which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith. 1 Tim. vi. 10.

senses.d: Very desirous; eager to obtain; — used in a good sense.
q: Covetous of wisdom and fair virtue. Shak.
Covetous death bereaved us all, To aggrandize one funeral. Emerson.

senses.d: Inordinately desirous; excessively eager to obtain and possess (esp. money); avaricious; — in a bad sense.
q: The covetous person lives as if the world were madealtogether for him, and not he for the world. South.

Covetous.syn: Avaricious; parsimonious; penurious; misrely; niggardly. See Avaricious.
Covetous.etym: [OF. coveitos, F. convoiteux. See Covet, v. t.]

senses.d: Strong desire.
q: When workmen strive to do better than well, They do confound their skill in covetousness. Shak.

senses.d: A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; excessive desire for riches or money; — in a bad sense.
q: Covetousness, by a greed of getting more, deprivess itself of the true end of getting. Sprat.

senses.d: A chimney cap; a cowl
The mature female of bovine animals.
The female of certain large mammals, as whales, seals, etc.

Cow.etym: [OE. cu, cou, AS. cū; akin to D. koe, G. kuh, OHG. kuo, Icel. kȳr, Dan. & Sw. ko, L. bos ox, cow, Gr. βου̑σ, Skr. gō. √223. Cf. Beef, Bovine, Bucolic, Butter, Nylghau.]

senses.d: To depress with fear; to daunt the spirits or courage of; to overawe.
q: To vanquish a people already cowed. Shak.
THe French king was cowed. J. R. Green.

Cow.etym: [Cf. Icel. kuga, Sw. kufva to check, subdue, Dan. kue. Cf. Cuff, v. t.]

senses.d: A wedge, or brake, to check the motion of a machine or car; a chock.

Cow.etym: [Prob. from same root as cow, v. t.]

senses.d: A contraction of cousin.
To make slight cracks; to make small, sharp, sudden noises, rapidly or frequently repeated; to crepitate; as, burning thorns crackle.
q: The unknown ice that crackles underneath them. Dryden.

senses.d: The noise of slight and frequent cracks or reports; a crackling.
q: The crackle of fireworks. Carlyle.

senses.d: A kind of crackling sound or râle, heard in some abnormal states of the lungs; as, dry crackle; moist crackle.

A condition produced in certain porcelain, fine earthenware, or glass, in which the glaze or enamel appears to be cracked in all directions, making a sort of reticulated surface; as, Chinese crackle; Bohemian crackle.
The making of small, sharp cracks or reports, frequently repeated.
q: As the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. Eccl. vii. 6.

senses.d: The well-browned, crisp rind of roasted pork.
q: For the first time in his life he tested crackling. Lamb.

senses.d: Food for dogs, made from the refuse of tallow melting.
A hard brittle cake or biscuit.

Cracknel.etym: [F. craquelin, fr. D. krakeling, fr. krakken to crack. See Crack, v. t.]

senses.d: Strength; might; secret power.
Art or skill; dexterity in particular manual employment; hence, the occupation or employment itself; manual art; a trade.
q: Ye know that by this craft we have our wealth. Acts xix. 25.
A poem is the work of the poet; poesy is his skill or craft of making. B. Jonson.
Since the birth of time, throughout all ages and nations, Has the craft of the smith been held in repute. Longfellow.

senses.d: Those engaged in any trade, taken collectively; a guild; as, the craft of ironmongers.
q: The control of trade passed from the merchant guilds to the new craft guilds. J. R. Green.

senses.d: Cunning, art, or skill, in a bad sense, or applied to bad purposes; artifice; guile; skill or dexterity employed to effect purposes by deceit or shrewd devices.
q: You have that crooked wisdom which is called craft. Hobbes.
The chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death. Mark xiv. 1.

senses.d: A vessel; vessels of any kind; — generally used in a collective sense.
q: The evolutions of the numerous tiny craft moving over the lake. Prof. Wilson.

Craft.etym: [AS. cræft strength, skill, art, cunning; akin to OS., G., Sw., & Dan. kraft strength, D. kracht, Icel. kraptr; perh. originally, a drawing together, stretching, from the root of E. cramp.]

senses.d: To play tricks; to practice artifice.
q: You have crafted fair. Shak.

senses.d: Dexterity in devising and effecting a purpose; cunning; artifice; stratagem.
q: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness. Job. v. 13.

senses.d: One skilled in some trade or manual occupation; an artificer; a mechanic.
Relating to, or characterized by, craft or skill; dexterous.
Possessing dexterity; skilled; skillful.
q: A noble crafty man of trees. Wyclif.

senses.d: Skillful at deceiving others; characterized by craft; cunning; wily.
q: With anxious care and crafty wiles. J. Baillie.

Crafty.syn: Skillful; dexterous; cunning; artful; wily; sly; fraudulent; deceitful; subtle; shrewd. See Cunning.

senses.d: A steep, rugged rock; a rough, broken cliff, or point of a rock, on a ledge.
q: From crag to crag the signal flew. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A partially compacted bed of gravel mixed with shells, of the Tertiary age.

Crag.etym: [W. craig; akin to Gael. creag, Corn. karak, Armor. karrek.]

senses.d: The neck or throat
q: And bear the crag so stiff and so state. Spenser.

senses.d: The neck piece or scrag of mutton.

Crag.etym: [A form of craw: cf. D. kraag neck, collar, G. kragen. See Craw.]

senses.d: A wading bird of the genus Grus, and allied genera, of various species, having a long, straight bill, and long legs and neck.

A machine for raising and lowering heavy weights, and, while holding them suspended, transporting them through a limited lateral distance. In one form it consists of a projecting arm or jib of timber or iron, a rotating post or base, and the necessary tackle, windlass, etc.; — so called from a fancied similarity between its arm and the neck of a crane See Illust. of Derrick.
An iron arm with horizontal motion, attached to the side or back of a fireplace, for supporting kettles, etc., over a fire.
A siphon, or bent pipe, for drawing liquors out of a cask.
A forked post or projecting bracket to support spars, etc., — generally used in pairs. See Crotch, 2.

Crane.etym: [AS. cran; akin to D. & LG. craan, G. kranich, krahn (this in sense 2), Gr. γέρανοσ, L. grus, W. & Armor. garan, OSlav. zeravĭ, Lith. gerve, Icel. trani, Sw. trana, Dan. trane. √24. Cf. Geranium.]

senses.d: To cause to rise; to raise or lift, as by a crane; — with up.
q: What engines, what instruments are used in craning up a soul, sunk below the center, to the highest heavens. Bates.
An upstart craned up to the height he has. Massinger.

senses.d: To stretch, as a crane stretches its neck; as, to crane the neck disdainfully.
to reach forward with head and neck, in order to see better; as, a hunter cranes forward before taking a leap.
q: The passengers eagerly craning forward over the bulwarks. Howells.

senses.d: Any arm which swings about a vertical axis at one end, used for supporting a suspended weight.
The American blue heron (Ardea herodias).
To break in pieces violently; to dash together with noise and violence.
q: He shakt his head, and crasht his teeth for ire. Fairfax.

Crash.etym: [OE. crashen, the same word as crasen to break, E. craze. See Craze.]

senses.d: To make a loud, clattering sound, as of many things falling and breaking at once; to break in pieces with a harsh noise.
q: Roofs were blazing and walls crashing in every part of the city. Macaulay.

senses.d: To break with violence and noise; as, the chimney in falling crashed through the roof.
A loud, sudden, confused sound, as of many things falling and breaking at once.
q: The wreck of matter and the crash of worlds. Addison.

senses.d: Ruin; failure; sudden breaking down, as of a business house or a commercial enterprise.
Coarse, heavy, narrow linen cloth, used esp. for towels.
The noise of many things falling and breaking at once.
q: There shall be . . . a great crashing from the hills. Zeph. i. 10.

senses.d: To ask with earnestness or importunity; to ask with submission or humility; to beg; to entreat; to beseech; to implore.
q: I crave your honor's pardon. Shak.
Joseph . . . went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus. Mark xv. 43.

senses.d: To call for, as a gratification; to long for; hence, to require or demand; as, the stomach craves food.
q: His path is one that eminently craves weary walking. Edmund Gurney.

Crave.syn: To ask; seek; beg; beseech; implore; entreat; solicit; request; supplicate; adjure.
Crave.etym: [AS. crafian; akin to Icel. krefja, Sw. kräfva, Dan. kræve.]

senses.d: To desire strongly; to feel an insatiable longing; as, a craving appetite.
q: Once one may crave for love. Suckling.

senses.d: An usher to a riding master.

Creat.etym: [F. créat, ultimately fr. L. creatus created, begotten; cf. It. creato pupil, servant, Sp. criado a servant, client.]

senses.d: Created; composed; begotten.
q: Hearts create of duty and zeal. Shak.

Create.etym: [L. creatus, p. p. of creare to create; akin to Gr. κραίνειν to accomplish, Skr. kṛ to make, and to E. ending -cracy in aristocracy, also to crescent, cereal.]

senses.d: To bring into being; to form out of nothing; to cause to exist.
q: In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth. Gen. i. 1.

senses.d: To effect by the agency, and under the laws, of causation; to be the occasion of; to cause; to produce; to form or fashion; to renew.
q: Your eye in Scotland Would create soldiers. Shak.
Create in me a clean heart. Ps. li. 10.

senses.d: To invest with a new form, office, or character; to constitute; to appoint; to make; as, to create one a peer.
The act of creating or causing to exist. Specifically, the act of bringing the universe or this world into existence.
q: From the creation to the general doom. Shak.
As when a new particle of matter dotn begin to exist, in rerum natura, which had before no being; and this we call creation. Locke.

senses.d: That which is created; that which is produced or caused to exist, as the world or some original work of art or of the imagination; nature.
q: We know that the whole creation groaneth. Rom. viii. 22.
A dagger of the mind, a false creation. Shak.
Choice pictures and creations of curious art. Beaconsfield.

senses.d: The act of constituting or investing with a new character; appointment; formation.
q: An Irish peer of recent creation. Landor.

Creation.etym: [L. creatio: cf. F. cr�ation. See Create.]

senses.d: One who creates, produces, or constitutes. Specifically, the Supreme Being.
q: To sin's rebuke and my Creater's praise. Shak.
The poets and artists of Greece, who are at the same time its prophets, the creators of its divinities, and the revealers of its theological beliefs. Caird.

senses.d: Anything created; anything not self-existent; especially, any being created with life; an animal; a man.
q: He asked water, a creature so common and needful that it was against the law of nature to deny him. Fuller.
God's first creature was light. Bacon.
On earth, join, all ye creatures, to extol Him first, him last, him midst, and without end. Milton.
And most attractive is the fair result Of thought, the creature of a polished mind. Cowper.

senses.d: A human being, in pity, contempt, or endearment; as, a poor creature; a pretty creature.
q: The world hath not a sweeter creature. Shak.

senses.d: A person who owes his rise and fortune to another; a servile dependent; an instrument; a tool.
q: A creature of the queen's, Lady Anne Bullen. Shak.
Both Charles himself and his creature, Laud. Macaulay.

senses.d: A general term among farmers for horses, oxen, etc.
One who credits, believes, or trusts.
q: The easy creditors of novelties. Daniel.

senses.d: One who gives credit in business matters; hence, one to whom money is due; — correlative to debtor.
q: Creditors have better memories than debtors. Franklin.

senses.d: A small inlet or bay, narrower and extending further into the land than a cove; a recess in the shore of the sea, or of a river.
q: Each creek and cavern of the dangerous shore. Cowper.
They discovered a certain creek, with a shore. Acts xxvii. 39.

senses.d: A stream of water smaller than a river and larger than a brook.
q: Lesser streams and rivulets are denominated creeks. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Any turn or winding.
q: The passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lands. Shak.

Creek.etym: [AS. crecca; akin to D. kreek, Icel. kriki crack, nook; cf. W. crig crack, crigyll ravine, creek. Cf. Crick, Crook.]

senses.d: To move along the ground, or on any other surface, on the belly, as a worm or reptile; to move as a child on the hands and knees; to crawl.
q: Ye that walk The earth, and stately tread, or lowly creep. Milton.

senses.d: To move slowly, feebly, or timorously, as from unwillingness, fear, or weakness.
q: The whining schoolboy . . . creeping, like snail, Unwillingly to school. Shak.
Like a guilty thing, I creep. Tennyson.

senses.d: To move in a stealthy or secret manner; to move imperceptibly or clandestinely; to steal in; to insinuate itself or one's self; as, age creeps upon us.
q: The sophistry which creeps into most of the books of argument. Locke.
Of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women. 2. Tim. iii. 6.

senses.d: To slip, or to become slightly displaced; as, the collodion on a negative, or a coat of varnish, may creep in drying; the quicksilver on a mirror may creep.
To move or behave with servility or exaggerated humility; to fawn; as, a creeping sycophant.
q: To come as humbly as they used to creep. Shak.

senses.d: To grow, as a vine, clinging to the ground or to some other support by means of roots or rootlets, or by tendrils, along its length.
To have a sensation as of insects creeping on the skin of the body; to crawl; as, the sight made my flesh creep. See Crawl, v. i., 4.
To drag in deep water with creepers, as for recovering a submarine cable.

Creep.etym: [OE. crepen, creopen, AS. creópan; akin to D. kruipen, G. kriechen, Icel. krjupa, Sw. krypa, Dan. krybe. Cf. Cripple, Crouch.]

senses.d: The act or process of creeping.
A distressing sensation, or sound, like that occasioned by the creeping of insects.
q: A creep of undefinable horror. Blackwood's Mag.
Out of the stillness, with gathering creep, Like rising wind in leaves. Lowell.

senses.d: A slow rising of the floor of a gallery, occasioned by the pressure of incumbent strata upon the pillars or sides; a gradual movement of mining ground.
Crawling, or moving close to the ground.
Growing along, and clinging to, the ground, or to a wall, etc., by means of rootlets or tendrils.
q: Casements lined with creeping herbs. Cowper.

senses.d: A Cretan
The Manx shearwater.
A company of people associated together; an assemblage; a throng.
q: There a noble crew Of lords and ladies stood on every side. Spenser.
Faithful to whom? to thy rebellious crew? Milton.

senses.d: The company of seamen who man a ship, vessel, or at; the company belonging to a vessel or a boat.
In an extended sense, any small body of men associated for a purpose; a gang; as (Naut.), the carpenter's crew; the boatswain's crew.

Crew.syn: Company; band; gang; horde; mob; herd; throng; party.
Crew.etym: [From older accrue accession, reënforcement, hence, company, crew; the first syllable being misunderstood as the indefinite article. See Accrue, Crescent.]

senses.d: A manger or rack; a feeding place for animals.
q: The steer lion at one crib shall meet. Pope.

senses.d: A stall for oxen or other cattle.
q: Where no oxen are, the crib is clean. Prov. xiv. 4.

senses.d: A small inclosed bedstead or cot for a child.
A box or bin, or similar wooden structure, for storing grain, salt, etc.; as, a crib for corn or oats.
A hovel; a hut; a cottage.
q: Why rather, Sleep, liest thou in smoky cribs, . . . Than in the perfumed chambers of the great? Shak.

senses.d: A structure or frame of timber for a foundation, or for supporting a roof, or for lining a shaft.
A structure of logs to be anchored with stones; — used for docks, pier, dams, etc.
A small raft of timber.
A small theft; anything purloined; a plagiarism; hence, a translation or key, etc., to aid a student in preparing or reciting his lessons.
q: The Latin version technically called a crib. Ld. Lytton.
Occasional perusal of the Pagan writers, assisted by a crib. Wilkie Collins.

senses.d: A miner's luncheon.
The discarded cards which the dealer can use in scoring points in cribbage.

Crib.etym: [AS. crybb; akin to OS. kribbja, D. krib, kribbe, Dan. krybbe, G. krippe, and perh. to MHG. krebe basket, G, korb, and E. rip a sort of wicker basket.]

senses.d: To shut up or confine in a narrow habitation; to cage; to cramp.
q: If only the vital energy be not cribbed or cramped. I. Taylor.
Now I am cabin'd, cribbed, confined. Shak.

senses.d: To pilfer or purloin; hence, to steal from an author; to appropriate; to plagiarize; as, to crib a line from Milton.
q: Child, being fond of toys, cribbed the necklace. Dickens.

senses.d: To crowd together, or to be confined, as in a crib or in narrow accommodations.
q: Who sought to make . . . bishops to crib in a Presbyterian trundle bed. Gauden.

senses.d: To make notes for dishonest use in recitation or examination.
To seize the manger or other solid object with the teeth and draw in wind; — said of a horse.
Any violation of law, either divine or human; an omission of a duty commanded, or the commission of an act forbidden by law.

Gross violation of human law, in distinction from a misdemeanor or trespass, or other slight offense. Hence, also, any aggravated offense against morality or the public welfare; any outrage or great wrong.
Any great wickedness or sin; iniquity.
q: No crime was thine, if 'tis no crime to love. Pope.

senses.d: That which occasion crime.
q: The tree of life, the crime of our first father's fall. Spenser.

Crime.etym: [F. crime, fr. L. crimen judicial decision, that which is subjected to such a decision, charge, fault, crime, fr. the root of cernere to decide judicially. See Certain.]

senses.d: A deep red color tinged with blue; also, red color in general.
q: Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. Is. i. 18.
A maid yet rosed over with the virgin crimson of modesty. Shak.

Crimson.etym: [OE. crimson, OF. crimoisin, F. cramoisi (cf. Sp. carmesi.) LL. carmesinus, fr. Ar. qermazi, fr. qermez crimson, kermes, fr. Skr. kṛmija produced by a worm; k�mi worm or insect + jan to generate; akin to E. kin. CF. Carmine, Kermes.]

senses.d: Of a deep red color tinged with blue; deep red.
q: The blushing poppy with a crimson hue. Prior.

senses.d: To dye with crimson or deep red; to redden.
q: Signed in thy spoil and crimsoned in thy lethe. Shak.

senses.d: To become crimson; to blush.
q: Ancient towers . . . beginning to crimson with the radiant luster of a cloudless July morning. De Quincey.

senses.d: One who creeps, halts, or limps; one who has lost, or never had, the use of a limb or limbs; a lame person; hence, one who is partially disabled.
q: I am a cripple in my limbs; but what decays are in my mind, the reader must determine. Dryden.

Cripple.etym: [OE. cripel, crepel, crupel, AS. crypel (akin to D. kreuple, G. krüppel, Dan. kröbling, Icel. kryppill), prop., one that can not walk, but must creep, fr. AS. creópan to creep. See Creep.]

senses.d: Lame; halting.
To deprive of the use of a limb, particularly of a leg or foot; to lame.
q: He had crippled the joints of the noble child. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To deprive of strength, activity, or capability for service or use; to disable; to deprive of resources; as, to be financially crippled.
q: More serious embarrassments . . . were crippling the energy of the settlement in the Bay. Palfrey.
An incumbrance which would permanently cripple the body politic. Macaulay.

senses.d: Swampy or low wet ground, often covered with brush or with thickets; bog.
q: The flats or cripple land lying between high- and low-water lines, and over which the waters of the stream ordinarily come and go.

senses.d: A rocky shallow in a stream; — a lumberman's term.
Curling in stiff curls or ringlets; as, crisp hair.
Curled with the ripple of the water.
q: You nymphs called Naiads, of the winding brooks . . . Leave jour crisp channels. Shak.

senses.d: Brittle; friable; in a condition to break with a short, sharp fracture; as, crisp snow.
q: The cakes at tea ate short and crisp. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Possessing a certain degree of firmness and freshness; in a fresh, unwilted condition.
q: It has been plucked nine months, and yet looks as hale and crisp as if it would last ninety years. Leigh Hunt.

senses.d: Lively; sparking; effervescing.
q: Your neat crisp claret. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: Brisk; crackling; cheerful; lively.
q: The snug, small room, and the crisp fire. Dickens.

Crisp.etym: [AS. crisp, fr. L. crispus; cf. carpere to pluck, card (wool), and E. harvest. Cf. Crape.]

senses.d: To curl; to form into ringlets, as hair, or the nap of cloth; to interweave, as the branches of trees.
To cause to undulate irregularly, as crape or water; to wrinkle; to cause to ripple. Cf. Crimp.
q: The lover with the myrtle sprays Adorns his crisped tresses. Drayton.
Along the crisped shades and bowers. Milton.
The crisped brooks, Rolling on orient pearl and sands of gold. Milton.

senses.d: To make crisp or brittle, as in cooking.

Crisp.etym: [L. crispare, fr. crispus. See Crisp. a. ]

senses.d: To undulate or ripple. Cf. Crisp, v. t.
q: To watch the crisping ripples on the beach. Tennuson.

senses.d: That which is crisp or brittle; the state of being crisp or brittle; as, burned to a crisp; specifically, the rind of roasted pork; crackling.
A bend, turn, or curve; curvature; flexure.
q: Through lanes, and crooks, and darkness. Phaer.

senses.d: Any implement having a bent or crooked end.
q: He left his crook, he left his flocks. Prior.

senses.d: A pothook.
An artifice; trick; tricky device; subterfuge.
q: For all yuor brags, hooks, and crooks. Cranmer.

senses.d: A small tube, usually curved, applied to a trumpet, horn, etc., to change its pitch or key.
A person given to fraudulent practices; an accomplice of thieves, forgers, etc.

Crook.etym: [OE. crok; akin to Icel. krōkr hook, bend, SW. krok, Dan. krog, OD. krooke; or cf. Gael. crocan crook, hook, W. crwca crooked. Cf. Crosier, Crotchet, Crutch, Encroach.]

senses.d: To turn from a straight line; to bend; to curve.
q: Crook the pregnant hinges of the knee. Shak.

senses.d: To turn from the path of rectitude; to pervert; to misapply; to twist.
q: There is no one thing that crooks youth more than such unlawfull games. Ascham.
What soever affairs pass such a man's hands, he crooketh them to his own ends. Bacon.

Crook.etym: [OE. croken; cf. Sw. kr�ka, Dan. kr�ge. See Crook, n.]

senses.d: To bend; to curve; to wind; to have a curvature.
q: Their shoes and pattens are snouted, and piked more than a finger long, crooking upwards. Camden.

senses.d: Characterized by a crook or curve; not straight; turning; bent; twisted; deformed.
q: he is deformed, crooked, old, and sere. Shak.

senses.d: Not straightforward; deviating from rectitude; distorted from the right.
q: They are a perverse and crooked generation. Deut. xxxii. 5.

senses.d: False; dishonest; fraudulent; as, crooked dealings.
The pouchlike enlargement of the gullet of birds, serving as a receptacle for food; the craw.
The top, end, or highest part of anything, especially of a plant or tree.
That which is cropped, cut, or gathered from a single felld, or of a single kind of grain or fruit, or in a single season; especially, the product of what is planted in the earth; fruit; harvest.
q: Lab'ring the soil, and reaping plenteous crop, Corn, wine, and oil. Milton.

senses.d: Grain or other product of the field while standing.
Anything cut off or gathered.
q: Guiltless of steel, and from the razor free, It falls a plenteous crop reserved for thee. Dryden.

senses.d: Hair cut close or short, or the act or style of so cutting; as, a convict's crop.
A projecting ornament in carved stone. Specifically, a finial.
Tin ore prepared for smelting.
A riding whip with a loop instead of a lash.

Crop.etym: [OE. crop, croppe, craw, top of a plant, harvest, AS. crop, cropp, craw, top, bunch, ear of corn; akin to D. krop craw, G. kropf, Icel. kroppr hump or bunch on the body, body; but cf. also W. cropa, croppa, crop or craw of a bird, Ir. & Gael. sgroban. Cf. Croup, Crupper, Croup.]

senses.d: To cut off the tops or tips of; to bite or pull off; to browse; to pluck; to mow; to reap.
q: I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one. Ezek. xvii. 22.

senses.d: Fig.: To cut off, as if in harvest.
q: Death . . . .crops the growing boys. Creech.

senses.d: To cause to bear a crop; as, to crop a field.
To yield harvest.

A gibbet, consisting of two pieces of timber placed transversely upon one another, in various forms, as a T, or +, with the horizontal piece below the upper end of the upright, or as an X. It was anciently used in the execution of criminals.
q: Nailed to the cross By his own nation. Milton.

senses.d: The sign or mark of the cross, made with the finger, or in ink, etc., or actually represented in some material; the symbol of Christ's death; the ensign and chosen symbol of Christianity, of a Christian people, and of Christendom.
q: The custom of making the sign of the cross with the hand or finger, as a means of conferring blessing or preserving from evil, is very old. Schaff-Herzog Encyc.
Before the cross has waned the crescent's ray. Sir W. Scott.
Tis where the cross is preached. Cowper.

senses.d: Affiction regarded as a test of patience or virtue; trial; disappointment; opposition; misfortune.
q: Heaven prepares a good man with crosses. B. Jonson.

senses.d: A piece of money stamped with the figure of a cross, also, that side of such a piece on which the cross is stamped; hence, money in general.
q: I should bear no cross if I did bear you; for I think you have no money in your purse. Shak.

senses.d: An appendage or ornament or anything in the form of a cross; a badge or ornamental device of the general shape of a cross; hence, such an ornament, even when varying considerably from that form; thus, the Cross of the British Order of St. George and St. Michael consists of a central medallion with seven arms radiating from it.
A monument in the form of a cross, or surmounted by a cross, set up in a public place; as, a market cross; a boundary cross; Charing Cross in London.
q: Dun-Edin's Cross, a pillared stone, Rose on a turret octagon. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A common heraldic bearing, of which there are many varieties. See the Illustration, above.
The crosslike mark or symbol used instead of a signature by those unable to write.
q: Five Kentish abbesses . . . .subscribed their names and crosses. Fuller.

senses.d: Church lands.
A line drawn across or through another line.
A mixing of breeds or stock, especially in cattle breeding; or the product of such intermixture; a hybrid of any kind.
q: Toning down the ancient Viking into a sort of a cross between Paul Jones and Jeremy Diddler. Lord Dufferin.

senses.d: An instrument for laying of offsets perpendicular to the main course.

Cross.etym: [OE. crois, croys, cros; the former fr. OF. crois, croiz, F. croix, fr. L. crux; the second is perh. directly fr. Prov. cros, crotz. fr. the same L. crux; cf. Icel. kross. Cf. Crucial, Crusade, Cruise, Crux.]

senses.d: Not parallel; lying or falling athwart; transverse; oblique; intersecting.
q: The cross refraction of the second prism. Sir I. Newton.

senses.d: Not accordant with what is wished or expected; interrupting; adverse; contrary; thwarting; perverse.
q: The cross and unlucky issue of my design. Glanvill.
The article of the resurrection seems to lie marvelously cross to the common experience of mankind. South.
We are both love's captives, but with fates so cross, One must be happy by the other's loss. Dryden.

senses.d: Characterized by, or in a state of, peevishness, fretfulness, or ill humor; as, a cross man or woman.
q: He had received a cross answer from his mistress. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: Made in an opposite direction, or an inverse relation; mutually inverse; interchanged; as, cross interrogatories; cross marriages, as when a brother and sister marry persons standing in the same relation to each other.
Athwart; across.
q: A fox was taking a walk one night cross a village. L'Estrange.

senses.d: To put across or athwart; to cause to intersect; as, to cross the arms.
To lay or draw something, as a line, across; as, to cross the letter t.
To pass from one side to the other of; to pass or move over; to traverse; as, to cross a stream.
q: A hunted hare . . . crosses and confounds her former track. I. Watts.

senses.d: To pass, as objects going in an opposite direction at the same time.
To run counter to; to thwart; to obstruct; to hinder; to clash or interfere with.
q: In each thing give him way; cross him in nothing. Shak.
An oyster may be crossed in love. Sheridan.

senses.d: To interfere and cut off; to debar.
q: To cross me from the golden time I look for. Shak.

senses.d: To make the sign of the cross upon; — followed by the reflexive pronoun; as, he crossed himself.
To cancel by marking crosses on or over, or drawing a line across; to erase; — usually with out, off, or over; as, to cross out a name.
To cause to interbreed; — said of different stocks or races; to mix the breed of.
To lie or be athwart.
To move or pass from one side to the other, or from place to place; to make a transit; as, to cross from New York to Liverpool.
To be inconsistent.
q: Men's actions do not always cross with reason. Sir P. Sidney.

senses.d: To interbreed, as races; to mix distinct breeds.
q: If two individuals of distinct races cross, a third is invariably produced different from either. Coleridge.

senses.d: To bend down; to stoop low; to lie close to the ground with the logs bent, as an animal when waiting for prey, or in fear.
q: Now crouch like a cur. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: To bend servilely; to stoop meanly; to fawn; to cringe.
q: Must I stand and crouch Under your testy humor? Shak.

Crouch.etym: [OE. cruchen, crouchen, crouken; cf. E. creep, G. krauchen, kriechen, or E. crook to bend, also crouch to cross.]

senses.d: To sign with the cross; to bless.
To bend, or cause to bend, as in humility or fear.
q: She folded her arms across her chest, And crouched her head upon her breast. Colerige.

Crouch.etym: [OE. cruchen, crouchen, from cruche, crouche, cross. Cf. Crosier, Crook.]

senses.d: To make the shrill sound characteristic of a cock, either in joy, gayety, or defiance.
q: The morning cock crew loud. Shak.

senses.d: To shout in exultation or defiance; to brag.
To utter a sound expressive of joy or pleasure.
q: The sweetest little maid, That ever crowed for kisses. Tennyson.
Sennacherib crowing over poor Jerusalem. Bp. Hall.

Crow.etym: [AS. crāwan; akin to D. kraijen, G. krähen, cf. Lith. groti to croak. √24. Cf. Crake.]

senses.d: A bird, usually black, of the genus Corvus, having a strong conical beak, with projecting bristles. It has a harsh, croaking note. See Caw.
A bar of iron with a beak, crook, or claw; a bar of iron used as a lever; a crowbar.
q: Get me an iron crow, and bring it straight Unto my cell. Shak.

senses.d: The cry of the cock. See Crow, v. i., 1.
The mesentery of a beast; — so called by butchers.

Crow.etym: [AS. crāwe a crow (in sense 1); akin to D. kraai, G. krähe; cf. Icel. krāka crow. So named from its cry, from AS. crāwan to crow. See Crow, v. i. ]

senses.d: A wreath or garland, or any ornamental fillet encircling the head, especially as a reward of victory or mark of honorable distinction; hence, anything given on account of, or obtained by, faithful or successful effort; a reward.
q: They do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible. 1 Cor. ix. 25.
Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. Rev. ii. 10.

senses.d: A royal headdress or cap of sovereignty, worn by emperors, kings, princes, etc.
The person entitled to wear a regal or imperial crown; the sovereign; — with the definite article.
q: Parliament may be dissolved by the demise of the crown. Blackstone.
Large arrears of pay were due to the civil and military servants of the crown. Macaulay.

senses.d: Imperial or regal power or dominion; sovereignty.
q: There is a power behind the crown greater than the crown itself. Junius.

senses.d: Anything which imparts beauty, splendor, honor, dignity, or finish.
q: The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness. Prov. xvi. 31.
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband. Prov. xvi. 4.

senses.d: Highest state; acme; consummation; perfection.
q: Mutual love, the crown of all our bliss. Milton.

senses.d: The topmost part of anything; the summit.
q: The steepy crown of the bare mountains. Dryden.

senses.d: The topmost part of the head (see Illust. of Bird.); that part of the head from which the hair descends toward the sides and back; also, the head or brain.
q: From toe to crown he'll fill our skin with pinches. Shak.
Twenty things which I set down: This done, I twenty more-had in my crown. Bunyan.

senses.d: The part of a hat above the brim.
The part of a tooth which projects above the gum; also, the top or grinding surface of a tooth.
The vertex or top of an arch; — applied generally to about one third of the curve, but in a pointed arch to the apex only.
Same as Corona.

Crown.etym: [OE. corone, coroun, crune, croun, OF. corone, corune, F. couronne, fr. L. corona crown, wreath; akin to Gr. κορώνη anything curved, crown; cf. also L. curvus curved, E. curve, curb, Gael. cruinn round, W. crwn. Cf. Cornice, Corona, Coroner, Coronet.]

senses.d: To cover, decorate, or invest with a crown; hence, to invest with royal dignity and power.
q: Her who fairest does appear, Crown her queen of all the year. Dryden.
Crown him, and say, “Long live our emperor.” Shak.

senses.d: To bestow something upon as a mark of honor, dignity, or recompense; to adorn; to dignify.
q: Thou . . . hast crowned him with glory and honor. Ps. viii. 5.

senses.d: To form the topmost or finishing part of; to complete; to consummate; to perfect.
q: Amidst the grove that crowns yon tufted hill. Byron.
One day shall crown the alliance. Shak.
To crown the whole, came a proposition. Motley.

senses.d: To cause to round upward; to make anything higher at the middle than at the edges, as the face of a machine pulley.
To effect a lodgment upon, as upon the crest of the glacis, or the summit of the breach.

Crown.etym: [OE. coronen, corunen, crunien, crounien, OF. coroner, F. couronner, fr. L. coronare, fr. corona a crown. See Crown, n.]

senses.d: Having or wearing a crown; surmounted, invested, or adorned, with a crown, wreath, garland, etc.; honored; rewarded; completed; consummated; perfected.
q: With surpassing glory crowned. Milton.

senses.d: Great; excessive; supreme.
To fasten to a cross; to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross or gibbet.
q: They cried, saying, Crucify him, cricify him. Luke xxiii. 21.

senses.d: To destroy the power or ruling influence of; to subdue completely; to mortify.
q: They that are Christ's have crucified the flesh, with the affections and lusts. Gal. v. 24.

senses.d: To vex or torment.

Crucify.etym: [F. crucifier, fr. (assumed) LL. crucificare, for crucifigere, fr, L. crux, crucis, cross + figere to fix, the ending -figere being changed to -ficare, F. -fier (in compounds), as if fr. L. facere to do, make. See Cross, and Fix, and cf. Crucifix.]

senses.d: Disposed to give pain to others; willing or pleased to hurt, torment, or afflict; destitute of sympathetic kindness and pity; savage; inhuman; hard-hearted; merciless.
q: Behold a people cometh from the north country; . . . they are cruel and have no mercy. Jer. vi. 22,23.

senses.d: Causing, or fitted to cause, pain, grief, or misery.
q: Cruel wars, wasting the earth. Milton.
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath for it was cruel. Gen. xlix. 7.

senses.d: Attended with cruetly; painful; harsh.
q: You have seen cruel proof of this man's strength. Shak.

Cruel.etym: [F. cruel, fr. L. crudelis, fr. crudus. See Crude.]

senses.d: In a cruel manner.
Extremely; very.
The attribute or quality of being cruel; a disposition to give unnecessary pain or suffering to others; inhumanity; barbarity.
q: Pierced through the heart with your stern cruelty. Shak.

senses.d: A cruel and barbarous deed; inhuman treatment; the act of willfully causing unnecessary pain.
q: Cruelties worthy of the dungeons of the Inquisition.
Macaulay.

Cruelty.etym: [OF. cruelté, F. cruauté, fr. L. crudelitas, fr. crudelis. See Cruel.]

senses.d: A small fragment or piece; especially, a small piece of bread or other food, broken or cut off.
q: Desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table. Luke xvi. 21.

senses.d: Fig.: A little; a bit; as, a crumb of comfort.
The soft part of bread.
q: Dust unto dust, what must be, must; If you can't get crumb, you'd best eat crust. Old Song.

Crumb.etym: [AS. cruma, akin to D. kruim, G. krume; cf. G. krauen to scratch, claw.]

senses.d: To break into crumbs or small pieces with the fingers; as, to crumb bread.
A cup or dish.
q: Take with thee . . . a cruse of honey. 1 Kings xiv. 3.

senses.d: A bottle for holding water, oil, honey, etc.
q: So David took . . . the cruse of water. 1 Sam. xxvi. 12.

Cruse.etym: [Akin to LG. kruus, kroos, mug, jug, jar, D. kroes, G. krause, Icel. krus, Sw. krus, Dan. kruus. Cf. Crucible, Cresset.]

senses.d: To press or bruise between two hard bodies; to squeeze, so as to destroy the natural shape or integrity of the parts, or to force together into a mass; as, to crush grapes.
q: Ye shall not offer unto the Lord that which is bruised, or crushed, or broken, or cut. Lev. xxii. 24.
The ass . . . thrust herself unto the wall, and crushed Balaam's foot against the wall. Num. xxii. 25.

senses.d: To reduce to fine particles by pounding or grinding; to comminute; as, to crush quartz.
To overwhelm by pressure or weight; to beat or force down, as by an incumbent weight.
q: To crush the pillars which the pile sustain. Dryden.
Truth, crushed to earth, shall rise again. Bryant.

senses.d: To oppress or burden grievously.
q: Thou shalt be only oppressed and crushed alway. Deut. xxviii. 33.

senses.d: To overcome completely; to subdue totally.
q: Speedily overtaking and crushing the rebels. Sir. W. Scott.

Crush.etym: [OE. cruschen, crousshen, Of. cruisir, croissir, fr. LL. cruscire, prob. of Ger. origin, from a derivative of the word seen in Goth. kruistan to gnash; akin to Sw. krysta to squeeze, Dan. kryste, Icel. kreysta.]

senses.d: To be or become broken down or in, or pressed into a smaller compass, by external weight or force; as, an eggshell crushes easily.
A violent collision or compression; a crash; destruction; ruin.
q: The wreck of matter, and the crush of worlds. Addison.

senses.d: Violent pressure, as of a crowd; a crowd which produced uncomfortable pressure; as, a crush at a reception.
q: Politics leave very little time for the bow window at White's in the day, or for the crush room of the opera at night. Macaulay.

senses.d: To make a loud call or cry; to call or exclaim vehemently or earnestly; to shout; to vociferate; to proclaim; to pray; to implore.
q: And about the ninth hour, Jesus cried with a loud voice. Matt. xxvii. 46.
Clapping their hands, and crying with loud voice. Shak.
Hear the voice of my supplications when I cry unto thee. Ps. xxviii. 2.
The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord. Is. xl. 3.
Some cried after him to return. Bunyan.

senses.d: To utter lamentations; to lament audibly; to express pain, grief, or distress, by weeping and sobbing; to shed tears; to bawl, as a child.
q: Ye shall cry for sorrow of heart. Is. lxv. 14.
I could find it in my heart to disgrace my man's apparel and to cry like a woman. Shak.

senses.d: To utter inarticulate sounds, as animals.
q: The young ravens which cry. Ps. cxlvii. 9.
In a cowslip's bell I lie There I couch when owls do cry. Shak.

Cry.etym: [F. crier, cf. L. quiritare to raise a plaintive cry, scream, shriek, perh. fr. queri to complain; cf. Skr. cvas to pant, hiss, sigh. Cf. Quarrel a brawl, Querulous.]

senses.d: To utter loudly; to call out; to shout; to sound abroad; to declare publicly.
q: All, all, cry shame against ye, yet I 'll speak. Shak.
The man . . . ran on,crying, Life! life! Eternal life! Bunyan.

senses.d: To cause to do something, or bring to some state, by crying or weeping; as, to cry one's self to sleep.
To make oral and public proclamation of; to declare publicly; to notify or advertise by outcry, especially things lost or found, goods to be sold, ets.; as, to cry goods, etc.
q: Love is lost, and thus she cries him. Crashaw.

senses.d: to publish the banns of, as for marriage.
q: I should not be surprised if they were cried in church next Sabbath. Judd.

senses.d: A loud utterance; especially, the inarticulate sound produced by one of the lower animals; as, the cry of hounds; the cry of wolves.
Outcry; clamor; tumult; popular demand.
q: Again that cry was found to have been as unreasonable as ever. Macaulay.

senses.d: Any expression of grief, distress, etc., accompanied with tears or sobs; a loud sound, uttered in lamentation.
q: There shall be a great cry throughout all the land. Ex. xi. 6.
An infant crying in the night, An infant crying for the light; And with no language but a cry. Tennyson.

senses.d: Loud expression of triumph or wonder or of popular acclamation or favor.
q: The cry went once on thee. Shak.

senses.d: Importunate supplication.
q: O, the most piteous cry of the poor souls. Shak.

senses.d: Public advertisement by outcry; proclamation, as by hawkers of their wares.
q: The street cries of London. Mayhew.

senses.d: Common report; fame.
q: The cry goes that you shall marry her. Shak.

senses.d: A word or phrase caught up by a party or faction and repeated for effect; as, the party cry of the Tories.
q: All now depends upon a good cry. Beaconsfield.

senses.d: A pack of hounds.
q: A cry more tunable Was never hollaed to, nor cheered with horn. Shak.

senses.d: A pack or company of persons; — in contempt.
q: Would not this . . . get me a fellowship in a cry of players? Shak.

senses.d: The crackling noise made by block tin when it is bent back and forth.

Cry.etym: [F. cri, fr. crier to cry. See Cry, v. i. ]

senses.d: Calling for notice; compelling attention; notorious; heinous; as, a crying evil.
q: Too much fondness for meditative retirement is not the crying sin of our modern Christianity. I. Taylor.

senses.d: The regular form which a substance tends to assume in solidifying, through the inherent power of cohesive attraction. It is bounded by plane surfaces, symmetrically arranged, and each species of crystal has fixed axial ratios. See Crystallization.

The material of quartz, in crystallization transparent or nearly so, and either colorless or slightly tinged with gray, or the like; — called also rock crystal. Ornamental vessels are made of it. Cf. Smoky quartz, Pebble; also Brazilian pebble, under Brazilian.
A species of glass, more perfect in its composition and manufacture than common glass, and often cut into ornamental forms. See Flint glass.
The glass over the dial of a watch case.
Anything resembling crystal, as clear water, etc.
q: The blue crystal of the seas. Byron.

Crystal.etym: [OE. cristal, F. cristal, L. crystallum crystal, ice, fr. Gr. κρύσταλλοσ, fr. κρύοσ icy cold, frost; cf. AS. crystalla, fr. L. crystallum; prob. akin to E. crust. See Crust, Raw.]

senses.d: Consisting of, or like, crystal; clear; transparent; lucid; pellucid; crystalline.
q: Through crystal walls each little mote will peep. Shak.
By crystal streams that murmur through the meads. Dryden.
The crystal pellets at the touch congeal, And from the ground rebounds the ratting hail. H. Brooks.

senses.d: The forearm; the ulna, a bone of the arm extending from elbow to wrist.
A measure of length, being the distance from the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger.

Cubit.etym: [L. cubitum, cubitus; elbow, ell, cubit, fr. (because the elbow serves for leaning upon) cubare to lie down, recline; cf. Gr. κύβιτον elbow, κύπτειν to bend, stoop, κυφόσ bent, stooping, humpbacked. Cf. Incumbent, Covey.]

senses.d: A creeping plant, and its fruit, of several species of the genus Cucumis, esp. Cucumis sativus, the unripe fruit of which is eaten either fresh or picked. Also, similar plants or fruits of several other genera. See below.

Cucumber.etym: [OE. cucumer, cocumber, cucumber, fr. L. cucmis, gen. cucumeris; cf. OF. cocombre,F. concombre.]

senses.d: That portion of food which is brought up into the mouth by ruminating animals from their first stomach, to be chewed a second time.
q: Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat. Levit. xi. 3

senses.d: A portion of tobacco held in the mouth and chewed; a quid.
The first stomach of ruminating beasts.
q: Chewed the thrice turned cud of wrath. Tennyson.
