Cud.etym: [AS. cudu, cwudu,cwidu,cweodo, of uncertain origin; cf, G. köder bait, Icel. kviðr womb, Goth. qiþus. Cf. Quid.]

senses.d: To rest upon as a troublesome or useless weight or load; to be burdensome or oppressive to; to hinder or embarrass in attaining an object, to obstruct or occupy uselessly; to embarrass; to trouble.
q: Why asks he what avails him not in fight, And would but cumber and retard his flight? Dryden.
Martha was cumbered about much serving. Luke x. 40.
Cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground? Luke xiii. 7.
The multiplying variety of arguments, especially frivolous ones, . . . but cumbers the memory. Locke.

Cumber.etym: [OE. combren, cumbren,OF. combrer to hinder, from LL. cumbrus a heap, fr. L. cumulus; cf. Skr. �� to increase, grow strong. Cf. Cumulate.]

senses.d: Trouble; embarrassment; distress.
q: A place of much distraction and cumber. Sir H. Wotton.
Sage counsel in cumber. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Encumbrance.
q: Extol not riches then, the toil of fools, The wise man's cumbrance, if not snare. Milton.

senses.d: Same as Cumin.
q: Ye pay tithe of mint, and cummin. Matt. xxiii. 23.

senses.d: To con (a ship).
To know. See Con.
Knowing; skillful; dexterous.
q: “Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white Nature's own sweet and cunning hand laid on. Shak.
Esau was a cunning hunter. Gen xxv. 27.

senses.d: Wrought with, or exhibiting, skill or ingenuity; ingenious; curious; as, cunning work.
q: Over them Arachne high did lift
Her cunning web. Spenser.

senses.d: Crafty; sly; artful; designing; deceitful.
q: They are resolved to be cunning; let others run the hazard of being sincere. South.

senses.d: Pretty or pleasing; as, a cunning little boy.

Cunning.etym: [AS. cunnan to know, to be able. See 1st Con, Can.]

senses.d: Knowledge; art; skill; dexterity.
q: Let my right hand forget her cunning. Ps. cxxxvii. 5.
A carpenter's desert Stands more in cunning than in power. Chapman.

senses.d: The faculty or act of using stratagem to accomplish a purpose; fraudulent skill or dexterity; deceit; craft.
q: Discourage cunning in a child; cunning is the ape of wisdom. Locke.
We take cunning for a sinister or crooked wisdom. Bacon.

Cunning.etym: [AS. cunnung trial, or Icel. kunnandi knowledge. See Cunning, a.]

senses.d: In a cunning manner; with cunning.

A small vessel, used commonly to drink from; as, a tin cup, a silver cup, a wine cup; especially, in modern times, the pottery or porcelain vessel, commonly with a handle, used with a saucer in drinking tea, coffee, and the like.
The contents of such a vessel; a cupful.
q: Give me a cup of sack, boy. Shak.

senses.d: Repeated potations; social or excessive indulgence in intoxicating drinks; revelry.
q: Thence from cups to civil broils. Milton.

senses.d: That which is to be received or indured; that which is allotted to one; a portion.
q: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me. Matt. xxvi. 39.

senses.d: Anything shaped like a cup; as, the cup of an acorn, or of a flower.
q: The cowslip's golden cup no more I see. Shenstone.

senses.d: A cupping glass or other vessel or instrument used to produce the vacuum in cupping.

Cup.etym: [AS. cuppe, LL. cuppa cup; cf. L. cupa tub, cask; cf. also Gr. κύπη hut, Skr. kūpa pit, hollow, OSlav. kupa cup. Cf. Coop, Cupola, Cowl a water vessel, and Cob, Coif, Cop.]

senses.d: To supply with cups of wine.
q: Cup us, till the world go round. Shak.

senses.d: To apply a cupping apparatus to; to subject to the operation of cupping. See Cupping.
To make concave or in the form of a cup; as, to cup the end of a screw.
One whose office it is to fill and hand the cups at an entertainment.
One of the attendants of a prince or noble, permanently charged with the performance of this office for his master.
A mongrel or inferior dog.
q: They . . . like to village curs, Bark when their fellows do. Shak.

senses.d: A worthless, snarling fellow; — used in contempt.
q: What would you have, you curs, That like nor peace nor war? Shak.

Cur.etym: [OE. curre, kur; cf. dial. Sw. kurre dog, OD. korre watchdog, and Icel. kurra to murmur, grumble, Sw. kurra to rumble, croak, Dan. kurre to coo, whirr; prob. of imitative origin.]

senses.d: To change into curd; to coagulate; as, rennet causes milk to curdle.
To thicken; to congeal.
q: Then Mary could feel her heart's blood curdle cold. Southey.

senses.d: To change into curd; to cause to coagulate.
To congeal or thicken.
q: My chill blood is curdled in my veins. Dryden.

senses.d: Care, heed, or attention.
q: Of study took he most cure and most heed. Chaucer.
Vicarages of greatcure, but small value. Fuller.

senses.d: Spiritual charge; care of soul; the office of a parish priest or of a curate; hence, that which is committed to the charge of a parish priest or of a curate; a curacy; as, to resign a cure; to obtain a cure.
q: The appropriator was the incumbent parson, and had the cure of the souls of the parishioners. Spelman.

senses.d: Medical or hygienic care; remedial treatment of disease; a method of medical treatment; as, to use the water cure.
Act of healing or state of being healed; restoration to health from disease, or to soundness after injury.
q: Past hope! pastcure! past help. Shak.
I do cures to-day and to-morrow. Luke xii. 32.

senses.d: Means of the removal of disease or evil; that which heals; a remedy; a restorative.
q: Cold, hunger, prisons, ills without a cure. Dryden.
The proper cure of such prejudices. Bp. Hurd.

Cure.etym: [OF, cure care, F., also, cure, healing, cure of souls, L. cura care, medical attendance, cure; perh. akin to cavere to pay heed, E. cution. Cure is not related to care.]

senses.d: To heal; to restore to health, soundness, or sanity; to make well; — said of a patient.
q: The child was cured from that very hour. Matt. xvii. 18.

senses.d: To subdue or remove by remedial means; to remedy; to remove; to heal; — said of a malady.
q: To cure this deadly grief. Shak.
Then he called his twelve disciples together, and gave them power . . . to cure diseases. Luke ix. 1.

senses.d: To set free from (something injurious or blameworthy), as from a bad habit.
q: I never knew any man cured of inattention. Swift.

senses.d: To prepare for preservation or permanent keeping; to preserve, as by drying, salting, etc.; as, to cure beef or fish; to cure hay.

Cure.etym: [OF. curer to take care, to heal, F., only, to cleanse, L. curare to take care, to heal, fr. cura. See Cure,.]

senses.d: To pay heed; to care; to give attention.
To restore health; to effect a cure.
q: Whose smile and frown, like to Achilles' spear, Is able with the change to kill and cure. Shak.

senses.d: To become healed.
q: One desperate grief cures with another's languish. Shak.

senses.d: Difficult to please or satisfy; solicitous to be correct; careful; scrupulous; nice; exact.
q: Little curious in her clothes. Fuller.
How shall we, If he be curious, work upon his faith? Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: Exhibiting care or nicety; artfully constructed; elaborate; wrought with elegance or skill.
q: To devise curious works. Ex. xxxv. 32
His body couched in a curious bed. Shak.

senses.d: Careful or anxious to learn; eager for knowledge; given to research or inquiry; habitually inquisitive; prying; — sometimes with after or of.
q: It is a pity a gentleman so very curious after things that were elegant and beautiful should not have been as curious as to their origin, their uses, and their natural history. Woodward.

senses.d: Exciting attention or inquiry; awakening surprise; inviting and rewarding inquisitiveness; not simple or plain; strange; rare.
q: A multitude of curious analogies. Macaulay.
Many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore. E. A. Poe.
Abstruse investigations in recondite branches of learning or sciense often bring to light curious results. C. J. Smith.

Curious.etym: [OF. curios, curius, F. curieux, L. curiosus careful, inquisitive, fr. cura care. See Cure.]

senses.d: In a curious manner.
Running or moving rapidly.
q: Like the current fire, that renneth Upon a cord. Gower.
To chase a creature that was current then In these wild woods, the hart with golden horns. Tennyson.

senses.d: Now passing, as time; as, the current month.
Passing from person to person, or from hand to hand; circulating through the community; generally received; common; as, a current coin; a current report; current history.
q: That there was current money in Abraham's time is past doubt. Arbuthnot.
Your fire-new stamp of honor is scarce current. Shak.
His current value, which is less or more as men have occasion for him. Grew.

senses.d: Commonly estimated or acknowledged.
Fitted for general acceptance or circulation; authentic; passable.
q: O Buckingham, now do I play the touch To try if thou be current gold indeed. Shak.

Current.etym: [OE. currant, OF. curant, corant, p. pr. of curre, corre, F. courre, courir, to run, from L. currere; perh. akin to E. horse. Cf. Course, Concur, Courant, Coranto.]

senses.d: A flowing or passing; onward motion. Hence: A body of fluid moving continuously in a certain direction; a stream; esp., the swiftest part of it; as, a current of water or of air; that which resembles a stream in motion; as, a current of electricity.
q: Two such silver currents, when they join, Do glorify the banks that bound them in. Shak.
The surface of the ocean is furrowed by currents, whose direction . . . the navigator should know. Nichol.

senses.d: General course; ordinary procedure; progressive and connected movement; as, the current of time, of events, of opinion, etc.
To call upon divine or supernatural power to send injury upon; to imprecate evil upon; to execrate.
q: Thou shalt not . . . curse the ruler of thy people. Ex. xxii. 28.
Ere sunset I'll make thee curse the deed. Shak.

senses.d: To bring great evil upon; to be the cause of serious harm or unhappiness to; to furnish with that which will be a cause of deep trouble; to afflict or injure grievously; to harass or torment.
q: On impious realms and barbarous kings impose Thy plagues, and curse 'em with such sons as those. Pope.

Curse.etym: [AS. cursian, corsian, perh. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. korse to make the sign of the cross, Sw. korsa, fr. Dan. & Sw. kors cross, Icel kross, all these Scand. words coming fr. OF. crois, croiz, fr. L. crux cross. Cf. Cross.]

senses.d: To utter imprecations or curses; to affirm or deny with imprecations; to swear.
q: Then began he to curse and to swear. Matt. xxi. 74.
His spirits hear me, And yet I need must curse. Shak.

senses.d: An invocation of, or prayer for, harm or injury; malediction.
q: Lady, you know no rules of charity, Which renders good for bad, blessings for curses. Shak.

senses.d: Evil pronounced or invoked upon another, solemnly, or in passion; subjection to, or sentence of, divine condemnation.
q: The priest shall write these curses in a book. Num. v. 23.
Curses, like chickens, come home to roost. Old Proverb.

senses.d: The cause of great harm, evil, or misfortune; that which brings evil or severe affliction; torment.
q: The common curse of mankind, folly and ignorance. Shak.
All that I eat, or drink, or shall beget, Is propagated curse. Milton.

senses.d: Deserving a curse; execrable; hateful; detestable; abominable.
q: Let us fly this cursed place. Milton.
This cursed quarrel be no more renewed. Dryden.

senses.d: A hanging screen intended to darken or conceal, and admitting of being drawn back or up, and reclosed at pleasure; esp., drapery of cloth or lace hanging round a bed or at a window; in theaters, and like places, a movable screen for concealing the stage.
That part of the rampart and parapet which is between two bastions or two gates. See Illustrations of Ravelin and Bastion.
That part of a wall of a building which is between two pavilions, towers, etc.
A flag; an ensign; — in contempt.

Curtain.etym: [OE. cortin, curtin,fr. OF. cortine, curtine, F. courtine, LL. cortina, curtian (in senses 1 and 2), also, small court, small inclosure surrounded by walls, from cortis court. See Court.]

senses.d: To inclose as with curtains; to furnish with curtains.
q: So when the sun in bed Curtained with cloudy red. Milton.

senses.d: A keeping or guarding; care, watch, inspection, for keeping, preservation, or security.
q: A fleet of thirty ships for the custody of the narrow seas. Bacon.

senses.d: Judicial or penal safe-keeping.
q: Jailer, take him to thy custody. Shak.

senses.d: State of being guarded and watched to prevent escape; restraint of liberty; confinement; imprisonment.
q: What pease will be given To us enslaved, but custody severe, And stripes and arbitrary punishment? Milton.

Custody.etym: [L. custodia, fr. custos guard; prob. akin to Gr. ������ to hide, and E. hide. See Hide to cover.]

senses.d: Frequent repetition of the same act; way of acting common to many; ordinary manner; habitual practice; usage; method of doing or living.
q: And teach customs which are not lawful. Acts xvi. 21.
Moved beyond his custom, Gama said. Tennyson.
A custom More honored in the breach than the observance. Shak.

senses.d: Habitual buying of goods; practice of frequenting, as a shop, manufactory, etc., for making purchases or giving orders; business support.
q: Let him have your custom, but not your votes. Addison.

senses.d: Long-established practice, considered as unwritten law, and resting for authority on long consent; usage. See Usage, and Prescription.
Familiar aquaintance; familiarity.
q: Age can not wither her, nor custom stale Her infinite variety. Shak.

Custom.syn: Practice; fashion. See Habit, and Usage.
Custom.etym: [OF. custume, costume, Anglo-Norman coustome, F. coutume, fr. (assumed) LL. consuetumen custom, habit, fr. L. consuetudo, -dinis, fr. consuescere to accustom, verb inchoative fr. consuere to be accustomed; con- + suere to be accustomed, prob. originally, to make one's own, fr. the root of suus one's

senses.d: To make familiar; to accustom.
To supply with customers.
To have a custom.
q: On a bridge he custometh to fight. Spenser.

senses.d: The customary toll, tax, or tribute.
q: Render, therefore, to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom. Rom. xiii. 7.

senses.d: Duties or tolls imposed by law on commodities, imported or exported.

Custom.etym: [OF. coustume, F. coutume, tax, i.e., the usual tax. See 1st Custom.]

senses.d: To pay the customs of.
To separate the parts of with, or as with, a sharp instrument; to make an incision in; to gash; to sever; to divide.
q: You must cut this flesh from off his breast. Shak.
Before the whistling winds the vessels fly, With rapid swiftness cut the liquid way. Pope.

senses.d: To sever and cause to fall for the purpose of gathering; to hew; to mow or reap.
q: Thy servants can skill to cut timer. 2. Chron. ii. 8

senses.d: To sever and remove by cutting; to cut off; to dock; as, to cut the hair; to cut the nails.
To castrate or geld; as, to cut a horse.
To form or shape by cutting; to make by incision, hewing, etc.; to carve; to hew out.
q: Why should a man. whose blood is warm within, Sit like his grandsire cut in alabaster? Shak.
Loopholes cut through thickest shade. Milton.

senses.d: To wound or hurt deeply the sensibilities of; to pierce; to lacerate; as, sarcasm cuts to the quick.
q: The man was cut to the heart. Addison.

senses.d: To intersect; to cross; as, one line cuts another at right angles.
To refuse to recognize; to ignore; as, to cut a person in the street; to cut one's acquaintance.
To absent one's self from; as, to cut an appointment, a recitation. etc.
q: An English tradesman is always solicitous to cut the shop whenever he can do so with impunity. Thomas Hamilton.

Cut.etym: [OE. cutten, kitten, ketten; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. cwtau to shorten, curtail, dock, cwta bobtailed, cwt tail, skirt, Gael. cutaich to shorten, curtail, dock, cutach short, docked, cut a bobtail, piece, Ir. cut a short tail, cutach bobtailed. Cf. Coot.]

senses.d: To do the work of an edged tool; to serve in dividing or gashing; as, a knife cuts well.
To admit of incision or severance; to yield to a cutting instrument.
q: Panels of white wood that cuts like cheese. Holmes.

senses.d: To perform the operation of dividing, severing, incising, intersecting, etc.; to use a cutting instrument.
q: He saved the lives of thousands by his manner of cutting for the stone. Pope.

senses.d: To make a stroke with a whip.
To interfere, as a horse.
To move or make off quickly.
To divide a pack of cards into two portion to decide the deal or trump, or to change the order of the cards to be dealt.
An opening made with an edged instrument; a cleft; a gash; a slash; a wound made by cutting; as, a sword cut.
A stroke or blow or cutting motion with an edged instrument; a stroke or blow with a whip.
That which wounds the feelings, as a harsh remark or criticism, or a sarcasm; personal discourtesy, as neglecting to recognize an acquaintance when meeting him; a slight.
q: Rip called him by name, but the cur snarled, snapped his teeth, and passed on. This was an unkind cut indeed. W. Irving.

senses.d: A notch, passage, or channel made by cutting or digging; a furrow; a groove; as, a cut for a railroad.
q: This great cut or ditch Secostris . . . purposed to have made a great deal wider and deeper. Knolles.

senses.d: The surface left by a cut; as, a smooth or clear cut.
A portion severed or cut off; a division; as, a cut of beef; a cut of timber.
q: It should be understood, moreover, . . . that the group are not arbitrary cuts, but natural groups or types. Dana.

senses.d: An engraved block or plate; the impression from such an engraving; as, a book illustrated with fine cuts.
The act of dividing a pack cards.
Manner in which a thing is cut or formed; shape; style; fashion; as, the cut of a garment.
q: With eyes severe and beard of formal cut. Shak.

senses.d: A common work horse; a gelding.
q: He'll buy me a cut, forth for to ride. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: The failure of a college officer or student to be present at any appointed exercise.
A skein of yarn.
Gashed or divided, as by a cutting instrument.
Formed or shaped as by cutting; carved.
Overcome by liquor; tipsy.
To deflect (a bowled ball) to the off, with a chopping movement of the bat.
To drive (an object ball) to either side by hitting it fine on the other side with the cue ball or another object ball.
To strike (a ball) with the racket inclined or struck across the ball so as to put a certain spin on the ball.
To drive (a ball) to one side by hitting with another ball.
A slanting stroke causing the ball to spin and bound irregularly; also, the spin so given to the ball.
A stroke on the off side between point and the wicket; also, one who plays this stroke.
The act or process of making an incision, or of severing, felling, shaping, etc.

Something cut, cut off, or cut out, as a twig or scion cut off from a stock for the purpose of grafting or of rooting as an independent plant; something cut out of a newspaper; an excavation cut through a hill or elsewhere to make a way for a railroad, canal, etc.; a cut.
Adapted to cut; as, a cutting tool.
Chilling; penetrating; sharp; as, a cutting wind.
Severe; sarcastic; biting; as, a cutting reply.
A musical instrument used by the ancients. It is supposed to have been similar to the modern kettle drum, though perhaps smaller.
A musical instrument of brass, shaped like a circular dish or a flat plate, with a handle at the back; — used in pairs to produce a sharp ringing sound by clashing them together.
A musical instrument used by gypsies and others, made of steel wire, in a triangular form, on which are movable rings.

Cymbal.etym: [OE. cimbale, simbale, OF. cimbale, F. cymbale, L. cymbalum, fr. Gr. κύμβαλον, fr. κύμβη, κύμβοσ, anything hollow, hollow vessel, basin, akin to Skr. kumbha pot. Cf. Chime.]

senses.d: A rule for construing written instruments so as to conform as nearly to the intention of the parties as is consistent with law.
A coniferous tree of the genus Cupressus. The species are mostly evergreen, and have wood remarkable for its durability.

Cypress.etym: [OE. cipres, cipresse, OF. cipres, F. cypr�s, L. cupressus, cyparissus (cf. the usual Lat. form cupressus), fr. Gr. ����, perh. of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. g�pher, Gen. vi. 14.]

senses.d: A thin, transparent stuff, the same as, or corresponding to, crape. It was either white or black, the latter being most common, and used for mourning.
q: Lawn as white as driven snow, Cyprus black as e'er was crow. Shak.

Cyprus.etym: [OE. cipres, cypirs; perh. so named as being first manufactured in Cyprus. Cf. Cipers.]

senses.d: Pertaining to Cyrene, in Africa; Cyrenaic.
A native or inhabitant of Cyrene.
One of a school of philosophers, established at Cyrene by Aristippus, a disciple of Socrates. Their doctrines were nearly the same as those of the Epicureans.
